Celtic 'a really good match' for record signing Hogh

BBC News Tue, 28 Jul 2026 14:43:18 GMT

Denmark striker Kasper Hogh has become Celtic's second summer signing

Denmark striker Kasper Hogh says Celtic are a "really good match" for him after becoming the club's record signing.

The 25-year-old has joined for a reported fee of £11m from Bodo/Glimt and becomes the Scottish champions' second summer recruit, following the arrival of Camilo Duran.

Hogh - who scored 54 goals in 103 games for Norwegians Bodo/Glimt, five of which were in last season's Champions League - has penned a four-year deal with the option of a further year.

The Dane's big-money arrival will ease some of the fan pressure on Celtic's board after Japan forward Daizen Maeda's exit to Ipswich Town.

"I'm so happy," Hogh told Celtic TV. "When I came into the room and saw the shirt, I was really excited.

"The history of the club is so big. I spoke with some people and with my family about the club.

"The feeling they had, and the feeling I had in my stomach, was that this was a really good match."

On his playing style, Hogh added: "I like to be in the box and score goals, but I also want to help my team-mates defensively and work hard for the team.

"I've trained throughout the summer and I've already played league games in Norway, so I feel ready. I just want to get started and be thrown into the fire."

Ipswich sign Japan forward Maeda from Celtic

Celtic to face Dundee Utd in League Cup last 16

Who has your Premiership club brought in & let go this summer?

Hogh's career has been a slow burner since he came through the youth ranks with local club Randers then was sold to second-tier Hobro after an injury-hit spell, including a loan to Valur in Iceland.

A switch to Danish Superliga club AaB followed in January 2022, but he was on the move again a year later, this time to Stabaek, who had just been promoted to the Norwegian Eliteserien.

It was there Hogh's career took off as they exercised their purchase option only six months into his year-long loan after he scored eight goals in 14 games.

Within another three months, he signed a pre-contract with Bodo/Glimt to join their top-flight rivals in January 2024.

Hogh would finish as his new club's top scorer with 12 goals as they retained the Norwegian title - and his seven goals in the Europa League made him the competition's joint top marksman as they reached the semi-finals.

He was also the club's top scorer for 2025 with 17 goals, albeit Bodo/Glimt finished second, one point behind Viking.

In January, he grabbed a double in a 3-1 Champions League win over Manchester City and the following week netted again in a 2-1 victory at Atletico Madrid.

Hogh was first called up to Denmark's senior squad in March and made his debut as a late substitute in a 4–0 win over North Macedonia.

In his second appearance, he came off the bench to head Denmark's equaliser in their World Cup play-off final against the Czech Republic only for his side to lose in a penalty shootout.

While unrest directed from the Celtic support towards the hierarchy has been verging on toxic, if it has not already reached that point, Martin O'Neill's side have yet to kick a ball in 2026-27 competitive action.

Nevertheless, the club have been working on a record deal for an incoming player.

The exit of Maeda, last season's title hero, following confirmation that Kelechi Iheanacho and Marcelo Saracchi would not be returning to Parkhead, cranked up the fury among the fanbase.

But does Hogh's arrival suggest the club are adopting a quality-over-quantity approach?

Celtic's wage bill and financial outlay on transfer fees in recent years point towards money being spent, but perhaps not being spent wisely.

It has felt impossible for fans and pundits to defend the fact the club had only one new face through the door less than a week before their Premiership title defence begins.

However, the signings of both Duran and Hogh come with a reported combined cost of about £15m, and the pair arrive with Champions League pedigree.

Duran has impressed in pre-season after scoring five of his 15 goals for Qarabag last term in Uefa's premier club competition. Hogh netted the same number in the same tournament as Bodo/Glimt defied the odds to reach the last 16.

Overall for Bodo/Glimt, the Denmark striker - who has scored once in four caps for his country - has averaged a goal every other game.

His underlying data and touchmaps suggest he is a penalty-box striker who has thrived in a fantastically well-coached system under Kjetil Knutsen.

O'Neill and his staff will back themselves to provide a platform for that success to be replicated in Scotland by their new big-money signing, whose CV shows he is capable of delivering at the highest level.

Can Burnham's vision for Manchester's schools really work for the rest of England?

BBC News Tue, 28 Jul 2026 14:03:55 GMT

Two years ago, I stood at the back of a conference room in Manchester Hall, sipping a coffee and watching Andy Burnham unveil his vision for transforming technical education in Greater Manchester.

He had announced plans for the Manchester Baccalaureate, or MBacc, the year before, and, armed with PowerPoint slides and guest speakers, was running through the ins and outs in front of a room full of education and business leaders.

Now, as prime minister, Burnham has announced plans to make that idea national, and overhaul the technical education system across the whole of England.

The details are still scarce at this stage. We know it will involve giving pupils the option to study more vocational courses and take up work experience from Year 10, but how it will work in practice is still up in the air.

One thing that is certain is that the thinking behind it, and the ambition, is the same as that which underpins the MBacc: a determination to give teenagers a clear, step-by-step route into more practical and technical jobs.

The trouble is, the MBacc itself can be quite a difficult concept to get your head around if you're not familiar with it.

Let's be clear from the start: it's not another type of qualification, like the T-levels and V-levels announced in England in recent years.

Instead, it's a framework that aims to give teenagers a "clear line of sight to good jobs" in vocational and technical areas.

The best way to think about it is a step-by-step route - picture a flow chart - that teenagers can follow from school into any given technical career.

It's set up in parallel to a more clearly defined academic route. During that conference event in July 2024, Burnham and other speakers made clear that those who want to go on to desk jobs can follow a well-trodden path of GCSEs, A-levels, and a university degree.

But for those who want more practical careers, the landscape is much more complicated.

The MBacc is best seen as an effort to simplify that landscape, spelling out for teenagers who want to go into more vocational or technical careers which courses they can study, and ensuring they have the opportunity to study them along with hands-on work experience.

It spells out routes to careers in seven different categories:

Its success is difficult to measure, since the MBacc is still in its infancy.

It's not until 2030 that it seeks to achieve its mission of guaranteeing every young person a clear path to good jobs. By 2035, the aim is for every young person to have 45 days of work experience by the time they're 19.

According to the most recent data, the MBacc has been rolled out across 101 secondary schools and colleges in Greater Manchester - about 40% of the total.

The Greater Manchester Combined Authority says 1,405 young people accessed workplace experiences during its second year.

Time will tell, as those teenagers leave school and enter the world of work, how transformative it will be.

And what works in Greater Manchester may not work everywhere else.

The prime minister has stated explicitly that he wants to expand the approach across England.

"I created the Greater Manchester Baccalaureate or MBacc... to bridge the gap between our schools and our employers," he wrote in the Times. "Now we're taking that idea national."

It may well be scalable. The seven MBacc "gateways" - although designed specifically around Greater Manchester's "fastest-growing industries" - are actually quite broad-ranging. They mirror some of the areas already targeted by efforts to boost technical education at a national level. There are T-levels in construction areas as well as in education and early years, for example.

But there will be challenges along the way.

The prime minister is clear that he wants technical and vocational education to be tied to local economies. He plans to work with local leaders, employers and schools, to "identify the industries driving growth in local areas and make sure that local kids have a clear route into them".

If that's to be the case, he will need to make sure that teenagers in all parts of England - including in areas without thriving industries - don't fall through the gaps.

Is it safe to travel to France and Spain right now?

BBC News Tue, 28 Jul 2026 13:54:20 GMT

Wildfires in Spain and France have caused mass evacuation and disruption, with more than 300,000 people forced to leave their homes and many sleeping in sports halls and other temporary shelters.

An official from one of the French departments affected by the fires has pleaded with visitors to stay away.

On Sunday, Sophie Brocas, prefect of the French department of Gironde, said, "I urge tourists not to come," while advising those already there to consider an alternative destination.

For those who have upcoming holidays to the affected regions, here is what you should know about how it might impact your plans.

The UK government has not specifically warned against travel to anywhere in France or Spain, but it does advise caution.

In France, it says access to affected areas may be restricted and roads may close at short notice. It adds that further evacuations may take place.

It has also issued a general warning about the high risk of wildfires in France during the summer season from April to October.

For those in an affected area in France or Spain or planning to travel there, the UK government recommends following instructions and updates from local authorities and emergency services at all times.

Those needing emergency help in France or Spain can call 112.

Travellers should also bear in mind the UK government's advice can and does change in response to moving events.

Anna-Marie Duthie, travel insurance expert at financial rating firm Defaqto, says that if this happens after you have booked your trip, "you may be covered for cancellation or curtailment".

"You may also be covered for additional travel and accommodation costs should your trip be disrupted due to a catastrophic event, if your insurer offers this cover or you've paid to include it," she adds.

To know if this applies to you, check your policy.

The UK government says parts of Gironde and Landes in the south west of France are affected.

As of Tuesday, the official French wildfire map gives Gironde the highest fire alert level. Meanwhile, Var has its second highest alert level.

The map says there are more than a dozen fires burning across the country, including on Corsica.

More than 42,000 hectares of land has been burnt in Gironde and some 240 homes have been destroyed.

In Spain, authorities have declared a national emergency because of wildfires in parts of Madrid and Ávila. The UK government says there are also reports of wildfires in other inland areas of Spain.

Once again, the answer depends on your policy.

"If your travel plans are disrupted by a wildfire and your policy includes trip disruption cover then travel insurance may cover some of the resulting costs," says Chris Bose, director of general insurance policy at the Association of British Insurers (ABI).

However, only half of travel insurance policies have "catastrophe" cover, according to analysis from Defaqto.

This means that, in many cases, travellers might not be covered by their insurance in the case of wildfires.

To know if this does or does not apply to you, speak to your insurer or check the wording of your policy.

In the case of cancelled flights or accommodation, Bose recommends seeking refunds from your airline, tour operator or accommodation provider in the first instance.

Duthie says if your airline cancels your flight due to wildfires then "they should offer you the chance to rebook, or provide a full refund".

She says if your holiday was booked as a package then this refund should cover "all elements", including flights, accommodation and transfers.

"But if you've booked everything separately, you'll need to deal with each provider independently. Your airline may refund your flight, but your accommodation provider may not if the property is unaffected."

Check what your insurance policy says about flights, accommodation or trip bookings first.

Rory Boland, editor of Which? Travel, says this is especially true for those not due to travel in the next week or two.

"Travellers who cancel now will likely forfeit their right to a refund or rebooking," he says.

As the UK government has not warned against travel to anywhere in the two countries, he says travellers are "unlikely to be able to claim on their travel insurance".

"As a rule, insurance firms won't make allowances for 'disinclination to travel'," Boland says.

"Instead, holidaymakers should wait until closer to the departure date to see if the holiday can go ahead or what flexible booking options are offered from the tour operator or airline.

"Travel companies will be prioritising anyone due to depart in the next couple of days."

The amount of land burned by wildfires across Europe has increased by 57% since summer 2022, according to the World Health Organization.

It adds that climate change is intensifying wildfires and increasing their frequency.

Duthie says insurance firms are adapting to "potential new and increasing risks involved in travel as a result".

In the near term, she says it is unlikely insurance providers will change their policies.

"Current clauses may refer to 'severe' or 'extreme' weather, but the definitions for these can vary and currently no providers go as far as to specify criteria such as maximum temperatures."

However, she says that "longer term there is a chance that we may end up seeing less insurable destinations and increased premiums".

Alonso's first Chelsea match was a tale of four strikers

BBC News Tue, 28 Jul 2026 13:28:28 GMT

Joao Pedro scored a hat-trick to cement his position as Chelsea's main striker

Xabi Alonso's first match as Chelsea manager was defined by four strikers - an untouchable one, one that struggled again and could leave, a promising talent, and one that could join.

The star was Joao Pedro, who scored a nine-minute hat-trick to help Alonso's side to a 6-4 win against Western Sydney Wanderers in a match that highlighted the gulf between Premier League and A-League teams.

Perhaps it was the disappointment of being left out of Brazil's World Cup squad that inspired the forward to showcase his finishing prowess as well as his power and pace in an entertaining spectacle at Accor Stadium.

Alonso described Joao Pedro as "very, very hungry" and "determined to have a great season".

For the most part however it was a sloppy and imperfect performance by Chelsea, with the Blues still adjusting to the effects of jet lag.

There were few other standouts other than Joao Pedro, but Dastan Satpaev was one.

The 17-year-old scored the first goal of Alonso's reign - and in spectacular fashion - after just six minutes.

Strangely, the Kazakhstan forward did so as a triallist - because he cannot formally complete his move from FC Kairat to Stamford Bridge until 12 August.

By contrast, his fellow starting forward Liam Delap again struggled, as he has in almost every appearance for Chelsea since his £30m move from Ipswich last summer.

Delap appears short of confidence and could now be sold, with Chelsea advancing talks to sign Danny Welbeck, 35, as an experienced replacement.

Welbeck has agreed personal terms and there is optimism at Chelsea that a deal can be reached, although his club Brighton are refusing to comment.

Chelsea are also in talks to sign midfielder Jordan Henderson, 36, from Brentford as they look to add experience and leadership to their squad after a disappointing 2025-26 season.

When asked about signing the two older players, Alonso replied: "We need balance, to have a complete squad and make a good team. For that, we have an idea and plan."

Beyond the narratives surrounding strikers, with injured Emmanuel Emegha and Nicolas Jackson also on the books, it was only a very early glimpse of what to expect from Alonso's Chelsea.

Chelsea begin Alonso reign with 6-4 win in Sydney - who stood out?

Why Chelsea want to sign older players

Satpaev is attempting to become the first Kazakh player to appear in a Premier League match.

In his homeland, he is a superstar. He has already played for his national team and attracted fans from his home country to both the open training session on Sunday and the match on Tuesday in Sydney.

Quick, sharp in the box and relatively small in stature, Satpaev is stylistically often compared to former Argentina and Manchester City striker Sergio Aguero.

Asked whether he will get a chance at Chelsea this season amid talk of a potential loan move, Alonso said: "We still have to take decisions.

"I knew Dastan from Almaty," added Alonso, who faced the player with his former club Real Madrid last season.

"He is a ball threat, he attacks the inner channel well and is good as a striker coming from the outside.

"He is really strong, really quick and I have been really impressed with him."

The former Liverpool midfielder, who was a vocal presence on the touchline, used the 4-2-3-1 system favoured by Enzo Maresca, who was Chelsea head coach this time last year.

With players still on holiday after the World Cup - including club record £117m signing Morgan Rogers - several youngsters were given an opportunity.

Midfield trio Mahdi Nicoll-Jazuli, Reggie Walsh and Reggie Watson all impressed, with the latter the only player to play the full game.

Nicoll-Jazuli and Watson, both 16, anchored the midfield together for long periods, while 17-year-old Walsh impressed in a more advanced role.

In his pre-match media conference, Alonso expressed surprise at how well the seven academy players drafted in to fill gaps in the squad had performed in training.

Landon Emenalo, 18, has also been given a significant opportunity, with no other left-backs available.

The only senior player other then Joao Pedro to particularly impress was winger Jamie Gittens, who made it three goals in three appearances in pre-season, following his two in behind-closed-doors friendlies against EFL opposition.

Booker Prize longlist: See the 13 'dynamite' novels up for this year's prestigious award

BBC News Tue, 28 Jul 2026 13:00:16 GMT

Elizabeth Strout, Douglas Stuart, Marlon James and Rebecca Perry are among the authors who have been longlisted for this year's Booker Prize.

The 13 chosen books include novels set in Mexico City, a remote Scottish island, an assisted suicide clinic in Zurich, 1980s Jamaica, post-apocalyptic Kent, and coastal Massachussetts before the 2024 US election.

Chair of the judges Mary Beard described the 13 novels as "dynamite", adding: "We are confident that our longlist of books has something for everyone."

The longlist, referred to as the Booker Dozen, will be whittled down to a shortlist on 22 September, before the winner is announced on 9 November.

The annual Booker Prize is the literary world's most prestigious award, recognising long-form fiction by writers of any nationality, written in English and published in the UK or Ireland.

The six shortlisted authors will receive £2,500 each and a specially bound edition of their book, while the eventual winner will receive a trophy and £50,000 in prize money.

High-profile authors who missed this year's longlist include Maggie O'Farrell, Ann Patchett, John Lanchester, Deborah Levy and Julian Barnes, who many predicted would be recognised for his final book Departure(s).

The Booker judges received 163 submissions for this year's prize before settling on the final 13.

Each of the five judges read all the submitted books, with Beard joking she "occasionally felt daunted as a new box of 30 or so gleaming volumes landed on my doorstep".

"But what I shall most remember is the eye-opening pleasure of it all, and what I learnt about reading and the power of fiction from my fellow judges."

Three of this year's authors in the Booker Dozen are previous shortlistees, including Elizabeth Strout, who is recognised for The Things We Never Say.

It follows a high school history teacher in Massachusetts who is grappling with isolation, post-pandemic social anxiety, and concern about the forthcoming 2024 US election.

The two other former shortlistees have also previously won the prize. Shuggie Bain author Douglas Stuart is recognised this time for John of John, about a young gay man who returns to his strict religious family on a remote Scottish island.

Another former winner, Marlon James, returns this year with The Disappearers, a 600-page book due to be released in September about eight gay men in Kingston, Jamaica, who are targeted by a violent mob during a play rehearsal.

James's is the longest book this year, while the shortest is Helen of Nowhere by Makenna Goodman - a 140-page novel which follows a disgraced professor touring an idyllic countryside house, learning about its previous owner.

Another longlistee, Rebecca Perry, won the Waterstones Debut Fiction Prize earlier this month for her novel May We Feed The King, about a curator of historic buildings who begins to explore the life of an almost-forgotten medieval king.

Two other authors are recognised for debut works - including Kenan Orhan for The Renovation, about a psychologist caring for her dementia-suffering father in Italy when some building work doesn't go to plan.

Fellow debut novelist Djamel White is recognised for All Them Dogs, which follows a man returning to west Dublin after being on the run for five years because he killed someone in a gang fight.

Aged 28, White is the youngest longlistee this year. The oldest is 81-year-old M John Harrison, for The End of Everything, a post-apocalyptic novel set in a Kent coastal town.

Switzy by Emma Cline, due to be published in September, is about a wealthy and accomplished man travelling to an assisted suicide clinic in Switzerland; while The Shadow of the Object by Chloe Aridjis sees an encounter in a Mexico City hospital lead to a life-changing friendship.

Gwendoline Riley's The Palm House, meanwhile, follows a London freelancer and her long friendship with a senior magazine editor; and Missouri Williams's The Vivisectors follows a graduate student in a decaying university city overrun by wild plants.

The list is completed by Luke Kennard's Black Bag, about a penniless out-of-work actor who is paid to zip himself inside a large black leather bag and sit silently at the back of a university lecture hall for a psychological experiment.

In a statement, Beard said: "Every writer on our longlist brilliantly musters the power of words on the page to take the reader to new places, to see old places from new angles, to change minds.

"Books are not mirrors: they don't simply reflect ourselves back to us. One of the many important things about fiction is that it helps us see what it might be like not to be us, to begin to understand the perspectives of others, and to imagine what it might be like to see the world differently.

"Great books are not cosy. In their various ways, the novels we have chosen are (we hope) dynamite."

Last year's Booker Prize was won by British-Hungarian author David Szalay, for his novel Flesh.

Mother and boyfriend guilty of murder of girl, two

BBC News Tue, 28 Jul 2026 12:49:20 GMT

Warning: This story contains distressing details

A mother and her new boyfriend have been found guilty of murdering her two-year-old daughter, with the man also convicted of sexually abusing the girl.

Isabelle Welsh suffered multiple injuries in the weeks before she collapsed with a fractured skull at her home in Thornaby in September 2025, Teesside Crown Court had heard.

Alexandra Walker, 25, and her partner Harrison Simpson, 22, were both found guilty of murder and child cruelty, with Simpson also convicted of sexual abuse of a child.

They will be sentenced on Thursday. Isabelle's family said she had her "whole life ahead of her" but it was "taken in the most heartbreaking way".

Prosecutors previously said the couple, who began a relationship in June 2025, were both responsible for a "wicked" campaign of sexual abuse and violence against Isabelle.

Walker and Simpson blamed each other for the girl's injuries and suffering.

Isabelle suffered her fatal injuries on the morning of 13 September while alone with Simpson, when Walker was upstairs in bed following a drink and drugs binge, the court heard.

Walker called 999 later that afternoon to say her daughter had collapsed at their home, with the two-year-old dying in hospital the following day.

The previously "happy and mischievous" girl was found to have a fractured skull and catastrophic brain injury, with doctors also discovering she was covered in bruises and suffered 21 broken bones in the weeks before her death.

Prosecutors said Isabelle's abuse started shortly after Simpson arrived in her life, with the extent of her injuries so obvious her mother must have known what was going on.

They said Walker prioritised her new relationship over the safety of her daughter, allowing Simpson to spend time alone with Isabelle despite suspecting he was a paedophile.

Simpson claimed he had no motive for harming Isabelle, while Walker said she did not hurt her daughter and was unaware of any abuse.

Jurors reached their verdicts after about six and a half hours of deliberation.

Simpson was unanimously found guilty of murder, cruelty and sexual assault of a child.

Walker was convicted of murder by a majority of 11 jurors to one and of cruelty unanimously.

She was found not guilty of sexually assaulting her daughter.

Ms Justice Norton said each murderer would get a life sentence, with the minimum term they would have to serve before being eligible for parole to be set by her on Thursday.

The judge thanked jurors for their work in the upsetting and distressing case.

In a statement released after the verdicts, Isabelle's family said: "Isabelle should have had her whole life ahead of her, but she was taken from us in the most heartbreaking way.

"She was so loved and our lives will never be the same without her.

"While today's verdicts cannot undo the pain caused or bring Isabelle back, it does mean justice has been served.

"We will remember Isabelle forever."

Det Ch Insp Steve Chatterton said Isabelle suffered "catastrophic injuries at the hands of the very people who should have loved, cared for and protected her".

Walker and Simpson "robbed Isabelle of her future" and "deprived her family of watching her grow up and achieve those milestones that so many take for granted", he added.

District crown prosecutor for the Crown Prosecution Service Kirstie Devine said Isabelle suffered "shocking violence" and "appalling abuse".

The "raft of evidence", which included phone records, CCTV and medical reports, showed "only the two adults who were regularly with Isabelle could have harmed her", she said.

Richard Hammond fined £999 for speeding offences

BBC News Tue, 28 Jul 2026 12:43:07 GMT

Former Top Gear presenter Richard Hammond has been fined £999 after being caught speeding twice in three weeks while driving luxury cars.

The 56-year-old was captured driving his Porsche Taycan Cross Turismo at 68mph in a 50mph limit on the A40 in Pencraig, Herefordshire on 2 December.

He was later clocked driving his Bentley Continental GT at 82mph in a 70mph limit on the M50 Rudhall Overbridge, also in Herefordshire, on 22 December.

Hammond pleaded guilty to two speeding charges through his solicitor. Two further charges that he had ignored the police letters and failed to identify himself as the guilty driver were withdrawn by police.

He was also given seven penalty points for his licence at the hearing last week.

Magistrate Ann Minton ordered him to pay a total of £1,771, comprising two fines of £333 and £666, £240 in costs and victim surcharges totalling £532.

Documents from the case show Hammond was first caught speeding by a police officer with a handheld speed camera at just before 13:00 GMT on 2 December and again at about 11:45 on 22 December.

West Mercia Police sent speeding tickets to a Grade II listed Herefordshire castle bought by Hammond in 2012 and a £1m farm estate near Hereford, but the letters were returned marked as "addressee gone away".

He was eventually tracked down to his £2m home near Abergavenny in Wales where more than 30 vehicles were currently registered, the court heard.

Police also set out in the court papers that Hammond had been accused of another driving offence in August last year.

Hammond, who hosted the BBC's Top Gear show with Jeremy Clarkson and James May between 2002 and 2015, received a three-month driving ban in France in 2013 after he and Clarkson were caught speeding while making an episode of the show.

To the charges of ignoring the police letters and failing to identify himself as the guilty driver, he said in a letter to the court read out by his solicitor: "He replied identifying himself as the driver. He sent the reply by First Class post. He posted the reply himself."

The force ultimately opted to withdraw the extra charges, as Hammond was prosecuted and convicted for the speeding.

Naga Munchetty to leave BBC Breakfast after 17 years

BBC News Tue, 28 Jul 2026 11:38:26 GMT

BBC Breakfast co-host Naga Munchetty is leaving the show after 17 years, and will swap the TV sofa for the presenter's chair on Radio 5 Live's breakfast show.

Munchetty has been one of the main hosts on BBC One’s Breakfast for the past 12 years.

She currently presents the TV show for three days a week and 5 Live's mid-morning programme for another three days. From January, she will present 5 Live Breakfast five days a week.

"It has been a privilege to be part of the BBC Breakfast TV team for the past 17 years, working alongside an incredibly talented and hard-working group of journalists who are not only outstanding colleagues but also great friends," she said.

"Presenting a flagship programme on 5 Live is an opportunity that was simply too good to pass up.

"It will take a huge amount of work and require 100% of my focus and energy, and I'm really looking forward to throwing myself into the role."

John McAndrew, the BBC's director of live and daily news, said Munchetty would be "hugely missed by the millions of viewers who've welcomed her into their homes each week".

He added: "I'm very pleased that Naga will be staying with the BBC and I wish her the best of luck at 5 Live."

Her replacement on BBC Breakfast has not yet been announced, while 5 Live Breakfast will get a new co-host to join Munchetty in the radio studio.

5 Live Breakfast's current hosts Rachel Burden and Rick Edwards announced on Tuesday's show that they will be leaving the programme.

Burden, who will move to Munchetty's Monday-to-Wednesday mid-morning slot on 5 Live, said: "After 15 years hosting 5 Live Breakfast, I've decided it's time for a change - and I'm really excited about launching my new show on the station."

Edwards, who will remain host of weekend sport quiz Fighting Talk, said he would miss "our wonderful audience", the team and Burden - who he described as "a colleague who has become a friend, and also a mentor, because she's so much older than me".

He added: "Two things I am of course looking forward to are not waking up at 3.45am, and vaping without fear of violent recrimination."

Munchetty, 51, is among the best-paid presenters on the BBC's star salaries list, earning about £360,000 a year, according to the latest accounts.

She has interviewed major celebrities and politicians on the programme over the years ranging from Hillary Clinton and Michelle Obama to Sir Keir Starmer, Sir David Attenborough and Sir Rod Stewart.

In 2016, she appeared on the BBC's Strictly Come Dancing.

She has also been at the centre of some controversies during her time on BBC Breakfast.

In 2019, she was initially found to have breached the BBC's guidelines over comments she made about a social media post from Donald Trump about four female politicians of colour.

However, the BBC's director general then reversed that finding after deciding her words were not "sufficient to merit" upholding part of the complaint.

In 2021, Munchetty and co-presenter Charlie Stayt were "spoken to and reminded of their responsibilities" after complaints about their reaction to a government minister's flag. Munchetty apologised for liking "offensive" tweets about the exchange.

In June 2025, the Sun reported details of two alleged incidents which the paper said caused BBC bosses to speak to Munchetty about her conduct.

That came amid reports of behind-the-scenes tensions on the show, and at the same time as the programme's editor Richard Frediani took extended leave following allegations about his behaviour.

Frediani returned to work two weeks later and remains editor of BBC Breakfast.

At the time, the BBC said it did not comment on individual cases but took all complaints about conduct at work extremely seriously. Munchetty and Frediani did not comment on the reports.

The programme won a Bafta TV Award last year for best news coverage for a special about the Post Office scandal.

How afraid should we be of Scotland's jellyfish?

BBC News Tue, 28 Jul 2026 05:11:31 GMT

When scuba diver and underwater photographer Ross McLaren encountered a jellyfish for the first time, he said all he felt was "sheer terror".

"I was diving in the Clyde and one of the instructors had to pull me out of the way of the tentacles as it was wafting above me," he said.

McLaren ended up with a sting across his upper lip but said it did not stop him from wanting to dive.

Many people are scared of jellyfish due to the fear of painful stings and the creature's unpredictable nature in the water.

But McLaren, who lives near the coast in North Ayrshire, believes there is more to the brainless, heartless and boneless invertebrates than people might think.

"Jellyfish have such a bad reputation but they are one of the most mesmerising and beautiful creatures underwater," he said, having completed almost 600 dives.

As we reach peak jellyfish season in Scotland, should we see them as a sight to behold or a reason to run?

July and August are peak months for jellyfish sightings in Scotland.

"The number and distribution of jellyfish are impacted by many different factors," said Anna Bunney of the Marine Conservation Society, which runs a nationwide survey of jellyfish.

"This includes sea temperatures, the availability of plankton for feeding, which peaks during the summer months when it is warmer, and ocean currents."

Sea temperatures tend to lag behind air temperatures, Bunney says.

The maximum air temperatures in Scotland usually occur in July and August, whereas sea temperatures are at the warmest in August and September.

When the sea starts to get warmer, it means a return of the jellyfish.

Bunney described jellyfish as weak swimmers or "passive drifters" which rely on ocean currents to carry them.

Calmer ocean conditions around the UK in the summer months help to push jellyfish gently towards the shore, meaning there are often more sightings of the creatures.

Breeding speed also increases with warmer conditions, allowing adult jellyfish to reproduce in large numbers, creating so-called blooms.

These blooms can look like a thick soup or pulsing cloud in the water and have been known to block boat engines.

In 2011, Torness nuclear power station in East Lothian was even shut down as a precautionary measure due to huge numbers of jellyfish found in sea water entering the plant.

McLaren added that while jellyfish season is normally April to October, the creatures can still be seen in Scotland's waters all year round.

"You see them in the winter months but they are far more prevalent and common during the summer," he said.

Jellyfish stings in Scotland are not usually life-threatening but can be very painful.

Depending on the type of jellyfish, the stingers may not be sharp enough or long enough to pierce the skin.

Bunney said most jellyfish have stinging cells but the severity and detectability of the sting varies widely between species.

Swimmers should be aware of the Lion's Mane, which is a brownish orange colour, and prevalent around Scotland's coastline in the warmer summer months.

They have long tentacles which can give a sore but not lethal sting.

The tentacles can break off and float around in the sea or become attached to chains on a boat, for example, but the stinging cells will stay alive even when not attached to the main body.

Bunney, who said she has been stung a lot by jellyfish, compared a mild sting to that of a nettle.

"There was one point when every time over a period of two years I was stung by a jellyfish when I was out in the sea," she said.

"But thankfully, it hasn't impacted how I feel about the ocean.

"In fact, what I often think is the most frustrating is when you are stung but you cannot see what you have been stung by."

McLaren said he has never been put off scuba diving by the prospect of a jellyfish sting but he can understand why swimmers might be nervous.

"When you're diving, as long as the visibility is good, you can negotiate your way around a jellyfish relatively easily, if you know what way the current is flowing and you pay attention," he said.

"Swimming, on the other hand, I totally get it - if I was taking my kids down to the beach and there were a lot of jellyfish I would probably stop them from getting in the water.

"When you're swimming you tend to have your head out of the water more so you can't always see what is underneath or know where the tentacles are going."

Both Bunney and McLaren added that it is important not to touch a jellyfish when it is washed up on a beach as it can still sting, even when presumed dead.

Bunney said to follow NHS guidance after a jellyfish sting.

It suggests using tweezers or the edge of a bank card to remove the tentacles as soon as possible as they can continue to sting while attached to the body.

A heat pack or immersion in hot water can reduce pain and swelling, and painkillers such as paracetamol can also help.

If symptoms because more severe or a sensitive part of body has been stung, seek medical help.

Unlike bees or wasps, which sting as a defence mechanism to protect themselves, a jellyfish sting is an automatic reflex, not a deliberate attack.

"A common misconception is jellyfish go after people but contact with a jellyfish is actually merely incidental and humans are not on their menu," Bunney said.

"They are not actively stinging, it is just when anything touches their tentacles as they are moving through the water, regardless of what it is."

Jellyfish tentacles are lined with thousands of venom-filled stinging cells.

When touched, these cells fire toxic harpoon-like tubes designed to paralyse prey, such as plankton and small fish.

"Do not be afraid but be cautious" is the advice from Bunney, who generally recommends swimming calmly away from jellyfish.

"Most of the species found in Scotland have very mild stings, which only cause minor irritation, and some are completely harmless," she said.

Bunney says it is important for people to learn about the different species of jellyfish and report sightings to the Marine Conservation Society.

"People think jellyfish are ugly," she said. "But they are really beautiful creatures that come in all different colours and sizes."

McLaren echoed the love for the marine invertebrate.

"People hate jellyfish but I always do my best to take a photo of one when I see it because they are impressive to see in the water," he said.

"It's almost like stars in the night sky when you are on the sea floor and looking up at the jellyfish above you.

"It's magical."

On the front line of Ecuador's drugs war, police fight gangs, guns and corruption

BBC News Tue, 28 Jul 2026 05:01:19 GMT

In the Ecuadoran city of Durán, riddled with drugs and rival gangs, Police Captain Jean Carlos Bustamante knows exactly what he is up against – not just the criminals who kill and sometimes dismember their rivals, but also the enemy within.

"We have many, many bad people inside our unit, inside the state, inside politics," he says. "We have many, many guys that are corrupt. They are in the pay of the gangs."

The only police officers he can trust, he says, are the ones right beside him - members of his hand-picked team. At 34, Captain Bustamante is the oldest among them and moves like the special forces officer he used to be.

With the sun setting, he leads his team into a hardscrabble neighbourhood where windows are sealed off behind metal grills, and lips are sealed by fear. This is the heart of gangland, controlled by a group called Los Aguilas (Spanish for The Eagles).

I ask what happens if local people speak out against the gangs. "They kill them," the captain replies. "So that's why they never say nothing."

Contains disturbing scenes.

He's heading for an abandoned house where he believes weapons have been hidden (gunmen don't keep their guns at home). He and his team line up, hugging the wall, heavily armed, and tightly packed. A battering ram gets them through the door.

They find two handguns – one rusty but the other ready to be fired - and ammunition for an assault rifle.

The captain says he's happy with the result. "The first reason is because we are safe," he says. "The second is that there are two guns less for the gangs."

But this is a small victory, in a war of attrition. He admits the gangs have "many weapons and much more money than the state".

He knows the risks only too well – having lost three close friends fighting the gangs. He has also lost his fear he says, "years ago", but his parents have not.

"My mum says 'be careful, maybe you can die there'," he tells me. "My dad calls all the time and asks 'my son, are you good? Tell me that you are good.'"

A line can be traced - in dollars and in broken lives - from the back streets of Durán to the hotspots of London, and other capital cities. Around 70% of the cocaine reaching Europe and the US is funnelled out of Ecuador, according to the country's President, Daniel Noboa.

How did it come to this?

The drug pours in from neighbouring Colombia and Peru – the two biggest producers in the world. Powerful home-grown gangs – with links to Mexican cartels and Albanian mafia groups – help smuggle the cocaine onwards. They take advantage of Ecuador's weak border controls, underfunded security forces, and long Pacific coast.

In the process what was a peaceful tourist haven in South America has – in under a decade - become a killing ground.

Last year the murder rate was one of the highest in the world, with more than 9,200 people killed, according to Ecuador's interior ministry. That's despite an iron-fisted crackdown by President Noboa over the past two years. Critics say it has backfired. Top crime bosses have been arrested, causing the gangs to fracture, but also to multiply.

Many here believe the war against the gangs will never be won.

Captain Bustamante keeps fighting.

When we join him for another operation he's lying in wait getting a bird's eye view of the back alleys from a drone. He sees three figures moving around at the edge of a playground – "micro-traffickers" - caught in the act, he says. They are at the bottom of the drug chain, selling locally, in minute amounts, not kilos.

Within minutes he and his team have tracked the suspects to their door. The battering ram is out again, and soon they are in the kitchen, where a middle-aged woman protests, and a young girl bursts into tears.

The police move from room to room, by torchlight - there's no power - opening wardrobes and lifting mattresses. Upstairs, they find a hiding place behind a window. A young suspect emerges and is detained. Two others are handcuffed in another room. All three are led away, denying that they were dealing drugs.

Nearby the captain finds tiny paper packets of "H" stashed in a flowerpot. It's a highly addictive mix containing small amounts of heroin sold by neighbourhood dealers for $1.00 (£0.75) per packet.

One of the suspects is charged, and if convicted, he could get five years in jail. Prosecutors release the other two. Senior officers say that happens a lot. They blame corruption in the justice system, and the prosecutor's office.

"We imprison them [gang members] and they release them," says Colonel Santiago Gavilanez, deputy commander of Durán police. "We know because when we carry out raids, we recapture them. Some of those who are released kill people and leave orphans behind." He tells us that the gangs have money to "buy laws, judges, and politicians".

We get an example of the buying power of the gangs from another police officer, in a different location. For his safety, we cannot reveal his name or where he is based.

He told us he was contacted twice by text and offered a massive bribe - "enough money to retire on". He turned it down.

Someone – a colleague perhaps – had informed the gang exactly where he worked and what he did.

"You never know who is watching," he said. We heard that a lot during a week in Durán, and surrounding areas.

Back at the playground it's the end of another long day in body armour, but Captain Bustamante says he has to keep going. "Maybe, I am a little tired," he admits, "but it's my work. I believe we can win this war. We have to do it."

As we speak, one of the main gang bosses in the area has been spotted nearby. "We know he controls the dealers," says the captain, "but we have no leads or evidence, so we can't arrest him".

But police here insist they are having an impact. The murder rate in Durán is down by half, they say, in the first six months of this year.

There are other indications of progress, they tell us, with streets no longer deserted after 19:00 local time, and bodies no longer found beheaded or dismembered. That used to be common, according to Colonel Gavilanez.

"We have managed to contain the gangs," he says. "Getting complete control is going to be a medium-term process."

Elsewhere the criminals are containing the police. Through a contact we arranged to meet a local gang on their home turf, about an hour's drive from the city. Their leader – whom we are calling Jonathan – told me he had four officers on his payroll.

"Whenever they're going to do an operation, they call me," he said. "They tell me to hide things, and to get out of here. When they arrive, they find nothing."

That early warning systems costs him about $1,500 (£1,100) to $2,000 (£1,500) a month.

At 37, Jonathan is just a few years older than Captain Bustamante, but he's across enemy lines. He says he joined a gang, at 18, to put food on the table.

He and his men (and boys) strolled through the rough-hewn streets, in broad daylight, brandishing weapons - including a semi-automatic rifle and a pistol. The youngest gang member we saw was a lean 17-year-old, wearing a bulletproof vest, and flip flops. All covered their faces.

Jonathan answered our questions inside a narrow room in a breeze block house, with his lieutenants crowding in. Most of the space was taken up by a bed. He admitted to being a drug pusher and a killer. "How many lives have you taken?" I asked.

"Well, until now about eight, I think. I don't remember well," he replied, with a handgun in his lap, pointing in my direction.

Jonathan claimed his gang didn't kill innocent people, just a rival criminal group trying to replace them. "They want to force their way in here," he said, "they come killing people, and we respond. The main thing for us now is to eliminate the other gang."

As we spoke, local people gathered near the doorway, children among them. Human rights workers in Ecuador told us boys can be recruited into gang life by the age of 12. Three years later they can be hitmen.

Jonathan makes no apologies for putting guns in the hands of teenagers or selling cocaine in the neighbourhood he claims to protect. He insists the drug trade cannot be rooted out.

"I think it's an issue that will never end," he says. "If they shut us down, another one [gang] will come along, and if they shut that one down, there will be another."

He expects to die, as he has lived – by the gun. "Death is paid by death," he said. "But if they come to kill me, I won't make it easy for them."

Two nights later, back in Durán, we saw how gangs settle scores. The body of a man was visible under flashing police lights, lying where he fell, beside a motorbike. Bullet casings were still on the ground. Neighbours stood looking on, mostly in silence.

A man and woman held each other and wept – relatives of the dead man.

Police suspected a revenge attack – one gang against another.

Forensic teams lifted the body onto a stretcher, and into the back of a refrigerated van: violent death, on repeat. Another corpse was already inside.

A witness was willing to speak – but not to be named. "He already had a bullet in his back," he told us. "As he fell, they finished him off with a shot to the head. He was shot six times by two men on a motorbike."

"We are used to this now because it happens every day," he said. "You might just step outside and catch a stray bullet. You can't even go out or talk to friends or family because someone could shoot you."

He does not expect the president's fight against the gangs to deliver any change.

"Criminals are like ghosts," he said, in a low voice. "They pop up wherever they please."

Then he melted away, into the warm night air.

You never know who is watching.

With additional reporting by Wietske Burema, Lee Durant, Chris Gibson, Thalie Ponce and Mauricio Torres.

Why attachment theory is everywhere right now and how it can help you

BBC News Tue, 28 Jul 2026 00:21:34 GMT

For Lizzy, relationships always seemed to end the same way. "I would get to a second or third date and find something wrong with them."

Just as things began to feel real, the connection she longed for would suddenly feel uncomfortable, even threatening. And she would pull away.

For years, she couldn't explain why - until she came across attachment theory.

And it was the description of a so-called fearful-avoidant - one of the four attachment styles - which felt strikingly familiar.

It describes someone who wants closeness, but worries that people in their life will eventually reject or abandon them.

"It was like I had found the missing piece to a puzzle that I've been trying to solve for years," Lizzy says.

She is not alone. Attachment theory has exploded into the public consciousness.

On TikTok, videos tagged #AttachmentTheory have racked up hundreds of millions of views.

And in popular culture it's used to explain everything from Marianne and Connell's relationship in the hit book and TV series Normal People to the lyrics of Sam Fender and Olivia Dean's record-breaking number one track Rein Me In.

"The first time I listened to it I started crying," Lizzy says.

For her, the song gave voice to both sides of avoidant attachment: the fear that can make love feel unbearable, and the confusion felt by the partner left behind.

First developed in the 1950s by British psychiatrist John Bowlby, attachment theory suggests that the bonds we form with early caregivers shape our expectations of relationships.

If support is consistently available, you are more likely to see others as reliable. If care is unpredictable or emotionally distant, you may develop strategies designed to protect yourself from disappointment or distress.

There are four attachment styles - anxious, avoidant, fearful-avoidant and secure. In simple terms they are defined as follows:

Research suggests that secure people tend to fare better not only in romantic relationships, but across life. They manage stress more effectively, cope better with setbacks like rejection or loss and are better colleagues and managers in the workplace.

And what began as a way to understand relationships is increasingly influencing how people navigate them.

Across social media, attachment styles are used to reassess friendships, make sense of family tensions or rule out potential partners.

And relationship coaches promise to reveal the hidden signs of emotional unavailability in a partner or the ways to heal anxious attachment.

Dr Pascal Vrticka, an associate professor of psychology at the University of Essex, has spent nearly two decades studying attachment.

He says the theory offers "one of the best explanations" for the differences in how people seek support and connection with others.

And while he's glad to see it reach a wider audience, he worries the way it is interpreted can be "outdated, misinformed and, in the worst case, harmful."

"I think one problem is that people are overgeneralising it and using it in contexts where it might not be the best framework to explain our behaviour," he says.

Part of the issue, he explains, is that initial assumptions around attachment theory have evolved since it was first developed.

Vrticka says one of the biggest misconceptions is that attachment styles are fixed.

Although studies have found that they can show a degree of stability over time, Vrticka says change is possible.

"The good news is that the evidence shows that secure attachment is the most stable. Which means that once you become secure, you tend to stay secure."

He says attachment is often reshaped during periods of transition, particularly during adolescence, when young people begin forming close relationships beyond their family.

Later events in our lives, like entering a new relationship, experiencing a breakup or dealing with bereavement, can also be influential.

But Vrticka says that change is gradual and professional support is likely to be needed for people with more entrenched attachment patterns.

It's that nuance, Lizzy says, which is often lost in discussions of attachment theory.

She says some people can be "quick to assume the worst" and reduce others to labels.

However, while she says people with insecure attachment styles should be viewed with more empathy, she acknowledges the importance of self-awareness.

"For me, I know that my avoidant tendencies are toxic and it would be unfair for me to date someone right now," she says.

But, she adds, that doesn't mean people with insecure attachments are incapable of healthy relationships. "It is on you to acknowledge it and put in the work to heal."

Few have played a more influential role in bringing attachment to the mainstream than Dr Amir Levine.

His book Attached, co-written with Rachel Heller, was first published in 2010 and has since sold millions of copies around the world.

But in his latest book, Levine shifts the focus from identifying attachment styles to ask a different question: how do you become secure?

Part of the answer, he argues, lies in what he calls "SIMIs" - seemingly insignificant minor interactions.

A text from a friend asking about your weekend. A smile from a stranger.

"The brain monitors small interactions all the time," Levine says. "That's what attachment is about. It's a monitoring system for safety."

And he says these interactions gradually shape what the brain expects from relationships.

Positive experiences build evidence that people can be trusted and relied upon, helping move someone towards what he calls "secure mode".

But equally, a delayed response or a friend failing to follow through on plans can trigger subtle stress responses in the nervous system.

Importantly, Levine says it's possible to have different attachment styles with different people.

So he encourages people to identify the relationships in their lives that already make them feel safe and understood, and to use them "as a vehicle for becoming more secure overall".

And the idea that security can be built through current relationships reflects a broader shift away from seeing attachment as just the result of childhood experiences.

For some, discovering attachment theory can involve re-examining family relationships, which can potentially lead to resentment. But Levine says "it's not just about where you started, but what happens afterwards".

"If that way of thinking helps you understand yourself and move forward, that's useful," he says.

"But if it makes you feel stuck or damaged, then it's not accurate because people really can change."

Levine also argues that insecure attachments can in themselves be strengths.

He says anxious people are often acutely tuned into relationships, spotting subtle shifts in mood, tone and behaviour that others miss, while avoidant people can be fiercely independent and perform well under pressure.

However, whilst Vrticka agrees that attachment styles shouldn't be seen as either good or bad, he stresses they "come with certain risks and difficulties", which he says shouldn't be disregarded.

But both agree that attachment theory is most useful when it helps people understand patterns rather than define themselves.

An island has been waging war on rats. They think they’ve finally won

New Scientist July 28, 2026

Thousands of screaming seabirds wheel through the air above and below me as I lean over the railings of a viewing platform halfway down a cliff. The chocolate backs of guillemots are packed so closely on the sheer rock face before me that they seem part of it. Higher up, on precarious ledges, they jostle with fulmars, kittiwakes and puffins, guarding their chicks and waiting for food from their mates.

It’s a wonderful sight, and one that draws in plenty of tourists. But it is not just the birds – much as I love them – that have prompted my trip to Rathlin Island in Northern Ireland. It is another animal that is really responsible for me being here, one that tends to evoke quite different feelings in the human psyche: the rat.

Rats are a huge threat to the seabirds on Rathlin, and the same is true on many islands across the world, where they, and other invasive predators like stoats and cats, eat eggs and chicks. There is now a growing movement for humans to step in and save the birds by killing all the rats. Predator eradication is difficult, but it is “one of the most powerful conservation interventions possible”, says conservation biologist James Russell at the University of Auckland in New Zealand.

Advertisement

Now, the strategy is being applied to Rathlin, one of the largest and most populated islands on which it has been attempted. Success isn’t guaranteed, but it is going well so far, thanks to a campaign involving lethal traps, poison, thermal drones and even a sniffer dog. I have come here to investigate what happens when you try to rid an island of rats, and where the idea goes next.

Rats have a long history of wiping out island birds, with their pawprints all over one of the world’s most famous extinctions, that of the dodo. This unfortunate bird disappeared within 100 years of Dutch sailors arriving on Mauritius, having been hunted by the settlers and their menagerie of pigs, dogs, cats – and stowaway rats.

Whenever rodents arrive on an island with ground-nesting birds that haven’t evolved any defences, they can cause an apocalypse. It is extremely difficult to stop rats from reaching any island that has boat traffic, as they stow away in transported goods, especially animal feed, and can even swim to new islands less than a kilometre away.

The Pacific Islanders fighting to save their homes from catastrophe

Their impact is notorious in New Zealand, whose fauna evolved in geographical isolation for 80 million years, with no rat-like predators – indeed, no native land mammals at all, other than bats. Since humans arrived, the country has suffered sequential invasions of three rat species across its 600-odd islands. The first was in the 13th century, as Polynesian settlers arrived in the north, bringing along Pacific rats.

A few centuries later, these were outcompeted by the larger black and brown rats that hitched rides with European sailors. By the 1960s, conservationists were watching in horror as rodents reached New Zealand’s small outer islands, which until then had been sanctuaries for multiple bird, bat and other native species experiencing precipitous declines on the country’s two main landmasses.

One teacher, Alistair McDonald, took matters into his own hands. In 1960, he was touring Maria Island, a 150-metre-long island off the country’s north coast, when he noticed hundreds of small, delicate-looking seabirds, white-faced storm petrels, floating dead in the water. Rats had finally reached the island.

McDonald turned saving the birds into a school project, encouraging children to fundraise for poisoned rat bait and taking them on hunting expeditions with his dog. Some children even used the more direct method of whacking rats over the head, McDonald told New Zealand Geographic. A park ranger visiting Maria a few years later confirmed the rats were all gone.

McDonald’s school project was one of the first island rodent eradications in the world. Since then, conservationists elsewhere have followed his lead and attempted to eliminate rats and mice from many hundreds of other islands, including those in Australasia, Europe and North America, as well as tropical islands with their unique ecosystems.

So far, there have been efforts to eradicate rodents on nearly 1000 islands around the world, with a 90 per cent success rate for rats and 75 per cent for mice (albeit with some reinvasions). Over the years, the techniques have become much more sophisticated. “We started in the 1960s with people crawling around on hands and knees throwing poison everywhere,” says Russell. “Now we use helicopters, sowing the poison aerially. We have gone from islands that were tens of hectares to hundreds of hectares to thousands of hectares.”

Conservationists had been discussing predator eradication on Rathlin Island for more than 20 years. Reports and feasibility studies were partly led by Liz Bell, a New Zealander who is a global leader in the field and who was drawn to Rathlin as the home to Northern Ireland’s largest seabird colony. At about 14 square kilometres, Rathlin isn’t the largest island to undergo predator eradication, but it is the largest one that is fully inhabited.

This is a serious obstacle, as it rules out using helicopters for bait distribution because the poison could be eaten by livestock, pets and possibly even children. “People don’t like poison dropping out of the sky,” says Russell. Instead, the poisoned bait has to go in containers that only rats or smaller creatures can access, which must be placed by hand, massively increasing the work involved.

An added complication was Rathlin’s feral ferret problem. Though there were fewer ferrets than rats, they are lethal predators. In 2017, one ferret managed to reach the cliff-side breeding area I visited, killing 27 puffins over two days.

Despite these difficulties, the idea of eradicating both rats and ferrets on Rathlin gained ground, promoted by conservationists, organisations such as the Royal Society for the Protection of Birds (RSPB) Northern Ireland and some islanders themselves.

The campaigners had to convince farmers and other residents to allow strangers onto their land to distribute lethal traps. But there would be clear benefits. If bird numbers recovered as expected, it would attract more birdwatchers and bring in more tourism, the island’s main source of income. Plus, ferrets and rats are agricultural pests, eating the food of livestock and attacking poultry. After numerous community meetings, several residents joined the campaign as employees or volunteers, and the eradication started in 2023.

The first job was to tackle the ferrets. This was done by placing 450 traps around the island, with non-lethal ones used near homes to ensure no pet cats were killed by mistake. In the end, 98 ferrets were killed.

Two years need to have passed since the last sighting for any eradication to be considered certain and, this March, the RSPB proudly announced success – having carried out the first eradication of feral ferrets on an inhabited island in the world.

The rats, however, were a far bigger problem.

With an estimated 10,000 living on Rathlin, it was a mammoth undertaking, requiring 7000 bait stations, designed so nothing larger than a rat could get in and eat the poison. These were placed at 50-metre intervals all over the island. Permission was needed from nearly every resident, as some bait stations had to go in barns, outhouses and even homes.

Synthetic biology may finally be ready to solve life’s biggest mystery

The farmland and residential areas weren’t the only problematic locations. Much of the shoreline is surrounded by steep cliffs, requiring professional climbers to abseil halfway down and dangle bait stations further down on long wires. “It’s about getting to every last place to make sure that you’ve got total coverage,” says Glenn Slade, project scientist for the RSPB. “If you leave just one pregnant female rat, you’ve potentially got recolonisation.”

The rat poisoning began in September 2024. Slade estimates that most of the rats were killed within the first month. “The vast majority of the decline happens in a short space of time, and then you spend a very long time chasing down those last ones,” he says. That final hunt involved innovative methods like bringing in thermal drones and a specially trained sniffer dog, both of which were used to find any remaining rats.

As far as we know, the last rat was killed in June 2025. So, if all goes well, the campaign could be declared a success by next summer. “I don’t want to jinx it, but, so far, we’ve been successful,” says Slade.

While the intensive part of the campaign is over, several Rathlin residents and volunteers have switched to the monitoring phase, with monthly checks of bait stations and camera traps to ensure no rats remain. They have added extra bait stations and cameras in the harbour area to spot any rats that arrive on boats. If any do, a new localised poisoning campaign would swing into action.

Charlie Bosanquet, a resident who is one of the harbour monitors, says the campaign works only with the islanders’ enthusiastic participation. She helped teach residents to spot signs of rats, giving out laminated sheets with pictures of scat from rats, mice and rabbits, as well as 3D-printed models of rat gnaw marks. The giveaway is that rats have two large front incisors, which leave distinctive grooves. Any resident who notices a rat knows to alert the RSPB.

The residents I speak to enthuse about the benefits of becoming a rat-free island. On my visit, I notice chickens strutting boldly around the lanes and fields, an unusual sight for a Londoner like me. Since rat numbers started falling, some non-farming residents began keeping chickens and ducks, says Marina McMullan, chair of the residents’ group, the Rathlin Development and Community Association.

All those I speak to on the island seem delighted with the campaign apart from one thing: it has led to a surge in rabbits, after the loss of ferrets, their only predators. As I take an evening walk, bunnies certainly bob up and down charmingly through long summer grass, but the next day, I hear how they ravage gardens and farmers’ fields.

I am shown a community allotment near the quay, where a whole row of sunflowers has just been beheaded. Similar destruction has been wrought on the strawberries, peas and herbs. As a keen allotmenteer myself, I feel the pain of this loss.

Then again, this outcome wasn’t wholly unexpected, seeing as the first ferrets were brought to Rathlin by residents in the 1980s specifically to control rabbits. When they got loose and started breeding, it must have felt like the song about the old lady who swallowed a fly.

I ask the RSPB what plans there are for the rabbits. For now, all a spokesperson will say is that their numbers are being monitored. Some of the islanders, however, mutter about taking matters into their own hands.

The rabbits may not seem like a big deal. Farmers elsewhere use various methods to keep their numbers down, including shooting them and gassing their warrens. But they show how, if one species disappears, the effects on an ecosystem’s complex web can be multiple and not always welcome.

When rats are eradicated, there is often a surge in mice, which are usually outcompeted by rats. “My prediction is that mice populations will explode now that the rats are gone,” says Wayne Linklater at California State University in Sacramento, who researches the impacts of invasive species.

Mice are also an agricultural pest and sometimes eat seabird eggs and chicks. On other islands where rats have been eradicated, the surge in mice has been bad news for some other species, like lizards.

When one Rathlin resident wonders aloud to me whether the next step could be eradicating mice, it starts to sound like a game of Whac-A-Mole. Mouse-eradication campaigns are possible, but they are generally harder because the animals are smaller than rats and have even faster breeding cycles.

In the short term, though, there is already an uptick in some seabirds, with about 1700 puffins recorded in 2025 by the RSPB, compared with 1200 in each of the previous two years. There have also been the first signs in decades of breeding by Manx shearwaters and storm petrels.

Zooming out, the global picture of rat eradication projects suggests they can have broader benefits than initially expected. On tropical islands, for example, restoring seabirds to their former numbers is thought to also boost coral and its fish, as the birds deposit nutrient-rich droppings. After rat eradication on two Indian Ocean islands in the mid-2000s, seabird numbers steadily rose, and nutrient levels in the surrounding water were found to be 13-fold higher than around similar islands that remained rat-infested.

Just how far could the eradication of introduced predators go? New Zealand is home to Predator Free 2050, a campaign launched by the government in 2016 to rid the entire country of its most harmful invasive predators by the middle of the century. While it first covered rats, possums and stoats, it later expanded to include ferrets, weasels and feral cats. “New Zealand’s ecosystem needs to remove these invasive predators for us to be able to have our seabirds, our land birds and our lizards and frogs back, and our massively cool invertebrates,” says Bell, who advises on aspects of the campaign.

Invasive species are now a major threat to wildlife, farms and people

But many conservationists think this goal is both misguided and unachievable. For one thing, it would take huge resources – requiring an estimated NZ$1 billion (US$570 million) a year, more than 0.5 per cent of the country’s GDP – that haven’t yet been made available. And these funds would be better spent in other ways, like protecting islands that are already free of predators, says Linklater, who critiqued the plan while he was based in New Zealand in 2018.

Although it may be unrealistic to eradicate the six invasive predators from the whole of New Zealand, the country has achieved stunning conservation successes through smaller-scale projects on many of its islands, including creating island sanctuaries for birds such as the kakapo, a large, waddling, frankly adorable parrot, and even the iconic kiwi.

Elsewhere in the world, work continues to suppress and eradicate invasive predators, including on both inhabited and uninhabited islands in the Scottish Orkneys and Hebrides.

With so many threats to wildlife from complex global problems like climate change and habitat loss, it is wonderful to work in a field that can count real successes, says Bell. “The recovery of these islands has been mind-blowing in a lot of places,” she says. “Plant recovery, bird recovery, invertebrates, reptiles – it’s magic.”

Jaguar makes epic 2100-kilometre journey across the Amazon

New Scientist July 28, 2026

A male jaguar has made an unprecedented trek, skirting 2100 kilometres of the southern edge of the Amazon rainforest. The journey – which crossed highways, farms, ranches and other human-modified landscapes – expands our knowledge of what these big cats are capable of.

The previous dispersal record for a tagged jaguar was about 60 to 100 kilometres, says Jon Morant at University College Dublin in Ireland. Knowing these animals are capable of travelling much longer distances reveals further challenges in protecting them. “Individuals that are travelling so far are more exposed to human-related risks like hunting or killing because of attacks on livestock,” says Morant.

Jaguar breaks records by swimming at least 1.3 kilometres

He and his colleagues have been tracking jaguars in Brazil via GPS collars as part of a larger ongoing project that started in 1999. The researchers wanted to better understand how jaguars use their environments along the Araguaia river, a potential wildlife corridor connecting the Cerrado grasslands with the Amazon.

Advertisement

They captured the male, dubbed Gaspar, as part of this work, fitting him with a collar on 11 November 2024. The 8-year-old jaguar then spent some time in his established range, about 700 square kilometres along the Araguaia river, before setting out on a massive southward trek, skirting the border of the Amazon to inland Cerrado.

Subscriber-only newsletter

The researchers recorded that Gaspar travelled 2122 kilometres, until his collar stopped transmitting locations in late Novemeber 2025, but that is as the crow flies. The actual distance is probably much more, says Morant.

While Gaspar mostly stuck to forested areas, he also crossed through heavily modified human landscapes, such as farms, ranches and roads. Dispersals, albeit shorter ones, are common in individuals aged 1 to 3 years old that are looking to establish a new territory, but it is unclear why an older adult like Gaspar made this move. He might have been searching for better food resources, mating opportunities or a better habitat in general, says Morant.

Jacob, an 11-year-old lion, has defied expectations by surviving for years after losing a leg – now we know his success is down to an innovative hunting strategy

“Beyond the extraordinary distance travelled, I find [it] especially intriguing that he apparently did not establish a territory despite more than a year of continuous movement through areas that were, at least in part, potentially suitable for jaguars,” says Jose Garcia Herrera at the Spanish National Research Council.

The findings also reveal an additional challenge in protecting such wide-ranging cats. In these human-modified areas, jaguars face threats from poaching, as ranchers often kill them to protect livestock. “Maybe we need to rethink how protected areas are framed and organised,” says Morant.

Gaspar’s fate is now uncertain. He may have been shot or poisoned, or the collar may have just stopped working, says Morant, which could mean Gaspar is still traversing the Brazilian landscape.

Ecology DOI: 10.1002/ecy.70441
