Matcha is under threat from climate change – can genomics save it?

New Scientist July 28, 2026

Climate change is wreaking havoc on matcha, traditional Japanese tea that has become a popular addition to iced lattes and even doughnuts around the world. Japan’s hotter nights and erratic spring temperatures are reducing yields and impacting the plant’s distinct umami flavour. But tea growers are starting to use genomic selection to overcome this, by identifying markers of heat tolerance in the plant’s seedlings.

Premium tencha, a green tea leaf that grows in shade and is ground into matcha, develops best during Japan’s spring, from March to May. Daytime temperatures ordinarily hover around 20 to 25 Celsius, then dip at night, which help develop the plant’s umami-producing amino acids.

Can climate change stay in the news agenda after Europe’s heatwave?

But spring temperatures in the Kyoto-Uji region, home to Japan’s finest matcha, have risen by roughly 0.6 to 1 Celsius over the past 100 years. Heat also causes tea plants to produce more catechins, defensive compounds that taste bitter.

Advertisement

“Climate change has altered growing conditions, and conventional cultivars [plants produced by breeding] are not always able to perform adequately under these changing conditions,” says Akiko Ogino at the NARO Institute of Vegetable and Tea Science in Makurazaki, Kagoshima in Japan.

Another problem is that tea breeding is slow. Breeders cross-pollinate carefully selected parent plants, each carrying different desirable characteristics, such as high yields or some degree of adaptation to warmer conditions.

But because the onset of these traits is complex and controlled by many genes, breeders must raise thousands of seedlings and identify the few that inherited the best combination of characteristics. Traditionally, they cannot judge whether a seedling has those traits until it matures, which can take around 15 years.

Subscriber-only newsletter

Now, genomic selection is accelerating this process, by identifying seedlings that seem to have good heat tolerance at a much earlier stage. This is already being incorporated into Japanese tea breeding programmes, says Takashi Ikka at Shizuoka University Research Institute of Green Science and Technology, Japan, who has co-authored a review on genomic approaches to tea breeding.

But it isn’t a perfect solution. It isn’t always possible to accurately predict a plant’s traits from its DNA and our existing genomic databases are relatively small, says Ikka. “[The] immediate value [of genomic sequencing] is not to replace field evaluation, but to prioritise parents and seedlings, and eliminate less promising candidates, before committing many years to clonal and multi-location trials,” he says. These trials involve growing promising plants at multiple sites over successive seasons to assess yield, flavour, disease resistance and adaptation to different growing conditions.

Japan’s tea cultivar registration system requires breeders evaluate 41 officially defined characteristics before a new one can be released, says Ogino. As a result, developing a cultivar still takes around 25 years.

Removing CO2 from the atmosphere by capturing the carbon from burning biomass is supposed to save the planet, but it looks like the flagship project will never happen

There’s also a possibility that heat tolerance could affect matcha’s flavour, however, Ogino doesn’t think this is a big risk. “At present, there is no clear evidence that tolerance to high-temperature conditions and bitterness or astringency are strongly linked at the genetic level,” says Ogino.

Ikka suggests that breeders may be able to select for both heat tolerance and a pleasant taste. “Regarding heat tolerance and flavour quality, I do not see an inevitable biological trade-off between them,” says Ikka. “In principle, breeders should be able to select for both simultaneously.”

Another possibility is that high temperatures increase catechin production regardless of how tolerant the plant is to heat, all of which will be revealed in time. “New research helps, but in the end, tea farming is still a waiting game,” says George Guttridge-Smith at Kyoto Obubu Tea Farms in Uji.

Breeding Science DOI: 10.1270/jsbbs.25050

Asteroid strike caused global firestorm that incinerated the dinosaurs

New Scientist July 28, 2026

The asteroid strike 66 million years ago caused a planetary-scale firestorm that burned dinosaurs to a crisp all over the world, according to simulations of the impact.

The so-called Chicxulub asteroid, which was 10 to 15 kilometres wide, landed in what is today the Gulf of Mexico at the end of the Cretaceous Period.

Why dinosaurs lived much more complex lives than we thought

Until now, it has been thought that most of the worst effects of heat and fires would have been relatively regional, and global extinctions were mainly caused by a “nuclear winter”, where dust blocks out the sun causes dramatic cooling.

Advertisement

Brandon Johnson at Purdue University, Indiana, and his colleagues analysed geological observations and impact simulations in the laboratory, which showed around five times more material was vaporised by the strike than previously thought.

The new work suggests that in the aftermath of the impact, a plume of rock vapour was blasted tens of thousands of kilometres into space and ended up being distributed high above the entirety of the planet.

Free newsletter

“After the impactor first strikes the Earth, it only takes about a second for much of the kinetic energy to be converted to heat, vaporising over 1000 cubic kilometres of rock,” says Johnson.

Just seconds later, the vapour plume expanded above much of Earth’s atmosphere into space, he says, leading to both dust and glassy, metallic beads called spherules, condensing from the vapour.

This immense vapour cloud ultimately turned into 1.6 trillion tonnes of dust, which blanketed the planet, sealing in heat, the study found. Meanwhile, the heavier spherules slammed back into the atmosphere.

“As this material re-enters the atmosphere over the coming hours, friction decelerates and heats the spherules, creating an approximately hour-long pulse of thermal radiation,” says Johnson.

“This would kill off creatures that were unable to shelter from it and was intense enough to ignite forest litter like grass and pine needles and may have even been enough to ignite trees.”

Dinosaur-killing asteroid impact site stayed hot for millions of years

The geologic record suggests the ensuing fires may have lasted for years and would have been reminiscent of the bushfires currently gripping Europe, except on a global scale, he says.

“The Cretaceous animals would have received 17 times the dose of thermal radiation that is 100 per cent lethal to humans,” says Johnson. “That should be enough to kill off even thick-skinned dinosaurs.”

Craig O’Neill at the Queensland University of Technology in Australia says the study shows that the dust layer encircling the planet was essentially opaque to infrared and visible light, trapping the heat.

“Every joule of heat created by incoming spherules is turned into a thermal pulse that bakes the surface of the Earth,” says O’Neill. “For about 30 minutes, the land is turned into history’s largest barbecue.”

However, this isn’t the whole story, he says. For example, life in the oceans was also badly affected by the event, driving many marine animals such as mosasaurs and ammonites extinct. This is better explained by the effects of a nuclear winter blocking out the sun on photosynthesising organisms, rather than an atmospheric thermal pulse, says O’Neill.

“We tend to think of mass extinction events as a murder mystery – if we can just find the murder weapon, we could solve the case. But mass extinctions seem more like a cascading system of failures,” he says.

Journal of Geophysical Research Biogeosciences DOI: 10.1029/2026JG009837

Unprecedented ‘fire clouds’ are fanning the flames in France

New Scientist July 28, 2026

A pyrocumulonimbus cloud, a looming thunderstorm generated by an intensely hot wildfire, has been observed with radar in France for the first time. These deadly “fire clouds” of rising hot air, smoke and moisture, which accelerate blazes with strong winds and soaring embers, are expected to become more common in Europe as wildfires there get bigger.

“You have this tilted column that is sucking air and then propagating embers in front, and it also creates lightning. That’s another way of lighting up fuels in front of the fire, so these cells are unstoppable,” says Jean-Baptiste Filippi at the University of Corsica, France. “You cannot stop a thunderstorm, and neither can you stop a firestorm, a strong pyrocumulonimbus.”

Alongside huge blazes in Spain, France has been suffering a wildfire in the Gironde region, which President Emmanuel Macron has called the country’s most severe crisis since the second world war. The fire has burned more than 420 square kilometres since last week, coming within 15 kilometres of the city of Bordeaux and forcing around 220,000 people to evacuate. It generated a pyrocumulonimbus cloud on 24 July and another on 25 July, according to regional officials. Embers and lightning ignited new fires around the original inferno.

Advertisement

“We faced another firestorm, the same incredible, unprecedented, unknown phenomenon as the one we saw on Friday, when we realised we were entering a new dimension,” Gironde prefect Sophie Brocas told journalists.

It is a miracle this pyrocumulonimbus-fuelled fire hasn’t claimed any casualties, Filippi says.

Sometimes called the “fire-breathing dragon of clouds”, pyrocumulonimbus are typically generated by massive wildfires in the forests of North America, Siberia and Australia. They’ve spurred on infamous fires like the Black Saturday bushfires that killed 173 people in Australia in 2009 and the conflagration that razed the Canadian oil city of Fort McMurray in 2016. Canada’s record-breaking wildfires in 2023 generated 142 of these storms.

In Europe, however, there have been only a handful of confirmed pyrocumulonimbus in Spain and Portugal, including one during Portugal’s devastating Pedrógão Grande fire in 2017, which destroyed hundreds of homes and killed 66 people. But that appears to be changing.

“You have to have two things happening at the same time: an extreme heat source and an unstable atmosphere that interacts with the fire,” says Francesca Di Giuseppe at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. “If… the heat from the fire increases, like it’s projected to increase from our studies, then yes, you should see more of these events.”

This firestorm begins to take shape when temperatures as high as 800°C send a plume of smoke into the sky. As the hot air rises and cools, water vapour condenses onto the ash to form pyrocumulus clouds, like the fluffy white clouds you might see on a summer day, only brown or grey.

If the plume is hot enough and the atmosphere is unstable enough, the cloud can keep rising to reach the upper troposphere at 10,000 metres, the cruising altitude of a passenger plane. It sometimes reaches the stratosphere, spreading as much smoke as a moderate volcano. It becomes a pyrocumulonimbus when the static electricity from colliding ice particles sparks thunder and lightning.

Although rain from the cloud often evaporates in the hot air, this kind of thunderstorm nonetheless creates its own weather system. The cloud’s updraft pulls in air, fanning the flames with winds reaching 160 kilometres per hour and accelerating the fire’s spread by up to five times, according to Filippi.

Meanwhile, strong downdrafts create erratic gusts that carry embers off to start new fires. Dozens of lightning strikes can ignite blazes as far as 100 kilometres ahead of the main fire. It can also create fire tornadoes of twisting flames. As the winds, embers and lightning strengthen and expand the wildfire, it releases more heat and smoke, a feedback loop that can amplify the rising cloud for many hours.

Both wind shear higher in the atmosphere and erratic gusts at the ground can take the fire in unpredictable directions, making it nearly impossible to contain its acceleration or plan targeted evacuations.

“The fire front is constantly shifting. We cannot fight it directly. It’s a David-versus-Goliath scenario,” Eric Brocardi of the National Firefighters Federation of France told local media about the Gironde fire on 2 August.

Wildfire plumes have expanded in height since 2003 in the western US, creating more pyrocumulonimbus clouds, an increase that’s projected to continue.

Pyrocumulonimbus will have more chances to occur in Europe as well, as the fastest-warming continent experiences more extreme heat, such as the record-breaking heatwave in June, and wildfires. Increasing “climate whiplash” could also contribute, such as when a wet spring last year boosted vegetation growth on the Iberian peninsula, only for record summer heat to dry it out. This led to Europe’s worst-ever wildfires, including a pyrocumulonimbus fire in Spain.

“We need to adapt, so get prepared,” Filippi says. “Burn-proof and reduce the amount of fuel around your house.”

A new kind of drug will help fight previously untreatable conditions

New Scientist July 28, 2026

I think we will look back at 2026 as a landmark in medicine, the year in which the first protac drug was approved. What’s special about protacs? Well, while most drugs simply block their targets, protacs utterly demolish them. Per molecule, protacs are far more potent, and they can also do things other drugs just can’t.

To put it in sporting terms, existing drugs tackle their opponents one-on-one, and sometimes that opponent evades them. Protacs are like a referee who red-cards an entire team, taking them off the field altogether – a game changer.

We may finally have a cure for many different autoimmune conditions

I first got excited about protacs in 2005 when I was a features editor at New Scientist, and promptly commissioned a piece about them. At that time, it was far from clear whether a brilliant idea could be turned into practical drugs, so it’s fantastic to see decades of hard work finally bearing fruit.

Advertisement

To understand why protacs are so revolutionary, we need to start with conventional drugs. Almost all the pills you pop – ibuprofen, say – contain drugs that consist of small molecules. The shape of these molecules allows them to bind to specific proteins, to block or stimulate them. For instance, ibuprofen binds to and inhibits enzymes that produce chemicals that promote inflammation.

Small-molecule drugs have some big advantages. They’re cheap to make, can get inside cells and can be taken as a pill because they can also pass through the gut lining and into the bloodstream. But their small size means they’re not that specific. They tend to bind to other molecules besides the one they are supposed to target and thus have undesirable side effects.

And in many cases, it simply isn’t possible to find a small molecule to block the activity of a protein. The issue is that each drug molecule can’t just bind to any part of a target protein. To have an effect, it must bind to the active site of the protein – the workface – but sometimes small parts of the active site don’t have a distinctive enough shape. Such proteins are referred to as undruggable.

That’s why many newer drugs consist of large molecules, most commonly proteins known antibodies. (Any drug whose name ends in “-ab” is an antibody.) The large size of antibodies means they can bind to targets with exquisite precision, making them highly effective and safer. To create them, you get immune cells to generate antibodies to the desired target and then pick the best one. It sounds easy, but it took many decades to perfect.

Free newsletter

The downside of antibodies is that they are really expensive because they can be made only in living cells. Their large size also means they must be injected because they can’t get through the gut. Nor can they get into cells once they’re in the bloodstream. So, while antibodies could bind to many undruggable proteins, they can’t get into cells to reach them.

The other thing to mention is that both small-molecule drugs and antibodies must be in contact with the target to work – the one-on-one part I mentioned above. Protacs work differently. Essentially, they stick a “recycle me” label on a protein in a cell. That means just one protac molecule can label and get rid of tens or hundreds of molecules of that protein. And because they’re not blocking or stimulating the target protein, they don’t have to bind to the active site. Anywhere on the target will do, making many undruggable targets druggable.

Craig Crews and Raymond Deshaies came up with the idea for protacs when they met at a conference in 1998. They knew that cells have waste disposal factories, called proteasomes, that break down and recycle faulty or excess proteins. They also knew that the “recycle me” label on proteins consists of a short chain of ubiquitin molecules. Add this label to a disease-causing protein and the proteasome will destroy it.

CAR T-cell therapy takes woman from bedridden to ‘perfectly fine’

But how? The “recycle me” labels are usually added to specific proteins by enzymes known as E3 ubiquitin ligases. Maybe it could be done by bringing an E3 ligase into close contact with the target protein by creating a molecule that binds to both, Crews and Deshaies speculated.

Within a few years, they had shown the answer was yes, it works. They called their creations proteolysis targeting chimeras, or protacs – the proteolysis bit of the name refers to the destruction of proteins, and the chimera bit to the fact that protacs are made by joining two parts that each bind to a different thing.

The first protacs were an academic exercise, Crews told me in 2020. The molecules were so large they had to be injected into cells – a non-starter for a drug.

In 2008, Crews set out to create small-molecule protacs. This is a challenge because each protac must bind to two molecules – the target protein and an E3 ligase – whereas conventional small-molecule drugs need bind only to one. While he succeeded in making protacs small enough to behave like small molecules, they are still somewhat larger than conventional drugs. “I call them large small-molecules,” he told me last week.

By 2013, Crews was confident enough to found a company called Arvinas. For its first products, Arvinas played it safe. Rather than going for undruggable proteins, it targeted hormone receptors in cancer cells. For instance, the growth of some types of breast cancer is driven by receptors that respond to oestrogen. There are already several drugs that work by targeting these receptors, but resistance can develop.

One way that cancers become resistant is by making more receptors, until even the highest tolerable drug doses can’t block all the receptor molecules – the one-on-one problem. “Since we’re actively degrading the receptor, we don’t have that limitation,” Crews said in 2020. In trials, people with advanced breast cancer that had spread around the body survived more than twice as long when given the protac drug vepdegestrant, compared with those given a conventional drug. As a result, vepdegestrant was approved by the US Food and Drug Administration in May.

“The approval is a milestone for the field,” says Crews. There was already huge interest in the idea of targeted protein degradation, with around 100 companies working on it and around 80 trials under way, he says. The approval will boost this even further. Increasingly, companies are starting to target undruggable proteins, too.

All sorts of variations on protacs are also being explored. For instance, simply linking two proteins together with a protac-type molecule can be a powerful tool. Crews himself recently developed “riptacs”, or regulated induced proximity targeting chimeras. Riptacs link a protein abundant in cancer cells to a protein essential for cell survival, blocking the function of both and killing the malignant cells. Riptacs performed so well in an initial trial against prostate cancer that US pharmaceutical firm Johnson & Johnson acquired the technology.

Of course, protacs are far from the only game in town. There are now a bunch of approaches based on stopping proteins being made in the first place, including CRISPR gene editing and epigenetic editing. These techniques are very promising, too, but they have limitations. For instance, delivery is a major challenge because of the large molecules involved. Nor do they get rid of existing proteins, says Crews, which can be important. “We’ve been able to show that a protac can degrade half of a protein population [in a cell] within 2 hours.”

So, I’m hopeful we will be seeing all kinds of new treatment based on protacs, ultimately helping billions of us. The approval of vepdegestrant may have received barely a headline, but if it is indeed the first of many, we will look back at it as a major milestone.

Peptides are the latest wellness trend – but do they work?

New Scientist July 27, 2026

Peptides are everywhere, so much so that wellness spas, massage parlours, chiropractor offices and rehabilitation clinics, particularly in the US but also in countries like the UK, are offering peptide injections.

Your body changes as you age and so should your diet – here’s how

Proponents claim peptides can help combat ageing, heal injuries, dampen inflammation, accelerate weight loss and treat a seemingly endless list of conditions, from osteoporosis to opioid withdrawal. There is little robust evidence to back up these claims, but that hasn’t stemmed people’s penchant for peptides. Estimates suggest the unregulated market for peptides is a $100 million to $3 billion industry.

“Because there’s no regulation, it’s like a free-for-all,” says Alexander Weber at the University of Southern California. “It’s like the Wild West right now.” That was part of the impetus behind what I found to be a shocking decision by an advisory committee to the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA). In a series of close votes, it recommended the agency lift regulations on several experimental peptides. Doing so would allow select pharmacies to manufacture the compounds and permit doctors to prescribe them.

Advertisement

On the one hand, this mitigates the risks associated with buying these products on the unregulated market. On the other, it sends the unfounded message that these compounds have been demonstrated to be safe and effective.

“What this announcement did, if anything, was increase the visibility of the peptide world,” says Changhan David Lee at the University of Southern California.

Once relegated to the fringes of the wellness movement, peptides now seem to be here to stay – and could cause unintended harm if they aren’t rigorously tested and regulated.

So how did we get here? Interest in peptides dates to the 1920s, when insulin became the first commercial peptide drug. Identifying and characterising peptides was a challenge, however, because of their small size. Most researchers define them as having fewer than 100 amino acids – the building blocks of proteins – whereas the FDA classifies them as having no more than 40. Compare that with the average human protein, which consists of 400 to 500 amino acids.

Detecting and analysing peptides became much easier about 25 years ago thanks to technological advances such as improved genetic sequencing. This opened a new biological frontier, says Lee. Nearly 2.3 million research papers mentioning peptides have been published since 2000 – double the number seen in the 20th century. In the past decade alone, the FDA has approved more than 40 peptide drugs for therapeutic use, one of which, semaglutide, has proven revolutionary. It is the main ingredient in medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which have transformed the treatment of obesity and type 2 diabetes. “[They] were a big step in the peptide space,” says Weber. They also propelled peptides into the mainstream.

Online retailers now ship them directly to doors across the US, UK, Canada and European Union, among other places. But most of these peptides aren’t approved drugs – they are experimental compounds meant only for research purposes, says Weber. This puts them in a regulatory grey zone. Because the FDA hasn’t yet deemed the compounds safe and effective, doctors can’t prescribe them as medications. Yet they can still be bought and sold legally, so long as the supplier doesn’t make any health claims about them. It is a situation comparable to vitamins and supplements. Similar grey areas exist for peptides in the UK and EU.

One of the glaring drawbacks of this set-up is the risk of contamination. “When substances aren’t regulated by the FDA, those companies could put, either knowingly or unknowingly, whatever they want into that bottle,” says Weber. A New Yorker article published in April found that some peptides purchased through one online retailer contained lead, signs of bacterial contamination or a significantly smaller dose than advertised.

This is probably one of the justifications for the FDA advisory committee’s decision. It recommended the agency add six experimental peptides – BPC-157, KPV, TB-500, MOTs-C, Semax and epitalon – to its compounding list, rejecting only one, emideltide. Unlike most medications, compounded products are made to order at select pharmacies, usually due to drug shortages or allergies.

Free newsletter

The recommendations passed on slim majorities. The week before the meeting, the US Department of Health and Human Services (HHS), which oversees the FDA, nominated eight new committee members, six of whom had ties to the peptide industry. “All committee members underwent the same ethics review and vetting process required of all FDA advisory committee members,” an HHS spokesperson told Reuters.

If the FDA accepts the committee’s recommendation, it would allow select pharmacies – which adhere to standards around product integrity, safety and purity – to manufacture the compounds. This would bring these six peptides under some regulatory purview. “We do not protect the patient by pushing them into the dark,” said committee member Haleem Mohammed – chief medical officer at Gameday Men’s Health, which offers peptides – during the meeting.

However, such a move would also lend each of these peptides an air of credibility. “Consumers will assume it is safe and effective,” says Weber, even though that hasn’t been established in clinical research.

How ultra-processed foods may damage your long-term brain health

In fact, none of these peptides has been tested in a scientifically rigorous way, with clinical trials involving a large number of participants, a control group and clear methods for evaluating efficacy. “There are no clinical trials, no clinical studies on the efficacy and safety of their use in humans,” says Weber. “Period. Full stop. End of story.”

Instead, most research comes from animal studies. For instance, Lee and his colleagues have found that MOTs-C, a peptide released naturally during exercise, can help regulate blood sugar and prevent obesity in mice. It can also improve speed and endurance in the animals. They are now evaluating whether it could delay age-related conditions, including Alzheimer’s, heart disease and cancer. But these studies are a far cry from the rigorous trials needed to determine its efficacy in humans.

There is also the question of side effects. TB-500 seems to accelerate tissue regeneration, helping it heal wounds in animals. But Weber says this ability may also spur cancer growth – a risk that has yet to be evaluated, even in animals.

Having a young biological age could help with weight loss

It also isn’t clear how these peptides should be administered. “What strength should you use? What frequency? How long do you cycle on and off? None of these things have been elucidated as to what is most effective,” says Weber.

It is possible that easing manufacturing restrictions on these peptides could accelerate research into their effects. But in the meantime, people will be treating themselves as guinea pigs.

The FDA compiled research on all seven peptides for the committee to review during its meeting. Briefs for each peptide conclude that there isn’t sufficient evidence to support them being added to the compounding list. Although the committee disagrees, the decision ultimately rests with the FDA. “Whatever the outcome is, one thing is for sure: research really needs to accelerate on all these peptides,” says Lee.

Mystery hominin left big footprints at ancient lake in Africa

New Scientist July 27, 2026

Footprints left by eight ancient hominins 1.43 million years ago beside a Kenyan lake have puzzled researchers because they don’t look quite as expected for species known to have lived there at that time.

Altogether, 21 hominin footprints have been found at the Lake Turkana site, known to researchers as GaJi10, part of which was first discovered in 1978.

How did Paranthropus, the last of the ape-people, survive for so long?

The tracks were made on what would have been mud in shallow water, between 2 and 10 centimetres deep, at the edge of the lake.

Advertisement

Fossil remains and other footprints discovered nearby and studied over many decades suggest there were two hominin species co-existing in the area: Homo erectus and Paranthropus boisei.

P. boisei, nicknamed “nutcracker man”, was a more ape-like hominin with a small body but large jaws and teeth.

Free newsletter

The shape of the footprints look similar to others made by P. boisei, but they are considerably larger. Previous estimates have suggested the largest members of the species were just over 160 centimetres tall, but analysis of the new footprints indicates that if they were made by P. boisei, they must have been over 180 centimetres tall.

While the tracks fit within the size range of the other species known from the area, H. erectus, the shape doesn’t.

“If these footprints are Paranthropus boisei, then they really increase the upper limits of body size in that species,” says Kevin Hatala at Chatham University in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, who worked on the study.

“If they are H. erectus, then they would imply that species has a range of variation in footprint morphology that far exceeds what we’ve observed in large samples of modern humans.”

The footprints have flatter arches and a big toe that is more angled away from the other toes, characteristics similar to other sets of prints in the area identified as P. boisei.

“Both of these features differ from what we usually see in modern humans, and that led us to hypothesise that footprints with that shape were more likely made by P. boisei,” he says. “We’ve also seen other footprints with human-like arches and human-like big toes, and we believe those were more likely made by H. erectus.”

The remarkable tale of how humans nearly didn’t conquer the world

The third possibility is that the footprints represent a different species. But that seems unlikely, says Hatala, since many fossils are known from this area and time period and have all been attributed to either P. boisei or H. erectus.

Whichever species left the tracks, the height of the group means that it probably consisted of males travelling together.

At around the same time as the hominins passed through, numerous other animals also walked across the same stretch of mudflats. They included two species of hippopotamus, as well as bovids, birds and equids – a scene not unlike what a visitor would see today in a modern African lakeshore environment.

“The presence of many hippos also indicates that this environment included some real dangers to the hominins, and that whatever brought them to the lakeshore – maybe they were seeking water or food – must have been worth the risk,” says Hatala.

PNAS DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2530996123

Getting a bit more gas from the North Sea doesn’t matter climate-wise

New Scientist July 27, 2026

I’m terrified by how fast weather extremes are ramping up as the world heats up, and there’s much, much worse to come unless we leave fossil fuels in the ground. The only way to do that is to end our dependency on oil and gas – and all the fuss about whether the UK will allow more drilling in the North Sea is a distraction from this.

Some people talk about the UK government’s current policy of not approving more licences for exploration in the North Sea as if it will reduce the amount of oil and gas that is burned, and thus help limit how much more carbon dioxide ends up in the atmosphere. But it won’t. All it will do is change where the oil and gas that gets burned comes from.

Solar energy is going to power the world much sooner than you think

What does matter is burning less fossil fuel. That means things such as getting more electricity from renewable sources, and more vehicles and heat pumps running on that electricity.

Advertisement

So I won’t be judging the climate credentials of the UK’s new prime minister, Andy Burnham, on whether or not his government decides to allow more drilling in the North Sea. It’s what is done to further reduce our use of fossil fuels that’s crucial in climate terms. And here Burnham has already made a good start by cutting the value-added tax (VAT) on electricity, which will make swapping gas boilers for heat pumps more appealing.

I’m not saying bans on drilling are a complete waste of time – they have a part to play in protecting vulnerable environments, such as the Amazon rainforest. But I don’t see how they will ever help limit emissions.

Free newsletter

At this point, you might be thinking, “but if enough countries ban drilling, it will make a difference”. There are already nearly 60 restrictions on fossil fuel production in 25 countries, according to the International Institute for Sustainable Development. But many of these are regional restrictions to protect places such as the Arctic, or bans on production methods such as fracking. And 15 have already been repealed. No major producers are planning to completely stop producing oil and gas, and the known reserves of fossil fuels are way more than enough to trash the climate. The bottom line is that some countries will keep on churning out fossil fuels as long as they can sell them, so the key is to reduce demand, not supply.

That said, most of the arguments used by supporters of further North Sea gas and oil exploration are false or misleading. For starters, more drilling is not going to bring down energy prices in the UK. North Sea oil and gas is sold at global market prices, and there’s not enough oil or gas left in the North Sea to make a dent in those prices.

Going all out on renewables, by contrast, would break the link between gas prices and electricity prices, and help bring down energy bills. This is what is Spain is succeeding in doing.

Another dubious claim is that more drilling is going to make oodles of money for the UK. But production in the North Sea already has to be supported by tax breaks and subsidies, and is declining year on year. More than 90 per cent of the oil and gas has already been extracted, so further drilling will, at most, slow the rate of decline. And what remains is harder to get out, so costs are higher. If the wars pushing up oil prices come to an end, it might not even be profitable – until recently, the world was building up a massive surplus of oil.

The secret weapon that could finally force climate action

Then there’s the exaggerated claim that North Sea gas is “four times cleaner” than imported liquid natural gas, or LNG. The emissions associated with producing LNG are around four times higher than those for North Sea gas, because of the energy required to liquefy it. But what matters are the total emissions, including those from burning the gas, and on this count North Sea gas emissions are only 15 per cent lower than those from LNG.

LNG now accounts for more than half of the gas imported by the UK. If that could be reduced by more North Sea gas production, there should be a little less CO2 emitted. It would also mean less money going to countries that obstruct climate action – the UK now gets 37 per cent of its gas from the US, for instance.

But the UK also gets gas from Norway via pipelines, and the production emissions of this are even lower than those of North Sea gas. So in climate terms, buying more Norwegian pipeline gas would be better than increasing North Sea production.

Overall, then, what happens in the North Sea just doesn’t matter much in the grand scheme of things – more drilling is neither a climate catastrophe, nor an economic panacea. Instead, the UK and other countries need to focus on what really matters – much more drastic action to replace fossil fuels or discourage their use. You only need to look at what’s happening in France and Spain to see why it’s so vital.

We’ve found the best example yet of an enormous wandering black hole

New Scientist July 27, 2026

Every massive galaxy astronomers have ever seen has a supermassive black hole at its centre. Some, though, ought to have so-called wandering supermassive black holes closer to their outskirts, too, and researchers have just spotted the most extreme example ever found.

True to their names, black holes don’t emit light, so Robert Stein at the University of Maryland and his team spotted this one only when it devoured a star in what’s known as a tidal disruption event, or TDE. A machine learning algorithm identified the burst of light as a possible TDE in data from the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) in California, and the researchers performed follow-up observations with several other telescopes to confirm it.

This TDE, called TDE 2025abcr, is the most distant from the centre of its host galaxy that we’ve ever seen. “We have a couple of examples of a tidal disruption event that’s very close to the centre of a galaxy but a little offset, and then we have examples where there’s a big galaxy and a little dwarf galaxy merging with it, and that dwarf galaxy has a TDE. This is just an empty patch of sky as far as we can tell,” says Stein. It is more than 30,000 light years from the centre of its galaxy – for comparison, our solar system is about 26,000 light years from the centre of the Milky Way.

Advertisement

We now know how a black hole can be flung across the universe

Wandering supermassive black holes usually begin their journeys away from a galactic centre due to a merger: two galaxies slam together, and one of their central black holes is flung away. Finding these black holes can tell us about the history and growth of their galaxies. “What’s exciting about this result is that we think it’s the tip of the iceberg,” says Stein. “If we can understand how many wandering supermassive black holes there are, then it can tell us about how many mergers the galaxy has been through and how it’s evolved over time.”

Black holes’ dark nature means that it is extremely difficult to find them; it is mostly accomplished by projects like ZTF that monitor the whole sky for flashes of light. The latest of these projects, the Legacy Survey of Space and Time (LSST) at the Vera Rubin Observatory in Chile, has just begun and is expected to find hundreds more in the coming years, Stein says.

Subscriber-only newsletter

In the meantime, there is a limit to how much we can learn about this particular black hole and its environs. The light from the star being devoured is still too bright to see much of anything else around it. “Some TDEs can last for years and years, so we might have to wait a long time to uncover what’s really going on here,” says Stein.

Most likely there is a small cluster of stars that is gravitationally tied to the black hole, and one of those caused the TDE as it fell in, but we can’t confirm that until the light fades. At least we don’t have to worry about black holes lurking near Earth, because the sun isn’t in such a cluster, Stein says: “I think it’s very, very unlikely that this is going to happen to our star.”

The Astrophysical Journal Letters DOI: 10.3847/2041-8213/ae77f3

David Tamihere, who was until recently one of the nation’s highest-profile double-murder convicts, returned to the High Court at Auckland today, four months after the Supreme Court quashed his convictions.

During a brief, routine pre-trial hearing attended by an unusually large contingent of media and documentary crew, Crown solicitor Alysha McClintock asked for an eight-week extension to determine whether a retrial will be sought over the deaths of Swedish tourists Sven Urban Hoglin and Heidi Birgitta Paakkonen.

The couple were last seen alive together in 1989 on the Coromandel Peninsula.

Justice Mathew Downs approved the Crown’s request to delay the decision, ordering the parties to return to court on October 7.

The Crown has been evaluating the file since March, when the Supreme Court found Tamihere’s 1990 trial to have been unfair - based partly on evidence that was “concocted to secure convictions”.

The nation’s highest court also found that the Crown’s later theories of what happened to the couple have never been tested in front of a jury.

Tamihere, now in his early 70s, has already served 20 years in prison.

He admitted before his trial that he stole the couple’s car and sold or dumped their possessions. But he insisted he had never met the backpackers.

His convictions were based in part on evidence from a fellow remand prisoner who, many years later, was discredited and prosecuted for perjury.

Hoglin’s remains were found in the bush by pig-hunters in 1991, many kilometres away from where they should have been if the prosecution’s theories were correct. Paakkonen’s remains have never been found.

Tamihere has always maintained his innocence, even after his release from prison in 2010. The case was reviewed twice by the Court of Appeal before the Supreme Court decision.

Craig Kapitan is an Auckland-based journalist covering courts and justice. He joined the Herald in 2021 and has reported on courts since 2002 in three newsrooms in the US and New Zealand.

Damian Spring, Executive Director and CEO of Santana Minerals. Photo / Santana Minerals.

Santana Minerals has spent more than $17 million pursuing fast-track approval for its proposed Central Otago gold mine after agreeing to a revised timetable requested by the expert panel considering the application.

The company told shareholders on Monday it had invested about $17.7m in costs associated with its Bendigo-Ophir Gold Project fast-track application, including environmental investigations, legal advice, cultural assessments and regulatory fees.

The update comes after the expert panel assessing the application asked Santana to revise the timetable to better align with the submission of the project’s final consent conditions.

The Environmental Protection Authority said processing of the application was due to resume on August 17, while the applicant had initially been expected to provide final workshopped consent conditions on September 11.

In Minute 41, the panel said it could “only confidently move into its assessment phase” once it had received “the most refined, robust and workable version of the conditions”.

It asked the applicant to reconsider its proposed timetable because the original dates would have left “very tight timeframes” for the panel to assess the application, prepare its decision and complete the statutory notification process.

The EPA said Matakanui Gold, the Santana subsidiary behind the application, had now indicated it would submit the final workshopped consent conditions by August 28 instead of September 11, giving the panel adequate time to incorporate them into its decision-making.

Santana said it would not seek any further pauses in the application process.

The company said it had spent about $10.1m on environmental, technical and supplementary forensic investigations, $4.7m on legal, planning and specialist advisory services, $1.9m on expert panel, Environmental Protection Authority, hearing and regulatory assessment fees, and $1m on cultural values work.

Chief executive Damian Spring said the panel had made it clear the revised timetable reflected the time needed to complete its statutory assessment and decision-making process.

“The project continues to advance through the Fast-track process, and the finalisation of consent conditions in August will allow the panel to move into substantive deliberations on its decision,” Spring said.

He said the company remained confident the project was well positioned to receive approval and, subject to consents, begin development early next year.

The proposed Bendigo-Ophir gold mine near Cromwell is among the highest-profile projects being considered under the Government’s fast-track consenting regime.

Since lodging its application, Santana said it had taken part in public hearings, 24 multidisciplinary expert conferences, multiple rounds of requests for further information, expert workshops and additional technical investigations as the assessment progressed.

How researchers say we could make New Zealanders richer

New Zealand Herald July 28, 2026

Improving your financial literacy could make you 25% more wealthy. Photo / RNZ

By Susan Edmunds of RNZ

There could be a simple way to make some New Zealanders 25% more wealthy, new research suggests – make them more financially literate.

AUT professor Bart Frijns has co-authored research looking at the long-term impact of financial literacy on wealth.

He said it sought to examine whether financial literacy was a cause or a consequence of financial success.

“Very often what we see is that people that are wealthier tend to be more financially literate but that’s simply because they have more money and therefore invest more in financial literacy.

“What we really wanted to figure out is, is there a really clear relationship between improvement in financial literacy and then better financial outcomes later in life?”

He used longitudinal data on Dutch households and connected financial literacy measured in 2011 with financial outcomes in 2019 for 475 individuals.

People were asked questions about the conception of inflation, diversification and other basic financial literacy questions.

“It’s a good proxy for what people know about money,” he said.

Frijns said the results were striking.

“An increase in financial literacy led to a 12% increase in income and a significant impact on savings as well, on wealth accumulation by 25%.

“There’s definitely a push from the literacy to becoming better off.

“A push from literacy into financial success but it also shows those people that invested in financial literacy in 2011 were still benefiting from that financial literacy eight years on.”

He said a one-point increase in financial literacy in 2011 was observed to lead to annual income increases of €4644 (about $7900 or a 12% increase relative to the average income in the sample), and savings increased by €12,540 ($21,000 or a 25% increase relative to the average savings in the sample).

He said it aligned with predictions that up to 40% of wealth inequality at retirement could be due to differences in financial knowledge.

He said the research also showed differences in how financial literacy was used.

Younger people tended to earn higher incomes when they were financially literate while older people were more likely to accumulate more savings.

“This suggests that people apply financial knowledge in ways that reflect their changing financial priorities over the life course. As a result, financial education may be most effective when tailored to specific life stages.

“Programmes aimed at younger people could focus on career development, income growth and early financial decision-making, whereas programmes for older adults may be better directed towards retirement planning and wealth accumulation.”

There were gender differences, though that did not bode as well for women.

The researchers found that while financial literacy had strong associations with higher income and savings among men, there were no significant relationships for women.

Frijns said the results suggested that gender differences may extend beyond financial literacy levels themselves.

They said that could be because traditional gender roles, unequal influence over household finances, labour market inequalities and other factors could be limiting how much women could turn their knowledge into decisions.

Previous research has consistently shown that women report lower levels of financial literacy than men.

He said the experience was likely to be similar in New Zealand.

“I don’t see a reason why you would expect different results in the relationship between financial literacy and wellbeing … I think it’s an important discussion for New Zealand.”

He said the results supported Government initiatives for financial literacy education in schools.

“That financial education is likely better targeted at maximising income, as our results show that is how young adults use their financial knowledge.”

He said it was also important for KiwiSaver.

“One could think about what this could mean for KiwiSaver balances if New Zealanders were provided with more targeted financial literacy education on their retirement savings.

“Finally, with average household debt at 90.6% of GDP, compared with the United Kingdom at 73.9% and the United States at 68%, improved financial literacy may result in better debt management strategies.

“Based on our findings that a one-point increase in financial literacy leads to a 25% increase in savings and the theoretical predictions that differences in financial knowledge can lead to a 30% to 40% wealth gap at retirement, improving financial literacy of those with the lowest financial knowledge could help close this gap.

“For all New Zealanders the message is clear: learning about and understanding your finances can lead to substantial improvements in wealth.”

Agricultural science underpins productivity, exports and economic growth - Dr Jacqueline Rowarth

New Zealand Herald July 28, 2026

Investing in the economic engine, the primary sector, is vital, writes Dr Jacqueline Rowarth. Photo / 123rf

THE FACTS

Agriculture is the bulk of the export economy.

It brings new money into the country (as does borrowing), which then circulates throughout businesses, from rural areas to the cities.

When money changes hands through spending, it creates income for someone else, who then spends it again.

Keynesian economics explains that this continuous cycle drives economic growth and keeps the economy expanding.

Without that new money, the pool already in the country will get smaller as Kiwis sell things to each other, paying taxes at each transaction (which gives income to the Government to invest in education, health, science and infrastructure) and saving a portion (or not, as the case might be).

John Keynes’ theory (termed the paradox of thrift) was that too much saving would result in decreased consumer demand, leading to reduced business revenues, redundancies and economic recession.

New money is important.

Hence agriculture is important.

Soare the science and research that underpins it, enabling New Zealand farmers and growers to adapt, increase productivity, and compete on the global market.

Last October, Pew Research Centre published the results of a survey involving more than 5000 respondents asking United States adults how much they thought people in 12 diverse occupations rely on an understanding of science to do their jobs.

The results indicated that Americans most closely associate biologists (97% of adults) and engineers (96%) with science: these professionals rely a lot or some on an understanding of science to do their jobs.

For farming, 94% of people recognise that farmers need a lot or some understanding of science to do their work properly.

Science for agriculture is important.

The new funding strategy for the science system makes this clear, and agriculture can fit into all four of the new investment pillars: Primary Industries and Bioeconomy, Technology for Prosperity, Environmental Sustainability and Resilience and Healthy People and a Thriving Society.

But with investment in science by the Government lagging well behind the OECD average, shifting the limited funds from productivity and environment to new technologies brings with it many risks.

The problem is that some of the advanced technologies rely on what is increasingly being recognised as old data.

The implication is that the promised returns might not materialise, and New Zealand farmers and growers could be misled about the most appropriate actions to take.

Research is showing that the predicted relationship between carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, warming temperatures and increased plant growth is not being seen in the paddock or plantation.

In an article published in the Journal (New Zealand Institute of Primary Industry Managers) last year, Rethinking the Assumption of Long Term CO2 Fertilisation, scientists Mike Dodd, Alec Mackay and Peter Clinton (all now members of the Bioeconomy Science Institute), stated that: “Despite generally optimistic future productivity improvement projections from rising atmospheric CO₂ concentration, long-term field studies of New Zealand’s two most important primary sector plant species – perennial ryegrass and radiata pine – show stagnant or declining productivity, the reasons for which are still unclear”.

Basic research is required to sort out the cause, to ensure future investments are targeted to drive appropriate solutions and avoid solutions that will prove maladaptive.

A recent parallel has been exposed in biomedical research where authors concluded: “This study is another wake-up call for biomedical research. If we don’t fully understand the genetics of the mice we’re using, we risk misinterpreting how diseases actually work.”

New Zealand’s new Public Research Organisations need enough funding to ensure critical mass of researchers in critical areas.

In biology, research indicates 21 people are needed to make progress on a project; in agricultural science, 10 people are needed.

A new way of thinking for research in New Zealand would be to have critical focus (larger teams) on the biological aspects in the BSI, with smaller groups involved as the research moves into the field for production testing.

This might be with the farmer levy-funded research.

The results could then be taken to the farmer by the levy body extension officers.

Areas of responsibility need identifying before more sandpit struggles for funding occur with money and time evaporating.

Further, the money should be targeted towards scientists with a track record in the appropriate area.

These are the scientists who have proved that they know what they are doing and where investment will achieve returns.

The authors of the Journal paper concluded that, “Given the value of the perennial pasture and radiata pine sectors to New Zealand’s economy, environment and society, any threat to the biological economy engine must be rigorously investigated and mitigated”.

More research is necessary; it always is, and so is more funding.

Investing in the economic engine, the primary sector, is vital.

- Dr Jacqueline Rowarth, Adjunct Professor Lincoln University, is a farmer-elected director of DairyNZ and Ravensdown. She is also a member of the Scientific Council of the World Farmers’ Organisation.

Pegasus Golf Course fast-track bid for 1000 homes lodged

New Zealand Herald July 28, 2026

The former Pegasus Golf Course was bought in a mortgagee sale by property developer Wolfbrook in May 2026. Photo / Anna Heath

A highly anticipated and controversial fast-track application has been lodged, proposing to build up to 1000 homes on a former championship golf course in North Canterbury.

Wolfbrook Property’s bid to transform the former Pegasus Golf Course has been met with staunch resistance from the Pegasus residents’ group, who presented a 16,000-strong petition to Parliament last week.

The proposed Pegasus West Development would require the 77.66ha property to be rezoned from a Special Purpose Zone to residential.

The Fast-track Approvals Act 2024 offers a permanent process for obtaining resource consents and a wide range of other approvals. According to the government website, “Fast-track brings these together into a streamlined process”.

The process is limited to infrastructure, housing and development projects with significant regional or national benefits. It involves all relevant authorities – but only as submitters, not decision makers.

The Minister for Infrastructure decides if projects are eligible for referral to the Fast-track pathway.

If so, the applicant can lodge a substantive application. Expert panels then consider applications before determining whether projects are approved or declined. Decisions can be appealed on points of law to the High Court.

As of February, the fast-track process was taking an average of 128 days for decisions to be made on substantive applications from when officials determine an application is complete and in-scope.

The golf course is believed to have been purchased for around $7 million and industry-led estimates suggest a residential rezoning could increase that value to around $400m.

Among the opposition to the course’s proposed conversion is cricketing great Sir Richard Hadlee, a long-time resident and first official member of the Pegasus Golf Club. Local member of Parliament for Waimakariri, Matt Doocey, has also publicly opposed the developer’s plans.

Former Bay of Plenty regional councillor Doug Owens’ latest court battle with Tauranga Marina Society

New Zealand Herald July 28, 2026

Former Bay of Plenty regional councillor Doug Owens has failed in his bid to have the Tauranga Marina Society liquidated, ahead of judicial review proceedings that Owens has also brought against the society.

The uncle of Tauranga Mayor Mahé Drysdale attempted to have the Tauranga Marina Society liquidated, in his ongoing battle with the society and Tauranga City Council over the marina’s operations.

Doug Owens, a former Bay of Plenty regional councillor who ran for Tauranga Mayor in the last election, made an application for liquidation, alleging the society has been “paying members for berth licences sold or surrendered to the society”, unlawfully allowing members to derive “financial gains”.

The society denies there are grounds for liquidation, and a judge has agreed there is “no suggestion that the society is insolvent”.

The society asked for the liquidation proceedings to be struck out as an abuse of process, as matters they referred to would be addressed in the judicial review Owens initiated in 2024.

Alternatively, the society sought a stay of the liquidation proceeding and an order restraining the trust from advertising the liquidation proceeding.

Associate Judge Grant Brittain, KC, agreed to stay the liquidation proceeding so the judicial review could be heard first.

“These issues are interrelated with other issues in respect of the berth holder licences that arise in the judicial review proceeding,” he said.

Associate Judge Brittain said it would be sensible for the trial judge in the judicial review to determine all related issues, and it would be an “inefficient use of judicial resources” to have two proceedings.

Owens – son of the late Sir Bob Owens, who was a Mayor of Tauranga Council and Mount Maunganui Borough Council in the 1970s and 1980s – owns a ketch that is moored at the marina.

He is a trustee of the Nereides Trust, which has a licence to occupy the berth, granted by the society.

As a dissatisfied member of the society, the trust initiated a judicial review of its operations, then separately sought an order for its liquidation.

The trust claims the society has been allowing berth holders to profit by selling their berth licences and this goes against section 22(1) of the Incorporated Societies Act 2022, which says that “a society must not be carried on for the financial gain of any of its members”.

It’s claimed that the continued dealing in berths “threatens [the society’s] financial liability”, because it “has paid for berth licences it cannot lawfully hold”.

Owens and his trust are represented by Gary Judd, KC, who told a hearing in the High Court at Tauranga this month that the society was carrying on “in a fashion that is against the law” and the longer it went on, the worse the situation would get.

However, the judge was concerned the basis of the liquidation bid mimicked the seventh cause of action named in the judicial review claims.

The review broadly focuses on the decisions and arrangements of the council and the society that resulted in the status quo in respect of the ownership and operation of the marina.

The relief sought is some 27 declarations and an order for inquiries and accounts, including declarations that the society has no power to grant or issue berth licences or to lease berths at the marina.

The judicial review is defended by the society and Tauranga City Council.

Judd said the liquidation proceeding was different in “nature, relief and procedure” and argued it should be allowed to go ahead.

If liquidation was refused, then the society could apply for a strike-out or stay of the seventh cause of action.

Associate Judge Brittain noted that if the two proceedings continued separately, they could produce “different findings of fact and law” on the same issues.

Judd suggested the trust could discontinue the sixth and seventh causes of action in the judicial review to avoid duplication, and not file them again without the leave of the court.

The judge found too many difficulties with Judd’s suggested approach, including overlapping issues outside those two clauses.

Associate Judge Brittain also said that Judd conceded the liquidation proceeding was, in part, the trust’s attempt to bring forward the judicial review hearing date – forcing the court to deal with that cause of action earlier.

He referred to a comment by Justice Pheroze Jagose, in an earlier High Court judgment declining interim relief in the judicial review, that the “trust seeks to disrupt nearly a decade of operation by the society, with indeterminate impact on actual and prospective licensees”.

Associate Judge Brittain said the trust had not applied for an urgent trial fixture in the judicial review.

Contact the Open Justice team.

“Grounds for urgency are not obvious. The liquidation proceeding should not be used for a tactical purpose to obtain a trial of a cause of action earlier than could otherwise be achieved.”

He determined that the judicial review proceeding was appropriate to deal with the issue of berth licences and any potential liquidation proceeding would be at the court’s discretion following that proceeding.

“In my view, the interests of justice are best served by a stay of the liquidation proceeding until the judicial review proceeding has been determined.

“In the meantime, advertising the liquidation proceeding should be stayed. There is no suggestion that the society is insolvent.”

In his view, the trust should pay the society’s costs on the application for a stay and restraint of advertising.

Hannah Bartlett is a Tauranga-based Open Justice reporter at NZME. She previously covered court and local government for the Nelson Mail and before that was a radio reporter at Newstalk ZB.

St Mary’s Bay sinkhole raises questions as intensification looms

New Zealand Herald July 28, 2026

A sinkhole in affluent Auckland suburb St Mary's Bay is sparking concerns about the resilience of the area’s ageing infrastructure amid ongoing intensification plans.

A sinkhole in an affluent Auckland suburb is sparking concerns about the resilience of the area’s ageing infrastructure amid ongoing intensification plans.

On Thursday, a section of Hackett St in St Mary’s Bay collapsed, forming a large hole 5m long and 3m wide.

The same part of the road was also damaged by flooding on Auckland Anniversary weekend in 2023, raising questions about the condition of the area’s underground infrastructure.

Tony Skelton was formerly chairmsn of the St Mary’s Bay Association and has lived in the area for 53 years with his wife.

He told the Herald there have been numerous other sinkholes in the area, with many residents concerned about upcoming plans to rezone the suburb.

Auckland Council has approved Plan 120, a move that would permit building heights of up to 15 storeys – increasing the strain on the suburb’s deteriorating water and wastewater network, Skelton said.

“The infrastructure is failing and we need a constant rate of repair.”

As a “crucial junction point for the entire network”, Skelton said the Hackett St engineered overflow point will be a serious concern during future severe weather events.

“There is potential for another catastrophic event in a storm.”

But a Hackett St resident said that in a historic area like St Mary’s Bay, the collapse was not surprising.

“Old stuff breaks,” they said. “It’s 100 years old.

“I think the thing that worries people is there’s been a hole there for three years and it just collapsed.”

The resident said Watercare had responded to the incident quickly but with the road expected to remain shut for two months, they were concerned about emergency access to the neighbourhood.

“The thing that worries me is what happens when someone needs an ambulance or a fire engine.”

On social media, the St Mary’s Bay Association wrote that the sinkhole had reinforced the community’s concerns about local infrastructure.

“St Mary’s Bay is an older coastal suburb with steep terrain, narrow streets and ageing underground services.

“These factors must be properly considered before further intensification is enabled through PC120.”

The association said it is “not seeking to apportion blame” and hopes to see proper planning around further development of the area.

“We want to work constructively with Watercare, Auckland Council and elected representatives to better understand the condition of local stormwater, wastewater, and potable water infrastructure.”

Watercare chief operations officer Mark Bourne said the organisation is still investigating the cause of the sinkhole and has closed the street for repairs.

“We know this work is disruptive to the community and we’re keeping residents of Hackett St and nearby streets updated. We sincerely appreciate everyone’s patience while we do this critical work.”

Bourne said the work is expected to take about two months, but the length of time required will depend on the ground conditions and construction progress.

“We are doing reactive water and wastewater works on Hackett St in St Mary’s Bay where an existing area of collapsed road has deteriorated above our pipes.

“This work will allow us to maintain water and wastewater services to the surrounding neighbourhood while we repair the damage to underground infrastructure and the road.”

Do the friends we make at 15 stay with us for life?

Sydney Morning Herald July 29, 2026

After bonding as teens in France, they lost touch for decades. But the impact of their friendship endured.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

The last time I saw Elsa, we were teenage girls in Melbourne, crying over a goodbye. Now, standing in a bustling square in France with my four daughters, I scan the crowd for a face I hope I will still recognise. What will it feel like to see each other again after all this time? More importantly, will our friendship still be there?

Then I spot her, making her way through the crowd. Time has changed us both, but her smile is unmistakable. She laughs, and I am transported back to the French village where we spent three months together, 35 years ago. Within seconds, we are in each other’s arms, talking over one another. There is an instant ease that feels both surprising and deeply familiar.

I was 15 when I went to France as an exchange student. I’d lobbied for the United States, but my Francophile parents were convinced France would be better for me. I, however, was terrified. My anxiety eased when I learnt my host family had a daughter my age. Coming from a family of five girls, I liked the idea of a ready-made sister. I collected brochures from a travel agency, imagining life in a French city … but they didn’t live in a city. After arriving in Paris, I took a train alone to a station in eastern France, where Elsa and her mother picked me up and took me to their tiny village. It was a shock. Rolling green hills and ancient stone houses in every direction. Elsa’s home was surrounded by dense pine forest and farms – a world away from the eastern suburbs of Melbourne.

The first few weeks were miserable. I was homesick, overwhelmed by a language I barely understood. Many nights I cried into my pillow. Starting school was particularly tough. One lunchtime, some boys in the cafeteria began teasing me. I couldn’t understand the words, but I recognised the tone. I just sat there, embarrassed, willing myself not to cry. Elsa quietly picked up my tray and moved us to another table.

The two of us bonded over music, chocolate, teenage crushes and badly dubbed episodes of the 1980s American TV soap series Santa Barbara. We laughed our way through conversations in a muddled mix of French and English. Elsa’s humour was wickedly dry. When I was served venison for Christmas lunch, she looked at my plate and said, completely deadpan, “Bambi’s father”. I was horrified. She dissolved into laughter.

Australia fascinated Elsa, who, at the time, had never been on a plane. She asked endless questions about its beaches, wildlife and culture. She loved horses and Harley-Davidsons, while I had posters of pop stars and tennis players on my bedroom walls. We seemed very different on paper, yet our friendship felt effortless.

When my three months ended, we cried and promised to meet again. From Melbourne, I wrote and received long letters on thin blue airmail paper that took weeks to arrive. A few years later, Elsa came to Australia and spent six months living with my family. But after that, the letters became less frequent and we drifted apart. Three decades passed before social media brought us back into each other’s orbit.

I arrange to meet Elsa in Annecy, a town I had visited with her family. While waiting, I don’t worry about whether I will recognise Elsa, I worry whether I will recognise the friendship. I needn’t have.

We wander alongside Annecy’s canals, talking and trying to make up for 35 years in a single afternoon. My daughters listen as Elsa and I trade stories (mainly in English, since my DuoLingo crash-course in French the month before our visit clearly wasn’t enough), interrupt one another and collapse with laughter. They are seeing something I had hoped still existed but wasn’t sure of until that moment: the friendship itself.

Over the next day, Elsa tells stories of riding across the US on a motorbike, becoming a martial arts champion and living in Russia as an ironworker. Her life has taken a different path from mine. Yet sitting beside her, I feel the same ease I experienced as a teenager. At one point she pauses and says quietly, “Meeting you changed the course of my life.” Hosting me all those years ago had sparked her curiosity to explore the world; her time with my family in Australia had consolidated her English, giving her the confidence to travel for work.

For years, I had thought of Elsa as the person who helped me navigate those difficult first weeks in France. I had never stopped to consider what our friendship meant to her.

As we say goodbye, my daughters are already talking about doing an exchange in France. Listening to them, I think about my own parents, who had packed a nervous 15-year-old onto a plane and hoped for the best.

“You know what, Michaela, I think the kids we were would be proud of us,” Elsa writes in a Facebook post after our reunion. “To everybody out there, be open-minded, generous and dare – it’s worth every bit of it.”

US diplomats stage UN walkout after France criticizes human rights record under Trump

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 21:39:51 GMT

France had also intervened after Trump administration had opposed the reappointment of UN human rights chief

US diplomats walked out of a United Nations meeting after France criticized the country’s human rights record under Donald Trump.

The staged walkout, which occurred on Monday during a UN security council meeting on the Ukraine-Russia war, came days after the Trump administration cited “forced labor” allegations as it imposed sweeping tariffs on dozens of countries.

Critics accused the US president of leaning on the claims as a “convenient” justification for the new duties, which were unveiled on Thursday.

The following day, the Trump administration criticized the credibility of the UN human rights system and opposed the reappointment of Volker Türk, the UN human rights chief, prompting an extraordinary intervention on social media from France’s UN mission in Geneva.

“The US used to be a beacon of human rights. Not anymore,” the French Geneva mission said in response. “Today, it stands alongside North Korea, Nicaragua, Mali & Russia, isolated. And the world no longer listens to it.

“#AmericaAlone,” it added.

Last March, Türk said he was “deeply worried by the fundamental shift in direction” in the US. In June, Türk took sharp aim at the Trump administration by calling for “prompt, independent, impartial and effective investigations” into the deaths occurring in US government immigration custody.

In addition to the US, nine other countries voted no to Türk’s re-appointment, including Russia, North Korea, Israel, Nicaragua and Mali. His re-appointment was ultimately approved, with 144 countries including France, China and the UK in favor, while 13 countries abstained.

In response to the French mission’s post, the US ambassador to the UN, Mike Waltz, wrote on X on Sunday and said: “It is disappointing – though not surprising – that this is how France deflects on its shameful vote to coddle some of the worst human rights abusers.

“France voted for someone who has been lecturing, free, sovereign democracies like the United States, the UK, and Israel, while cozying up to the world’s worst oppressors.”

The US continued to criticize France during Monday’s meeting, with Dan Negrea, the US deputy ambassador, claiming that the US “remains the beacon of liberty for the world”.

“As such, we will not be affording them the benefit of listening to their politicized drivel until they renounce their condescending and disrespectful rhetoric and behave in a manner commensurate with their seat on this council,” said Negrea.

France’s UN ambassador, Jérôme Bonnafont, did not mention the walkout, instead saying on Monday: “The United Nations was created with the goal of working towards international peace and security, human rights and development,” the Associated Press reports. “All of that forms the spirit in which France works within the United Nations … to preserve this institution, its independence, its ability to act in service of the charter and act to serve human rights and peace.”

The US walkout came after Trump faced bipartisan criticism over his use of “forced labor” as “a pretext” for imposing controversial new tariffs of between 10% and 12.5% on imports from more than 80 countries. Those include longstanding allies such as the UK, Canada, Australia, and the European Union, alongside Mexico, India and China.

Criticizing the tariffs, Richard Neal, the top Democrat on the House’s ways and means committee, said last week: “Forced labor is a real and pervasive problem in our supply chains and demands serious enforcement. It should never be cheapened into a pretext for a tariff policy built on dubious legal theories and personal grievances.’’

Abusive chanting against immigrants in English football on rise, new data reveals

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 21:30:14 GMT

Reported incidents of all discrimination reach new high

Reports of abuse in grassroots football rose for fifth year

Abusive chanting against immigrants has become a feature of football matches in England, according to new data from Kick It Out.

Last season 39 reports of anti-immigrant chanting were made to the anti-discrimination charity, more than the previous two seasons combined. Phrases such as “stop the boats” and “send them back” were reported as being heard “at all levels of the game”, as part of a growing trend of discriminatory “mass chanting” at matches, Kick It Out said.

The growth in anti-immigrant rhetoric was consistent with a broader rise in reports of discrimination, at matches and online. Kick It Out received 1,744 reports of discriminatory behaviour in total during the 2025-26 season, a record and a 25% increase on the previous campaign.

The number of reported incidents increased across every type of discrimination to new highs. Reports of racism remained the most common, rising 19% year-on-year, the 792 reports making up 45% of the total. Complaints of sexist behaviour rose 12% to 216, homophobia rose 46% to 203, antisemitism rose 43% to 93, ableism rose 20% to 89, and Islamophobia rose 88% to 60. Kick it Out said all six areas had seen their biggest totals in five years.

Reports of abuse in grassroots football rose for a fifth consecutive year, up by 33% in 2025-26 to a record 248 reports. Equally, the 98 reports of abuse against match officials was the same as the past three seasons combined.

Samuel Okafor, chief executive at Kick It Out, said such behaviour at matches and in online spaces was matched by a rise in hateful rhetoric elsewhere in British society, but he praised the willingness of supporters – and players – to speak out.

“These figures show that discrimination remains deeply embedded across the game at a time when we’re also seeing rises in hate crime and divisive political rhetoric in Britain,” he said. “But they also show that people are more willing to stand up to abuse when they see it, and it’s encouraging to see professional players set that example last season.”

For example, in March, a 60-year-old man was given a suspended sentence for sending offensive messages to the England Women defender Jess Carter, who went public over the attacks during the European Championship last year. In the men’s game, Antoine Semenyo drew attention to the racist abuse he had received over the course of the season, with a charge of racially aggravated behaviour against one man scheduled to go to trial in September.
