Burnham to seek cross-party consensus over urgent reforms to social care

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 21:30:13 GMT

Prime minister invites Badenoch and Davey – but not Farage – to discuss how to fix decades-old funding crisis

Andy Burnham has promised “problem-solving, not point-scoring” before a speech on social care in which he will set out his strategy for resolving one of the most intractable issues in British politics.

The prime minister has invited Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, and Ed Davey, the Liberal Democrat leader, to discuss how to enact urgent reform on social care, as he attempts to find common ground across party lines. Davey confirmed he would attend via videocall while the Conservatives said they would send the shadow health secretary, Stuart Andrew, in Badenoch’s place as she was having pre-planned minor surgery.

However, the suggestion that the main Westminster parties could finally reach consensus to fix the crisis that has eluded a generation of political leaders in England already appeared optimistic after the Tories imposed their own red lines and amid negative headlines about inheritance tax.

Several Labour MPs also expressed concern over how to manage the financial burden of a reformed care sector.

Before his speech on Wednesday, Burnham said: “We need a different kind of politics: problem-solving, not point-scoring. Nowhere is that more urgent than social care. For decades, governments have kicked this issue down the road because they’ve seen it as too risky, too difficult, and too complicated.

“Politicians might have different views but I’m serious about fixing this issue and to do that, we have to find common ground and listen to others to find a way forward. It’s time to draw a line under people playing politics when the human cost of that means carers struggling, families paying the price and our NHS buckling under the strain.”

The prime minister is expected to stop short of unveiling plans for a new social care system in this speech, instead confirming plans, first revealed by the Guardian, to speed up the independent review led by Louise Casey that has been considering possible options.

Lady Casey, who will launch the Big Conversation on Care on Wednesday to give the public their chance to share their views on the future of adult social care in England via an online platform, has warned that money alone won’t fix the problem.

However, Burnham’s push for a solution is set against a tightening economic backdrop with the economic thinktank NIESR warning of “very difficult trade-offs” in the autumn budget if the Iran war keeps oil prices and inflation high.

He is understood to be committed to exploring a new system that would be free at the point of use, the same principle as the NHS. He is understood to regard other options, such as a care costs cap, as less attractive, though they would be significantly cheaper for the taxpayer.

A middle-ground option would be a model similar to Scotland’s, where personal care costs are paid by the state but other costs, such as accommodation and food in care homes, are borne by individuals and their families.

Whichever option the government eventually pursues is likely to involve significant extra investment over the long term, most likely through increases in taxation.

When Burnham first proposed a universal system of social care as health secretary under Gordon Brown, he suggested replacing inheritance tax with a 10% levy on all estates. At the weekend he did not to rule out this option, which could raise as much as £18bn.

Before visiting a care home on Wednesday, Burnham said: “This comes down to a choice. We can carry on passing the problem to the next generation, or we can face it head on and work together to build a care system that gives people dignity, security and the support they deserve.

“This is about bringing back hope that we can finally fix the difficult issues that have been ignored for too long, and making Britain believe again. That’s why I’m making this choice and I’m prepared to put everything I’ve got behind it.”

An average of 13,600 people a day were stuck in hospital beds last month despite being medically fit to leave, including some delayed because of the availability of adult social care, underlining the pressure on the NHS.

While Labour MPs have broadly welcomed the prospect of reform, several cautioned that there would have to be serious consideration of how to protect people from losing their homes to care costs or penalising those who had already saved for retirement and care with new taxes.

One minister said the prime minister “must exercise a lot of care” in managing the sensitive trade offs between the quality of care versus the cost and who pays for it.

“There are no easy answers, and I don’t think we can just dive straight into saying ‘this is the solution and this is what’s going to happen’, because we have a prime minister and in many ways a government … with no specific mandate on a specific measure.”

A centrist Labour MP said: “It’s vital that the UK at least tries to do something because we will never be able to contain the rising costs of the NHS. Our ability to genuinely improve the quality of health care will be stymied if we don’t have a quality social care service that relieves pressure.”

Others on the party’s left urged the government to consider adopting a full NHS-style system that would rely on some taxation, but would also highlight that Burnham’s premiership is ready to not just “talk the talk but also walk the walk”.

“If we’re talking big and bold we shouldn’t shy away from this option. It took from 1945 to 1948 to get the NHS up and running. We’ve still got years to start the process but we have to really try to shake this broken system,” one said.

“Andy doesn’t have the goodwill from the electorate that Keir did in 2024 because we messed it up over the last two years so people feel betrayed and ignored,” another added. “This is a moment where we now have to prove ourselves.”

A Tory source said: “If Burnham was serious about working cross-party he would have given us more than 18 hours’ notice for a 30-minute meeting during recess and the invitation wouldn’t have been immediately press released. It’s almost like it’s only being done for show.”

Davey posted on X: “I’m with my family in France and as people know I have a disabled son who needs 24/7 care so I can’t be back in Westminster tomorrow but I look forward to meeting Andy Burnham over Zoom. I’m hopeful this call may prove to be the first step towards fixing our broken care service.

Nigel Farage, who has not been invited to attend as he is not currently a sitting MP and Reform has just seven seats, accused Burnham of “conspiring behind closed doors with the failed political establishment”.

The Reform leader and candidate for Clacton added: “If Andy Burnham is serious about putting politics aside to solve Britain’s biggest problems, it’s remarkable that he’s chosen to ignore the party that led over 300 national opinion polls and represents thousands of councillors and millions of Britons across the country.”

Amy Hunt settles for 100m silver as Zoe Hobbs secures Commonwealth gold

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 21:20:01 GMT

New Zealand sprinter wins in personal best of 10.93sec

Emmanuel Eseme surges to men’s 100m victory in 9.83

On a night of spite and might in Glasgow, England’s Amy Hunt had to settle for 100m silver as New Zealand’s Zoe Hobbs ran the race of her life to take Commonwealth gold.

The filth and unrelenting fury of the rain had left the track sodden and conditions far from ideal, but Hobbs ran a huge personal best of 10.93sec from lane seven to take a surprise victory, with Hunt second in 10.98. Australia’s Torrie Lewis ran an Australia record of 10.99 to claim bronze.

True, this was nowhere near as deep a final as it could have been. Six of the 10 fastest 100m women this year come from the Commonwealth. None of them were taking to the blocks when the gun went off at 9.40pm. But that won’t bother Hobbs, who produced a sensational run to take victory.

Earlier, Cameroon’s Emmanuel Eseme defied Australia’s Lachlan Kennedy in the final strides to take gold in the men’s 100m.

For 95 metres of the race, Kennedy ran a stormer. But moments before the line he stuttered slightly, as Eseme charged from third to first to come through in a Commonwealth Games record of 9.83sec. For Kennedy there was a compensation of a silver medal and an Australian record of 9.85. Nigeria’s Kanyinsola Ajayi took bronze in 9.90, and Wales’s Jeremiah Azu was fifth in 10.03.

There was another gold for Australia minutes earlier as Ky Robinson sprinted clear to win 10,000m gold in 27min 48.93sec, ahead of India’s Gulveer Singh. Not far behind was the Isle of Man’s David Mullarkey, who won bronze – and his island’s first track and field medal at a Commonwealth Games.

But this day will live longest in the memory for the rain, which flitted from the heavy to the biblical and never really eased. The high jumpers looked particularly miserable when they were introduced to the crowd shortly before 6.30pm. No wonder, given the weather in Glasgow bore a closer resemblance to late October than the height of summer.

As the rain hammered down, some high jumpers sported umbrellas in between jumps. Others winter coats. The Indian Pooja Singh, the 19-year-old Asian champion, took even fewer chances. She wore a thick coat, a woolly hat and gloves.

Outside the stadium, the volunteers were joyously shouting: “No Scotland, no party” but – for the first time at these Games – no one was joining in. Unsurprisingly it was the field events that were affected most of all, with officials fighting a largely losing battle with their huge squeegee rollers designed to suck up water from the infield.

Eventually the women’s high jump was halted for nearly 90 minutes after the conditions turned for the worse. And while the women’s hammer did start on time, the wet weather affected some athletes’ grip.

The first thrower in the competition, Scotland’s Angela McAuslan-Kelly, found the protective net. So did Australia’s Stephanie Ratcliffe, who went second. No wonder there were ironic cheers when the third competitor to throw, England’s Charlotte Payne, found the field.

Things were better in the sprints, at least, with the new lightning fast Mondo track at the Scotstoun Stadium producing several very fast 100m semi-final times. Eseme was quickest to make the final in 9.89, with Kennedy running a lifetime best of 9.94 behind him.

However those in lanes one, two, and three in those semi-finals found themselves disadvantaged as their lanes were unprotected by the stadium roof – and so had to run through surface water.

England’s Elliot Jones seemed to be affected most of all as he bombed out after running 10.24 – nearly two-tenths slower than his time in the heat.

“There was water all over the lane,” said Jones, a part-time sprinter who works as football operations manager at Uefa. “When I got in the blocks I was pushing water out my lanes, then there was a false start and the water all came back. It’s a Scottish summer, isn’t it?”

Things didn’t get any better when the gun went off. “It felt like I couldn’t get any traction,” Jones said. “I didn’t feel like I was moving anywhere. It was freezing. Then we had a false start. We had to reset, and your nervous system’s up and down and up and down. It’s frustrating.”

Conditions had eased slightly by the time the women’s high jump resumed at 9.08pm. However, conditions were far from ideal and England’s Morgan Lake went out early having failed three attempts at 1.82m, her opening height.

Teenager dominates men’s 200m breaststroke final

Win makes him island’s most successful Games athlete

Filip Nowacki secured his status as Jersey’s most successful Commonwealth Games athlete by storming to a historic gold medal in the men’s 200m breaststroke.

The 18-year-old led from start to finish in a commanding display, touching the wall in 2min 07.87sec before erupting in celebration as he climbed on to the lane dividers and slapped the water in delight while soaking up the enthusiastic applause around the Tollcross International Swimming Centre as Jersey flags waved. Canada’s Oliver Dawson claimed silver, with Australia’s Olympic champion, Zac Stubblety-Cook, taking bronze.

Having captured silver in the 100m breaststroke earlier in the Games, Nowacki arrived as the favourite and delivered under the weight of expectation. The Jersey teenager took control from the opening 50m, remained in front at halfway and produced a superb pull-out after the turn to extend his advantage.

By the 150m mark, Nowacki had opened up a lead of more than seven tenths of a second and never looked in danger of surrendering it, powering home to claim Jersey’s first Commonwealth swimming gold.

It was Jersey’s first Commonwealth gold medal in any sport since Colin Mallett won the individual fullbore shooting title in Auckland in 1990 before teaming up with his father, Cliff, to take bronze in the pairs.

Nowacki’s triumph marks another milestone in the remarkable rise of the world junior and British senior champion, who is widely viewed as the heir to the British breaststroke great Adam Ramsay-Peaty, having already finished ahead of the Olympic champion in the 100m breaststroke final in Glasgow.

England’s teenage sensation Amalie Smith claimed her second medal of the Games with bronze in the women’s 200m individual medley. The 16-year-old, who won silver in the 400m individual medley on her Games debut on Monday, again impressed against an experienced international field, finishing third behind Australia’s Jenna Forrester and South Africa’s Aimee Canny.

Smith qualified third fastest for the final, with Forrester the quickest and the favourite for gold. Scotland’s Katie Shanahan delighted the home crowd by leading at the halfway stage after 100m, while Smith remained firmly in contention throughout. The English teenager briefly hit the front during the closing stages before Forrester surged clear to win in 2:09.24, with Canny securing silver.

Smith held on for bronze, adding another podium finish to an outstanding first Commonwealth Games campaign. Shanahan narrowly missed out on a medal in fourth after her fast start, while Wood was unable to challenge for the podium.

Earlier, Scotland’s Stephen Clegg claimed gold in the men’s S14 50m freestyle, with the five-time Paralympic medallist touching the wall in 24.73sec to secure an impressive victory. South Africa’s Nathan Hendricks finished second in 24.84, while Canada’s Nicolas-Guy Turbide took bronze in 24.96. The triumph comes days after the 30-year-old won silver in the men’s S13 100m freestyle, where his brother James narrowly missed the podium in fourth place.

Former Gavin Newsom aide shares fresh details of affair

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 21:15:14 GMT

Ruby Rippey writes in Vanity Fair of relationship with then San Francisco mayor and appears to contradict his account

A former aide to Gavin Newsom has publicly shared for the first time her full account of their affair, which took place more than two decades ago when Newsom was mayor of San Francisco.

In a new essay published in Vanity Fair on Tuesday, Ruby Rippey writes about her struggles with alcoholism, substance abuse and her relationship with Newsom while she worked as his appointments secretary and was married to his deputy chief of staff and later the manager of the mayor’s re-election campaign.

The essay provides the most detailed look yet at Rippey’s relationship with Newsom, now in the final year of his second term as governor of California – and is likely to rekindle interest in the scandal ahead of his widely expected run for the White House in 2028. In the essay, Rippey does not refer to Newsom by name, but as her “boss” and the “mayor”.

“For my former boss, it is a footnote in a longer arc of ascent,” Rippey writes in the Vanity Fair essay, titled How I Blew Up – Then Rebuilt – My Life. “For me, it is the fracture that split my life into before and after.”

Newsom, who was single at the time, publicly admitted to the relationship in 2007, memorably telling reporters at a city hall press conference: “Everything you’ve heard and read is true.” In his new memoir, Newsom describes their relationship as “the briefest of affairs”. But Rippey’s telling complicates his account of their story.

Newsom writes in his new book that he “came clean” to her husband and his top aide Alex Tourk – a version Rippey says gives Newsom “credit for something I had already done”.

“Technically defensible, perhaps, but one that leaves the unmistakable impression that he, not I, was the one who told Alex the truth,” she writes.

In the essay, Rippey describes the early days of the newly elected mayor’s administration, her marriage, pregnancy, struggles with alcohol and her ensuing relationship with Newsom as it veered into an extramarital affair.

She eventually went to rehab and left her job with the mayor’s office.

After the story became public, Rippey was inundated with calls from journalists and was the subject of frenzied media coverage about the affair.

Jennifer Siebel Newsom, the first partner of California who started dating Newsom shortly afterward, told journalists in 2007 that Rippey was the “culprit”– remarks she later apologized for.

The office of the governor and a spokesperson for Siebel Newsom did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

In the aftermath of the incident, Kamala Harris, then the district attorney, contacted Rippey, she writes. Rippey was being urged to speak publicly about the incident, she told Harris, who advised her to pause and that taking time would give her “better perspective”.

“It turns out to be the best advice I receive. I am newly sober and still inside the wreckage – unable to make sense of anything, let alone speak clearly about it,” Rippey writes.

Rippey and her husband eventually divorced.

For years, Rippey said little publicly about her relationship with Newsom. During the MeToo movement, she observed a new narrative about their relationship emerge in which Rippey saw herself cast as a “powerless subordinate”, she writes.

At the time, Rippey said she was doubtful it applied to her situation. Although she was Newsom’s “subordinate”, she said in 2018, she was also “a free-thinking, 33-year-old, adult married woman and mother. Also happened to have an unfortunate inclination toward drinking-to-excess and self-destruction.”

Taking responsibility felt like the last form of agency, Rippey writes in the essay. But since the reckoning, she has re-evaluated the role power can play in a relationship between a subordinate and their boss.

“Both things are true,” she writes. “I am responsible for what I did. Power does not distribute consequences evenly.”

Rippey is now 20 years sober, she writes, and has remarried and rebuilt her relationship with her ex-husband.

Gomorrah: The Origins review – a mob prequel so stylish you’ll look for Al Pacino

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 21:05:13 GMT

There’s a cheekiness, freshness and tenderness to this show that sets it apart from standard crime dramas. It’s so wonderfully rich that the Godfather cast wouldn’t be out of place

It’s worth it just for the leather. The prequel to formidable Neapolitan mobster saga Gomorrah hurls us into the filthy bustle of Secondigliano, a broken quarter of northern Naples which, in 1977, has been abandoned by God and government, leaving organised crime as the only alternative to destitution. But even in this purgatory, the style of the city and the late 70s abides: the young men of Secondigliano might not be able to escape their fate, but they’ll look fantastic trying.

Sashaying forcefully through the throng is Angelo (Francesco Pellegrino), with his messianic collar-length curls, eyes that seem to mascara themselves and an array of spectacular leather jackets. Kids gather to gawp when his car skids to a dusty halt and Angelo, chest hair and medallion nestling in the open collar of a patterned silk shirt in two exquisite shades of brown, emerges and strides to his next appointment. Angelo is in his early 20s and is the hippest gangster in his neighbourhood, but he bears the pained intensity of the thwarted: on a citywide level he has no sway, and he’s worked out that the cut of the action the big bosses give him is a paltry percentage of the overall pie. His crew, sporting their own leather outerwear in boxy mustard or calf-length burgundy, are happy enough, but Angelo wants more.

Observing him from afar is a kid who’s even further down the food chain. Pietro (Luca Lubrano) is in his mid-teens, with a greasy parting and bumfluff. Every day he wears the same jumbo corduroy coat, which looks sad next to Angelo’s sharp clobber while still being, in our eyes, pretty cool. Pietro has nothing but his wits, yet his desire to improve himself makes him the natural leader of his cheerful gang of petty-thieving urchins, and if he can prove his worth to Angelo, his ascent can begin. His surname is Savastano … Gomorrah fans know that, in 30 years’ time, Pietro Savastano will be a king.

The dashing Angelo and determined Pietro soon become colleagues, at first when Angelo’s team are ambushed on their own turf when they’re keeping cash on the premises overnight. Evidently there is a rat in the operation who must be found and mercilessly dealt with, a classic mafia tale told here with mournful elegance, as the rain pours down and Pietro’s eyes open. Not for the last time, we attend a lavish funeral where everyone in attendance knows that the murderer is among them and that the deceased had it coming.

The two new allies grow closer as Angelo, desperate to mix in with the older, all-powerful dons – majestic double-breasted suits; impossibly large, square, tinted spectacles – embroils himself in a drugs operation that pits family against family and young against old. There is always a boyish, even vaguely Bugsy Malone cheekiness offsetting the seriousness of the business being conducted, for instance when Angelo and Pietro pull off a dock heist by distracting security guards using a football and 22 10-year-olds.

But Gomorrah: The Origins is respectful of its characters’ predicament. The word “freedom” keeps popping up in the dialogue, forever promised to foot soldiers in return for their loyalty, but never actually given to anyone except the men at the top. Angelo and Pietro’s difficult backgrounds mean their chances of success are small – we see how impoverished Pietro is, while Angelo’s troubled youth is summed up by a recollection from his uncle, who doesn’t have many lines but does utter this corker: “You know what your mum did after she shot your dad’s killer? She came home to breastfeed you!”

As he’s plotting his way into the mob, meanwhile, Pietro meets a girl, Imma (Tullia Venezia), who has a comfortable life in the nice apartment she shares with her loving parents. Imma tells Pietro about her dream of studying music at Juilliard; Pietro quietens when he’s asked what his dream is, since poor boys like him aren’t allowed them. Again, Gomorrah fans know how that story turns out, and it starts with Imma realising that organised crime’s tentacles touch her family too, which means she isn’t free either.

With children and young adults as its protagonists, Gomorrah: The Origins may not have the heft of other premium gangster stories, but although it delivers familiar, wonderfully rich mob-drama set pieces – at a fabulous garden party where the various families meet, eat and furiously scheme against each other, you half-expect a young Al Pacino to walk into shot – its youthful main characters lend it a freshness and tenderness that standard crime sagas lack. Dust off your wildest vintage fabrics and hit the streets.

Shabaz Asks: Are Billionaires Bad? review – a hilarious spoof that’s like Philomena Cunk meets Louis Theroux

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 20:50:13 GMT

TikToker Shabaz Ali uses his uber-dry wit to make the mega-rich look ridiculous in this very silly satire

BBC Three’s latest documentary opens with a man floating down a London street in a smart black turtleneck and grey suit jacket, increasingly alarmist string music swelling around him. “In a world of ever-widening economic divides,” he begins, gesticulating wildly to the camera as he walks through lavish Knightsbridge, “the BBC have asked me, Shabaz Ali, to answer one burning question: are billionaires bad?” You would be forgiven for thinking that this was another documentary of the kind the channel is known for: well-intentioned and well-made programmes, fronted by presenters such as Stacey Dooley and Zara McDermott.

Then the camera zooms out to reveal another camera pointed in Ali’s face, and the music stops: “Er, yeah,” he says. “They are!” He strides off, mock end credits playing at triple speed. As it turns out, Shabaz Asks: Are Billionaires Bad? isn’t one of those BBC Three documentaries that boils down important societal goings-on for gen Z, but rather a parody of the genre. It’s a bit of a risk to send up one of the things your channel is best known for, as if ITV started broadcasting spoof versions of those dark psychological thrillers where a heavy-drinking police detective is haunted by an unsolved case from 20 years ago.

Somehow, though, Shabaz Asks: Are Billionaires Bad? works. Much of its success is down to Ali himself – a former teacher turned TikToker and self-proclaimed “povvo king” from Blackburn. He rose to internet fame in lockdown, reacting to outlandish, out-of-touch content on social media with a straight face (“You can barely afford a meal deal from Tesco, let alone $5,000 worth of caviar. Why? Because you’re poor …”) Here, he disarms the mega-rich and those in their orbit by appearing slightly gormless, promising at the outset to “[do] the Louis Theroux stare when I can’t think of a comeback”. He then uses his uber-dry wit to take the mickey out of his subjects (at the “winter home” of Phones 4u founder John Caudwell in Colorado, Ali asks his unimpressed host whether he has “a Batcave, or one of those big boards where you have a world map [for] conquering stuff”). Elsewhere, the economist Faiza Shaheen schools Ali in the economics of becoming a billionaire. But he has a more pressing question: “What’s billionaire shortbread?” At the back of a get-rich seminar hosted by Joseph Valente, a former winner of The Apprentice, the camera pans to Ali, doodling the letter S on his notepad.

It might all sound a bit Philomena Cunk, more of a comedy performance than anything else. Yet, Ali has actually managed to make a decent documentary, by going so ham on the ridiculousness of the issues at hand that the very concept of a billionaire does start to feel silly. The Green party leader, Zack Polanski, has a particularly good comeback when Ali asks him whether his party are scapegoating billionaires. “I’m very happy to scapegoat billionaires”, he counters, “because otherwise we’re scapegoating migrants, trans people, disabled people, people who can’t get a job …” Mic drop!

Much of the time, though, the “povvo king” shtick gives way to what are clearly Ali’s real thoughts and opinions. When he meets Emily Abraham – who sells luxury bags to celebrities and royals – he is incredulous. “I grew up working class, my dad was a taxi driver, my mum was a housewife,” he explains, “but they could afford 20 years ago to buy a house … hard-working people, teachers, could go on holidays. Now, it’s not the case. The gap is becoming so wide that an average person can’t do normal things.” At Abraham’s shop, £190,000 can buy you an Hermès Faubourg Birkin, modelled after the Paris street of the same name. In Blackburn, he says, it could buy an actual two-bedroom house. Abraham grew up in poverty and agrees to an extent with what he says. “But the reality is that we do have people with money, and they do want to spend it …”

Are Billionaires Bad? is a pilot of what one day might become a series, with Ali doing that part-Theroux, part-Cunk thing and doing it well. But if it does continue, its makers will need to decide whether it is a proper documentary, a comic endeavour, or the funniest, most cutting hybrid of the two that TV has ever seen. Maybe the super-rich are just too easy a place to start; indeed, says Caudwell, “I’m not a fan of billionaires either.”

Shabaz Asks: Are Billionaires Bad? aired on BBC Three and is on iPlayer now.

The Vampire Lestat review – a mega-fun glam-rock musical … with bloodsucking

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 20:45:13 GMT

Velvet jackets and opera glasses are out, tight trousers and a hoofing glitter stomp are in. Interview With the Vampire’s taken quite the turn

It starts with drums, heavily reverbed: da-doom-ba-CHA, da-doom-ba-CHA, da-doom-ba-CHA, da-doom-ba-CHA-CHA. Cheap, chugging electric guitars kick in. A song plays, and although it’s an original composition it is at least 60% Blockbuster by Sweet. What in the Tony Visconti is happening? This is meant to be season three of Interview with the Vampire! Has it turned into a glam-rock musical?

Yes. Yes, it has. The show based on Anne Rice’s Vampire Chronicles books – a text it is serially unfaithful to while remaining loyal to the source material’s essence, a camp melange of the sinister, sordid and the deeply, sincerely emotional – was previously set in a lush vision of the past, starting in New Orleans in 1910. There romanced the vampires Louis de Pointe du Lac (Jacob Anderson) and Lestat de Lioncourt (Sam Reid), a sensitive pupil and wild, brittle master whose tumultuous relationship was remembered in a second timeline set in 2022 during an interview with Louis conducted by the journalist Daniel Molloy (Eric Bogosian). At the close of season two, Molloy published the titular book.

In this new series, the old theme music, an orchestral crescendo resolving menacingly into a dissonant scream, has been replaced by that hoofing glitter stomp. Velvet jackets and opera glasses are out; tight trousers and lines of coke are in. Lestat has responded to the salacious biography by forming a glam band, and recorded an album that channels his rage. Now touring it around the US, we join him in 2025 as he storms through a bloodily chaotic stopover in Detroit. A flashforward has taken us to the near future, where an elite auctioneer sells memorabilia relating to the project, including an extensive audio diary, committed by Lestat to vinyl and forming the show’s voiceover. The auctioneer refers, tantalisingly, to “the events of the 2025 album and supporting tour, and the global catastrophes that sprung from [them]”.

This has not come from nowhere: Lestat becoming a rock singer happens in the Rice books. But, as the critically panned 2002 movie Queen of the Damned and Elton John’s swiftly forgotten 2006 Broadway musical Lestat both demonstrated, the part of the oeuvre where vampires mesh with popular music is a tricky proposition.

Canon or not, the wholesale shift of tone in The Vampire Lestat, as signalled by the show changing its name, is a risk. Although Lestat choosing 1970s-style guitar music as his route to fame in the 2020s, and doing so successfully, can perhaps be justified by his immortal powers transcending time and fashion, it still threatens to turn what was the sleekest, cruellest and perhaps best TV vampire drama into a bad mashup of Hedwig and the Angry Inch and Daisy Jones & the Six.

To be into it, you have to go along with Reid’s uninhibited performance as a Jim Morrison-style lizard king, while forgiving the retro cheesiness of the songs – pitched somewhere between Iggy Pop, Mott the Hoople and the Dandy Warhols – and the narration’s refusal to acknowledge a limit on how cringeworthy a rock frontman’s pronouncements can be. “I baptised them ‘The Beautiful Unwell’,” says Lestat of his fanbase, an identikit collection of freaks and rejects. Of his constant fraternising with women, whom the old-school pop stars he’s based on might have referred to as groupies, he explains that his undead status has given him “an immortal erection”. Reid’s chewy attempt at an aristocratic mid-Atlantic drawl adds an extra layer of spoofy irony.

Get past all that and The Vampire Lestat is roaring fun, from the man hired by the band’s management to impersonate Lestat on nights out after gigs, thus giving him an alibi for any killing he does while in town – the best doppelganger they can find is an Albanian gangster, also played by Reid – to the scene where Lestat nearly has an overdose because a fan’s blood is so rich in MDMA and LSD, which the tripping vampire bizarrely refers to as “the Torvill and Dean of hallucinogenics”.

More substantial are the easy but rewarding comparisons made between the famous artist and the undead bloodsucker, each of them hiding alienation behind hedonism, each of them elevated above regular society and sometimes yearning to return to normality. Vampires draining the blood of mortals has always been an obvious metonym for casual sex, and the show capitalises on a vampire celebrity taking that exploitation to another level. Lestat in particular is empty-hearted due to romantic disappointment, which heightens the loneliness of the platinum-selling singer.

The Vampire Lestat demands to be taken seriously and works to earn your solemn respect, before mercilessly mocking you with more silliness if you give it what it wants. Trusting it fully would be a mistake, but there’s something invigorating about a drama that never apologises and knows no shame. Let it in and surrender.

The Vampire Lestat aired on BBC Two and is on iPlayer now

Apple becomes second $5tn company as investors flee AI stocks

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 20:33:14 GMT

Share price rally driven by strong product demand as well as decision to sit out AI spending race, amid wider tech sell-off

Apple has become only the second company to pass the $5tn valuation mark, as it benefited from investors fleeing AI and semiconductor stocks amid a wider tech sell-off.

The iPhone maker’s shares hit a session high ⁠of $342.89 on Tuesday, giving it a market ⁠capitalisation of $5.04tn (£3.78tn), then eased back down to $340.08 – around the $5tn mark.

Apple became the world’s most valuable company earlier this month, overtaking the chip giant Nvidia, which had been ⁠at the top since June 2025 and became the first company to breach the $5tn threshold last October.

The US consumer electronics company’s rally has been driven ⁠as much by strong demand for its products as its decision to sit out the ​AI spending race that is sapping cash ‌flows at big tech ‌rivals.

Its fresh high valuation came amid an intensifying sell-off of AI stocks around the world driven by rising concerns about AI companies’ borrowing to fund datacentre expansion.

US chip stocks extended their recent losses when Wall Street opened on Tuesday, with Intel, Advanced Micro Devices, Sandisk, Western Digital and Seagate Technology all down by more than 4%.

The Nasdaq 100 index of leading tech stocks fell by as much as 1.8% at one point, meaning since its early June record high it had fallen more than 10% – the technical definition of a market correction.

Meanwhile South Korea’s stock market slid to its lowest level since mid-April, with semiconductor companies SK Hynix and Samsung Electronics falling by more than 10%.

Analysts attributed the sell-off to renewed worries over AI investment spending, and competition from cheaper Chinese companies, after a report by the Information that China had begun mass production of homegrown deep ultraviolet (DUV) chip-making tools.

Investors may also be growing jittery about the “circular funding” at the heart of the AI industry, through which artificial intelligence companies finance one another.

They have also been spooked by the announcement from Google last week that it was further increasing capital spending this year to as much as $205bn to fund its AI plans, while reporting negative free cashflow for ​the first time in its history, burning through $5.9bn in the three months to the end of June.

Apple has been shielded somewhat by being something of an AI laggard. Its difficulties in developing in-house models meant it has instead relied on Google’s ‌technology to power new services such as a revamped Siri. That has spared it the hefty infrastructure costs that have left big tech investors wary.

Apple’s decision to hold iPhone prices steady last month when it announced increases for MacBooks and iPads has also bolstered demand as buyers scooped up the company’s flagship device before expected ‌price hikes later this year, analysts have said.

To aid demand, Apple on Tuesday also launched a device leasing programme in the US through the payments ​firm Klarna, under which monthly payments start at $17.99 for an iPhone, $11.99 for an Apple Watch or iPad, and $24.99 for a Mac.

“Apple has resisted the AI spending race, betting that customer experience – not infrastructure investment – will ultimately determine the winners,” said Dipanjan Chatterjee, a vice-president and principal analyst at Forrester. “The ⁠new leasing programme is a clever response: it doesn’t reduce the price ​of an iPhone, but ​it changes how consumers perceive the cost ​by replacing sticker shock with a predictable monthly payment.”

Including session gains, Apple ​stock has jumped ‌24% so far this year, ​widely outperforming the ​other six of the “Magnificent Seven” cohort of US technology stocks.

Film-maker Mike Leigh has said his next film is likely to be his last.

According to Indiewire, the Oscar-nominated writer-director was speaking at a recent Golden Globes-hosted roundtable in London about his next film Tender Loving Care, a drama set to premiere during this fall festival season.

The 83-year-old, whose films include Secrets & Lies, Mr Turner and Another Year, said another film would be “very difficult” and is “not going to be possible” as a result of his health.

Leigh has previously spoken about being diagnosed with myositis, a disease that affects the immune system and causes chronic muscle inflammation.

When asked if Tender Loving Care will be his last film, he responded: “Absolutely. I think very likely, yes. I mean, I know the girls don’t like to hear me say that, but I think that is the case.”

The film is a comedy drama starring Leigh’s longtime collaborator and partner Marion Bailey and recent Widow’s Bay breakout Kate O’Flynn. Specific plot details are unknown, but it has been described as “an insightful exploration of the contemporary world”.

The film will have its Canadian premiere at the Toronto film festival with a world premiere at the Telluride film festival predicted just before it.

“I was lucky in making this last film – people were very helpful,” he said. “You’ll see when I get up, that my two friends all helped me to stand up. So I probably can’t do much more. And doing a play is even more physically demanding, strangely enough, than making a film, because on a film you can be moved around.”

Leigh’s last film Hard Truths, starring Marianne Jean-Baptiste, was a critical hit two years ago. The Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw called it “a deeply sober, sombre, compassionate drama” in a four-star review.

Hard Truths marked the final time Leigh worked with his longtime cinematographer Dick Pope, who died in October 2024.

Is the World Cup for sale? Here’s what Fifa’s plans mean and what happens next

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 19:10:09 GMT

Gianni Infantino is under fire from Uefa over plans to sell off commercial rights for the tournament but he says they are ‘about the democratisation of football worldwide’

A week after the World Cup finished, Fifa has yet to announce whether Argentina will be punished for the violence seen on the pitch at the end of the final. What it has been able to do, however, is devise an entirely new way of running international football, which – in the words of its president, Gianni Infantino – “is about the democratisation of football worldwide”. It is also an idea to allow private investors to take a stake in Fifa’s competitions and potentially make money from the World Cup.

After reporting in the Times and the Financial Times broke the news on Tuesday afternoon, Fifa published a lengthy statement extolling the new venture. To be known as Fifa Forward Enterprise, or FFE, the new body would sell all of Fifa’s commercial rights – across broadcast, sponsorship, ticketing and licensing – and also take charge of “operational delivery” of Fifa tournaments. It would focus all Fifa’s money-making endeavours in one place and the governing body would “retain sole control of FFE”, but it would also “invite third parties to make minority, non-controlling investments”. These investors “would be selected against clear long-term, governance, and strategic criteria”.

Well, only a small “non‑controlling” bit of it. But whose game is it anyway? And yes, Fifa confirmed to the Times that the proposed lead investor to take a stake in FFE would be Joshua Kushner, the brother of Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared, but why should that matter? As Infantino pointed out on his 15-slide Instagram post on Monday, Fifa has been “on the front lines organising, working hard, and delivering the best show in the world”. Maybe give Fifa a break?

Sources have told the Guardian that the FFE plans would not allow investors to take dividends from the scheme (though the investors could later sell their stake). The governing body’s messaging, meanwhile, is very much focused on the financial benefits the scheme would bring to its member associations. Fifa has promised that any external investment would deliver an “optional” $20m in extra funding to any nation that wants it. It has also promised an increase in annual disbursements and predicted a total of $10bn in extra funding would eventually be shared around. Fifa has said that a majority of its 211 members must express an interest in taking the extra funding if the external investment is to be allowed. Many nations are already dependent on Fifa in order to run their operations, however, and this year Infantino said that without the governing body “there would be no football in 150 countries in the world”. So he would seem likely to receive the necessary expressions of interest.

Yes, he announced a deal with the Japanese investment management firm Softbank to fund the development of the Club World Cup in 2018 until a backlash brought it down. Reports in the Times suggested that that Infantino could become chief executive of the FFE once he leaves Fifa – he is poised to win an unprecedented fourth term next year which would extend his stay until 2031. Fifa also insists that joint ventures are par for the course – Uefa has one such with the group known as European Football Clubs to sell the commercial rights to its competitions. Fifa said: “Many major sporting organisations have restructured their commercial operations in similar ways in recent years in pursuit of the same long‑term goal – sustainable growth that can be reinvested in the sport itself.”

The Guardian reported on Tuesday that the launch of the FFE – which has been planned since well before the World Cup – has caught the rest of football by surprise. Members of the key decision‑making body, the Fifa council, were unaware of the scheme and not included in its development. Uefa, meanwhile, has released its second statement in a month warning of a Rubicon being crossed. There will probably be further expressions of discontent and questions will be asked as to the process that led to these events. But whether any football stakeholder will actually do anything to stop the plans is uncertain.

Retaining Rodri is key to Manchester City success under Enzo Maresca

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 19:00:11 GMT

New manager’s No 1 priority must be to persuade World Cup-winning captain to stay as Real Madrid circle

“Welcome home,” was Khaldoon al-Mubarak’s warm greeting to Enzo Maresca on his appointment last month as Manchester City manager. Now, after two previous spells at the club, the Italian’s task is to keep the chair content, and ensure a three-year contract does not end early. To achieve that, Maresca’s tenure must continue Pep Guardiola’s glittering legacy of 20 trophies across a decade of excellence.

The key to the 46-year-old, who was Guardiola’s assistant during the 2022-23 treble season and City’s elite development squad leader two years before that, being successful can be summed up in two words: “Keep Rodri”. Yet with Real Madrid almost certain to launch a bid for the peerless No 6, and him seemingly wanting to play for the Spanish giants, a move away from City may become inevitable.

Maresca’s best hope of avoiding “doing a David Moyes” – who succeeded Sir Alex Ferguson at Manchester United in May 2013 and lasted a mere 34 Premier League games – and thriving as the man who follows the man is to retain Rodri, who has just captained Spain to World Cup glory, winning the Golden Ball as best player in the process. The 30-year-old is contracted until June. City’s stance is that they have no wish to sell and remain intent on persuading him to sign the new terms that have been on offer for a while.

Saying City will definitely be contenders for the biggest prizes next season if they retain Rodri may sound simplistic until you examine his CV and are reminded of the pivotal role he has played for the club. Rodri was key to City’s treble glory, including scoring the winner in the Champions League final against Inter. Then there was the 74-game unbeaten sequence with him in the colours that ran from February 2023 to May 2024. “He’s unbelievable, irreplaceable,” said Guardiola. “The best midfielder in the world by far.”

The World Cup triumph also came after Rodri had been part of Spain’s Euro 2024 glory and City’s 2023 Club World Cup success, again winning the player of the tournament in each. In the two seasons before the World Cup, injury plagued him, however. The result: no Premier League titles in either year for City, halting a record four-in-a-row run for Guardiola’s garlanded team.

Rodri’s ability to mould and control contests was reiterated by his World Cup displays. Exhibit A: the chokehold imposed on France in the semi-finals. At domestic and international level, this is a priceless quality. So if Maresca can field Rodri, City will be feared in the league and on the continent. The back injury for which Rodri underwent surgery on Monday is minor, but the desire to broaden his club horizons – primarily in Spain – remains, meaning there is no certainty he will stay put. Particularly so given the initial resistance of Real Madrid’s president, Florentino Pérez, to acquiring Rodri has shifted, due, surely, to his resurgence at the World Cup and maybe José Mourinho, returning as head coach, expressing a need for the player’s calm and elan.

City have invested £116m on Elliot Anderson this summer, an England first-choice midfielder who may be joined by another midfielder in Lille’s Ayyoub Bouaddi, the 18-year-old who also impressed at the World Cup for Morocco, and would cost around £85m. However, neither of them or Tijjani Reijnders, Mateo Kovacic nor Nico González can claim to be in the class of Rodri, who may well be in line to claim a second Ballon d’Or following his World Cup exploits.

Maresca won the Championship with Leicester in 2024 and the following season led Chelsea to fourth in the Premier League and to a Conference League triumph, following that up with glory at the expanded Club World Cup, which featured the 3-0 demolition of Paris Saint-Germain in the final. All of this convinced al-Mubarak and his chief executive, Ferran Soriano, that Maresca is the one who can thrive after the era-defining Guardiola.

Joško Gvardiol has signed a new five-year contract with Manchester City, the defender stating that “great things” can be achieved with Enzo Maresca, the new manager.

While the terms include an option of a further 12-months, the Croatian is confident that the Italian’s first season will be successful. “I remember when he was at Chelsea [2024-26] it was difficult to play against them – especially away. However, as Maresca made clear with his “after Sir Alex [Ferguson]” reference in his unveiling on Friday, directly following greatness can be treacherous. The comparison between him and Moyes is hardly precise, though. Moyes arrived at United trophyless and with no experience of the pressures of an elite club. Maresca’s résumé shows a season and a half in the Chelsea hothouse and, with his prior experience of City, he is versed in the organisation where he now plays a crucial role.

City have five weeks of the market remaining to try to persuade Rodri his future is at the club. Guardiola’s stance was never to stop any player exiting who wished to do so. The logic is understandable: what is the point in retaining an unhappy employee? In this case it would also be one who wants to return to his native city. “Having played for Atlético [Madrid] before would not prevent me from playing for Real Madrid,” Rodri said in March. “There are other players who have done that before. Maybe not direct transfers, but eventually. You can’t turn down one of the world’s best clubs.”

Even Real Madrid boycotting Rodri’s Ballon d’Or-crowning ceremony in November 2024 in protest at Vinícius Júnior’s failure to win the vote has clearly not dissuaded the midfielder that the Bernabéu can be the home al-Mubarak characterises City as for Maresca.

Zelenskyy and Netanyahu brave the whims of Trump’s darkly confounding White House

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 18:53:04 GMT

Ukrainian and Israeli leaders converge on Washington with criss-crossing fortunes, but knowing they can count on little from US counterpart

The converging visits of Benjamin Netanyahu and Volodymyr Zelenskyy to Washington offer an unusually eloquent snapshot of a world in turmoil, unmoored from decades-old certainties.

Some things remain the same. The US is still an almighty military and economic power and for both foreign visitors, a White House encounter with Donald Trump is critical to their governments and the wars they are fighting.

The imperial presidency Trump has tried to forge is in decline, however, in large part as a result of his own erratic leadership. He may see his visitors as client-potentates flying in from the edges of empire to kiss his ring. But they will be as aware of Trump’s weaknesses as they are of their own.

Netanyahu and Zelenskyy arrive in Washington on opposite trajectories. The Israeli prime minister’s star has declined dramatically since he persuaded Trump to join him in an ill-conceived war on Iran five months ago, on the groundless promise that the Tehran regime would quickly collapse.

Since then, a viscerally disappointed president has publicly scolded Netanyahu and insisted Netanyahu would ultimately do his bidding, while the White House has liberally leaked Trump’s foul-mouthed tirades belittling him.

Israel has been left out of negotiations with Iran, and its views were ignored when it came to selling F-35 stealth fighter planes to Turkey, or making a nuclear deal with Saudi Arabia. An Economist/YouGov survey found that nearly half of Americans polled thought that Netanyahu should be arrested on arrival for war crimes.

By contrast, Zelenskyy arrived in Washington in the ascendant. Ukraine has defied the US administration’s predictions of inevitable defeat to Russia’s might, his country is now a world leader in drone warfare, and parts of the Magaverse are now warming to the accidental war leader they once scorned as a loser.

In traditional administrations, both men and the countries they represent would be natural allies and both could be sure of solid welcome in the Oval Office. It is telling that the occasion of their coinciding visits was the funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, a Republican hawk of the old school who could be relied on for wholehearted promotion of the Israeli and Ukrainian war efforts. In that respect, he was one of a dying breed.

But this is no normal administration, led by a president who rules on a whim, and neither visitor can predict how he will be received. Neither wanted cameras in the room. Trump began his presidency by throwing all-in support behind Netanyahu and his wars, dropping even the pretence of concern for the lives of Palestinians or the people of southern Lebanon that had tempered backing for Israel from earlier presidents.

Facing a hostile electorate, the president is trying to extricate himself from the region, but in doing so is finding Israel the most recalcitrant party on every front.

In Ukraine, Trump threw out the American foreign policy handbook altogether, proposing peace deals that often echoed Moscow’s talking points, rewarding aggression with territory Russia had not even won on the battlefield.

Rather than capitulate, Ukraine showed it could fight on despite drastic cuts in US military aid, relying more on Europe and its own hard-won improvised expertise.

Now Zelenskyy finds himself the unlikely darling of far-right Maga influencers such as Lara Loomer, formerly an apologist for the Russian invasion, who interviewed the Ukrainian president in his garden last week, and called for “moral clarity” in Kyiv’s support.

Zelenskyy’s recent ascent may mirror Netanyahu’s simultaneous decline, but that does not mean they came to Washington with comparable status. When it comes to the Trump administration, they arrive from very different starting positions.

Just about anything would count as an upgrade for Zelenskyy compared with his infamous White House ambush in February 2025 by Trump and the vice-president, JD Vance, who tried to humiliate the Ukrainian visitor in front of the cameras, demanding gratitude and acceptance of defeat with “no cards” left to play.

Zelenskyy does have cards this time but well short of a winning hand without US support. The Ukrainian’s immediate aim is modest: for Trump to honour Senator Graham by backing a Russia sanctions bill he was pushing at the time of his death. He knows that direct US military aid to Ukraine is not likely to return in meaningful quantities any time soon.

The Patriot interceptors and other weapons Ukraine once counted on for its defence have been used up wholesale in the Middle East, many of them to protect Israel. It will take years for the US to rebuild its own stocks. Netanyahu may be out of favour in the current White House, but the US is committed to Israel’s defence in a manner and on a scale of which Ukraine can only dream.

Netanyahu and Zelenskyy came to Washington on different paths and footings but they do at least share an awareness that their relationship with the administration can be upended with scant notice, without any clear reasons, in a matter of mere seconds in the court of the irascible, flagging would-be emperor.

Donald Trump hosted back-to-back White House meetings with Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Benjamin Netanyahu on Tuesday, as Ukraine seeks more firepower for its air defenses and the Israeli prime minister tries to repair his strained relationship with the US president.

It was Netanyahu’s first visit to the Oval Office since he and Trump launched their joint military campaign against Iran on 28 February.

Netanyahu’s relationship with Trump has been complicated in recent weeks by his push to keep fighting Iran and Hezbollah in Lebanon, even as Trump pursued a diplomatic opening with Tehran.

Tensions between the pair have risen as the war has drifted inconclusively, with Trump calling the Israeli premier “crazy” and declaring: “Without me, there would be no Israel.”

The two men are each facing pressure at home, with Netanyahu in a tough re-election fight, and Trump under pressure to end an unpopular war that has pushed up prices before November’s midterms.

Trump signaled some of that friction beforehand. Asked on Fox & Friends on Tuesday morning about reports that Netanyahu planned to brief him on intelligence about Iranian activity at Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected nuclear site Trump has threatened to bomb, he said he knew “exactly what’s going on at Pickaxe”, adding that Netanyahu raises it because “he wants me to stay involved”.

Far outside the White House, behind the fences, protesters chanted: “Netanyahu, you’re a tyrant” and “Bibi, you’re not welcome here” on Tuesday.

The closed-door meeting, which lasted about an hour, was expected to cover Iran, a framework deal the US and Israel signed with Lebanon, and a possible expansion of the Abraham accords, according to a White House official.

Netanyahu also faces the task of reassuring Trump he will not obstruct US-led diplomacy in Gaza and Lebanon, as support for Israel among the US public has slipped, with a new AP-Norc poll showing a sharp decline amid accusations, denied by Israel, that its conduct in Gaza amounts to genocide.

Zelenskyy’s meeting was described by both sides as positive. In a statement, Zelenskyy said he had discussed licensing arrangements to let Ukraine manufacture its own interceptors for Patriot missile systems.

“We also spoke about diplomacy – it’s important that the diplomatic process be reinvigorated,” said Zelenskyy. “Our teams will arrange the details of their further communication. I am grateful to the United States for its firm support.”

He opened by offering condolences over the death of the US senator Lindsey Graham, calling the late foreign policy hawk “a true friend of Ukraine”.

“A vote of confidence in British business,” trumpeted Andy Burnham, seizing the political gift of GSK splashing out £400m on a shiny new research and development centre in Cambridge.

For positive vibes, it definitely beats the early pharma news his predecessor as prime minister received. That was the painful tale of how AstraZeneca, frustrated by indecision in the Treasury, cancelled its intended £450m expansion of a vaccine plant in Speke in Liverpool.

In reality, GSK’s investment in Britain is a specific one in Cambridge. The group’s historic Stevenage facility will close and most of the scientists (or as many as want to go) will move to the Fens.

One shouldn’t be surprised. Around the world, life sciences companies increasingly gather in clusters. Cambridge – thanks to its university, Addenbrooke’s hospital, various science institutes and a healthy biotech and biopharma start-up scene – is a genuine world-class rival to Boston and Basel. The Cambridge biomedical campus is the natural place for GSK to be in the UK in the interests of “acceleration” of research and development. Only a cynic would suggest literal proximity to AstraZeneca’s facilities could come in handy for a future merger.

The switch of UK research location is the most eye-catching big decision by Luke Miels, the chief executive since the start of the year, but Tuesday’s first-half numbers contained three sources of encouragement for shareholders.

First, GSK thinks it can put at least 20 potential medicines into late-stage trials this year, an increase from 10 at the last count. Part of the boost flows from the near-£8bn acquisition of the US-based cancer specialist Nuvalent last month. But the rest probably owes something to Miels’s focus on which drug programmes should be backed harder and which cut. If the 20-plus target indicates more ruthlessness in prioritisation, investors will applaud. It is easy to talk, as Miels has done, about displaying “scientific courage”, but you still need candidates to come through the drug pipeline to make it happen.

Second, Miels surprised the market with a plan to cut £1.9bn of annual costs by 2029. Even for a company the size of GSK, that’s a big number to find from the general wash of procurement, frontline sales forces, AI efficiencies and a leaner manufacturing presence amid the shift from general medicines to specialist drugs.

after newsletter promotion

Third, the dark cloud hanging over GSK – the expiry during 2028-30 of patents on the HIV medicine dolutegravir, which accounts for about a fifth of group sales – looks less threatening if the group’s latest forecasting proves correct.

A critical line in the results was the prediction that operating profits margins will be “stable to improving” even during the patent crunch. Thanks to the intended cost savings, that is a notably clearer statement than the group has offered before now. Meanwhile, the grand target of hitting £40bn-plus of revenue in 2031 is “on track” with “accelerating growth” thereafter.

Longstanding GSK shareholders know from experience never to underestimate the scope for disappointment. The past 20 years have witnessed many false dawns; improvements under Miels’s predecessor, Emma Walmsley, ran into bad luck in the form of US litigation over a heartburn drug from the 1990s.

But the tone has definitely improved. It’s still too soon to speak about GSK replicating AstraZeneca’s remarkable 15-year blueprint for growth under Pascal Soriot (which also started with expansion in Cambridge). But the big-picture pieces are falling into place. The 2031 revenue target gets more credible with every telling; the pipeline is fuller; the patent cliff is less daunting; the share price is perkier. Put the merger talk on hold.

The Guardian view on India’s gen Z revolt: the cockroaches are coming together

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 17:25:39 GMT

A youth movement born from exam leaks and online mockery has pierced Narendra Modi’s aura of invincibility and may yet reshape Indian politics

“What if all cockroaches come together?” was the question that humbled India’s strongman prime minister, Narendra Modi. It was posted on X by Abhijeet Dipke, an Indian student in the US with a master’s in public relations. Enraged that India’s top judge likened unemployed youths to insects and “parasites”, and that millions saw medical exams compromised by leaks, Mr Dipke lit a fuse. For India’s nearly 400 million gen Z, public exams are often the only ladder to a secure future. When papers leak or tests are cancelled, that ladder is kicked away. By June, young people were protesting peacefully in Delhi as the Cockroach Janta party (CJP), a parody of Mr Modi’s Bharatiya Janata party (BJP). They demanded the resignation of the education minister, Dharmendra Pradhan.

This weekend, Mr Pradhan became the first senior minister in Mr Modi’s 12 years in power to be forced from office by a mass-protest movement. It came after credible reports suggested police officers attacked protesters marching to parliament. Security sources say it was they who were attacked. This may be just the beginning. The concession has taught the Cockroach movement’s leadership that pressure works. They could have declared victory and gone home. Instead they have accused the government of breaching the terms of the settlement offered by Mr Modi’s government. The CJP claims at least 100 people have been arrested, many on non-bailable charges. Its leaders are now demanding the release of detainees and threatening to remobilise nationally.

Mr Modi has built an authoritarian order which rested upon Hindu majoritarianism and demonising Muslims. Education in the country has been subordinated to ideology and political patronage. But corruption in public exams cannot be divided so easily along religious lines. A Hindu graduate in northern India and a Muslim graduate in its southern cone experience the same anger over leaked papers and worthless qualifications. The grievance, crucially, creates an economic identity that cuts across the BJP’s preferred religious cleavage.

Until Mr Pradhan’s resignation, ministerial accountability to public protest had all but disappeared; loyalty to Mr Modi’s ideological project had mattered more. The CJP has also broken the spell of fear that has dominated the public square. The movement’s leadership were not requesting generosity; they were asserting a claim to clean administration, fair exams and ministerial accountability. Writing in the Guardian, the historian Mukul Kesavan says the CJP’s social-media dexterity is crucial. Like New York’s mayor, Zohran Mamdani, they combine eloquence, message discipline and composure, making Mr Modi look leaden. Their victory may have produced not merely a protest movement, but a new generation of political leaders.

A similar kind of unrest during an anti-corruption movement in 2011 paved the way for Mr Modi to wrest power from the ruling Congress coalition 12 years ago. The next general election is in 2029 and predicting its outcome today is not a worthwhile exercise. But the political scientist Christophe Jaffrelot argues that the CJP represents a much deeper revolt than just anger over exam leaks. It has, he says, become the voice of educated young Indians trapped by jobless growth, poor education and insecure work. Many Indians are either cockroaches now or in the process of becoming them. If they were to come together in a meaningful political way then Mr Modi may be in much bigger trouble than he is in today.

The Guardian view on noise pollution: keep it down

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 17:23:27 GMT

New research linking the issue to Parkinson’s disease adds to the evidence of serious health repercussions from traffic volume and other sources

The roar of late-night traffic is not just annoying for those trying to sleep. It can also have profound effects on their health. A pioneering new study, published this month, has found a clear link between road noise and Parkinson’s disease. The research, which followed more than 3 million Danish participants, found a modest but consistent effect: for every 11.5dB rise in noise level, the risk of the degenerative disorder rose by 3% over the 18-year study.

The study adds to the growing body of evidence that auditory nuisance is associated with serious physical consequences. The European Environment Agency reported last year that more than 110 million people across the continent suffer high levels of health-damaging noise pollution, with physiological stress and sleep disturbance leading to 66,000 early deaths annually as well as heart disease, diabetes and depression. It found that the harm caused was greater than from secondhand tobacco smoke exposure.

Yet a 2023 report from the UK parliamentary science and technology committee described noise as a neglected pollutant, poorly understood and regulated. In the US, the 1972 Noise Control Act pledged to promote “an environment for all Americans free from noise that jeopardizes their health or welfare”, but exposure to harmful noise levels remains widespread. That may be partly because it is unequally felt. Many neurodivergent people are markedly more sensitive to unwanted noise, for example. But research in the US in 2017 found that neighbourhoods with higher proportions of poorer and of black or minority ethnic residents were measurably louder. Wealthier people are also more able to soundproof their homes.

Road traffic noise is not the only issue, though it is a big one. Automated hand dryers and leaf blowers proliferate. Sparser decor has made cafes and restaurants louder environments. The mayor of London, Sir Sadiq Khan, recently said that he is “particularly sensitive to the misery” that tube noise causes residents, following complaints that the screech of metal wheels on tracks is not being adequately dealt with. But he gave short shrift to campaigners seeking to challenge all new applications for pub and bar licences in central London, arguing: “Complaining about nightlife when you *checks notes* choose to live in Soho is like living in South Kensington and complaining about the museums”. What sounds objectionable to some is convivial to others.

Noise is not an uncontrollable part of city life. China’s official statistics, as well as anecdotal reports, suggests significant improvements there in the last decade. That’s not just down to the rise of electric vehicles, declining construction and closures of loud venues. Authorities have also installed sound barriers and laid tens of millions of square metres of quieter road surfacing.

Improved engineering and even lower speed limits can pay dividends. Sound insulation for homes and reliance on noise-cancelling headphones should be a last resort. One of the subtler consequences of auditory pollution is not what it imposes on us, but what it takes away. Animals and even aquatic plants are acutely sensitive to loud noises, and can be damaged by them. Traffic noise drowns out the rustling of trees. Those who learn to tune out what’s around them no longer heed the birdsong. Not all noise is unwelcome. But we should do more to address the sounds that bring misery, not least so that we can experience those that bring joy.

‘They’re part of folklore’: storks return to Derbyshire after 600-year absence

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 17:22:08 GMT

Conservationists are thrilled at the arrival of three juvenile birds at Willington Wetlands, hoping more will follow

A long orange beak poked curiously out from its wooden crate, followed by a sleek head and slender body. Then the first white stork of the morning flapped its wings and took to the air. Moments later a second emerged tentatively to stalk through the long grass, followed closely by a final sibling who stretched its wings and explored the length of the enclosure.

The trio of juvenile white storks have just arrived at their new home in Willington Wetlands in Derbyshire and conservationists are hopeful that their presence will kickstart the return of the birds to the Midlands after an absence of more than 600 years.

“It feels absolutely incredible,” said Katie Last, the living landscape officer for Derbyshire Wildlife Trust, who has overseen the project and manages the nature reserve. “To see white storks back at Willington feels like a real milestone. We’ve put years of work into restoring this landscape. I’m over the moon with how it all went. Our next aim is to get to the point where they’re a sustainable population and they can live outside, flying around and people can see them moving through the landscape.”

White storks disappeared across Derbyshire and the Midlands around the 14th century, largely due to habitat loss and hunting. Recent sightings of birds have increased in the region but none have yet stayed to breed. The hope is that the trio of juveniles – one male, one female and one of yet-to-be-determined sex – will act as a “magnet flock” to attract wild birds moving through the Trent Valley and encourage others to settle and lead to a healthy breeding population.

“White storks seek safety in numbers, so it’s been proven that white storks will settle around other white storks,” Last said. “We’ve got wild white storks migrating over from Africa. We’ve had white storks recorded in nearby Matlock and Ashbourne, so this is the perfect opportunity. We’ll also be putting artificial platforms up in existing trees to give birds space and encourage nesting.”

Watched by an excited gathering of staff, volunteers, donors and birders, the freshly released birds soon settled into their new home. They were bred at Celtic Rewilding’s captive breeding facility in Staffordshire before being moved to their new, purpose-built enclosure, which is predator-proof, with an electric fence to defend against foxes and minks, and fine netting to keep smaller birds out and protect the storks from avian flu.

Over time, Derbyshire Wildlife Trust hopes to see white storks successfully breeding in the area and to manage releases from the enclosure into the reserve as part of the ambitious species-recovery programme. The first pair will be carefully monitored. Depending on how they settle and progress, additional birds may be shipped into the reserve in future. “Our long-term hope is that white storks become part of the Midlands landscape once again, but success is about much more than one species,” said Rachel Bennett, the director of wilder landscapes and wilder communities at Derbyshire Wildlife Trust. “Success means thriving wetlands, more wildlife across the landscape, and communities that feel connected to nature and invested in its future.”

The £309,000 project has been funded by the Veolia Environmental Trust through the Landfill Communities Fund. “This whole project is about more than the return of an iconic bird,” said Last. “It’s about reigniting people’s sense of wonder in nature. If you can create the kind of healthy, dynamic landscape that supports white storks, you’re also creating habitats that benefit countless other species.”

The wetlands, a 40-hectare (100-acre) rewilding site that was previously an area of gravel pits, has been identified as a critical stepping stone for stork recovery. Years of restoration work has helped create wet grassland, open pools and reed beds, which provide ideal foraging and nesting conditions for storks, and it is also home to Derbyshire’s first resident beavers in more than 800 years, after two pairs of Scottish beavers were released in 2021, which has helped create a “fluid, dynamic wetland habitat”, Last explained.

Storks “have a really strong connection with people across Europe, and they’re part of lots of folklore. They migrate and arrive in spring, so they’re a sign of new life, which is why they’re associated with delivering babies – there’s the story that birthmarks are where the stork carried the baby, leaving their mark on them. Because they have that history with us, they’re great at inspiring people to reconnect with nature. They’re an iconic species that capture people’s imaginations but what they really represent is healthier wetlands, healthier ecosystems and a landscape that’s becoming richer for wildlife.

“This has got to be the ultimate wetland that acts as a space for protection for wildlife but on a larger landscape scale,” added Last. “We want to see this reserve extending out and for the River Trent to be a wildlife corridor. We want land-owners to work with us, get onboard and give a bit of space for wildlife to move freely. We want landowners to work with us and engage with wetland habitat, to create corridors, so when the storks migrate, they have an abundance of food and rest points. We want the wildlife we’ve got here to be able to move freely in and out across Derbyshire and beyond.”
