‘A control freak’: murderer James Desborough convicted of two further killings

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 16:58:49 GMT

Man already serving life for killing his cellmate while awaiting trial also murdered and dismembered his friends Claudio Aquilino and Daniel Coleman

On a spring day last year, James Desborough marched up to Cornwall’s county hall in Truro and began bombarding the offices with dozens of eggs stolen from a supermarket.

It was a drug- and drink-addled protest at his plight – homeless, jobless and generally angry at the world. He expected to be arrested and messaged a friend: “If I’m going to get nicked, might as well round the charges up.”

He certainly did that. In the weeks and months after the egg incident, Desborough committed three murders.

He killed two vulnerable friends, Claudio Aquilino and Daniel Coleman, whose dismembered and burnt bodies were found in woodland close to a shack where he sometimes lived off-grid in south Cornwall.

Then while awaiting trial, he murdered Steven Kempster, his cellmate in Exeter prison, strangling him to death because he was annoyed with his snoring.

Desborough, 40, is already serving a life sentence for the prison killing. After a jury at Winchester crown court convicted him of murdering his two friends, he may never be released. Mr Justice Saini will sentence Desborough on Wednesday, and made it clear he could face a whole-life term.

The judge described the circumstances – a person being sentenced for two murders while already jailed for life for killing someone in prison – as “unique”.

Acquaintances have said Desborough was a “control freak” with a terrible temper – he has an old conviction for grievous bodily harm – and was furious at what he saw as his bad luck in life. A civil engineer by profession and a father, he had fallen on hard times.

Quite what tipped him over into an explosion of violence is unclear. He used Aquilino’s and Coleman’s bank cards after he killed them, but police do not believe it was a simple matter of theft.

The prosecutor in his trial, Ahmed Hossain KC, put it to Desborough that he might have killed them because he considered them worthless, deserving to die because of their troubled lifestyle and because they were “dinlos” – a local slang term for fools. Had he simply got annoyed with them and snapped? “I thought they were OK,” he replied in court. “They were good friends.”

The trial has certainly put the focus on a different Cornwall to the one most holidaymakers to the county love. It highlighted not surfing beaches and historic landscapes, but the deep-rooted social issues that make life for many in the far south-west of England difficult. There are pockets of serious deprivation in Cornwall where people experience homelessness and addiction problems.

Desborough, Aquilino and Coleman were among those who – in the words of the defence barrister, Sean Brunton KC – had slipped through the cracks in society. The three got to know each other when they lived in a hostel for homeless people in the seaside resort of Newquay.

In the months before he died, Aquilino, 57, was taking hard drugs, suffering from depression and subjected to “cuckooing”, in which dealers take over the home of a vulnerable person. Coleman, 43, abused alcohol and had cirrhosis. He had been kidnapped and stabbed at the age of 13, leaving him with post-traumatic stress disorder.

The police were first called in after Coleman was reported missing. He had last been seen on 3 June 2025, drinking with Desborough. Police thought they had solved the case quickly when they found a body in woodland between Truro and the village of Probus.

It turned out not be Coleman though, or Aquilino, but a third man, Lee Hockey, who had vanished from Truro. Police believe he too may have been murdered, but have not linked his death to Desborough.

Attention began to focus on Paramoor Woods, near Sticker, once a mining settlement now popular with people who work in the town of St Austell.

Desborough had inherited land there from his grandfather and built a shack, though, to his frustration, he did not have the correct planning permission and had been told by the council that he was not allowed to live there permanently.

He would let homeless friends camp there, grew cannabis and had a “stash tree” where he hid class A drugs in a hollow. Machetes, knives and saws were also scattered around the property.

Police searched the woods for five months, eventually finding the remains of Coleman and Aquilino. The latter had last been seen alive on 18 April 2025, also drinking with Desborough.

Codenamed Operation Honeyfall, the search was extraordinary. More than 700 officers and scientists were involved, with Devon and Cornwall police drawing on resources from five other forces. Dog teams, soil experts and anthropologists were brought in.

The weather was very hot and the nature of the terrain jungle-like and boggy. Officers sometimes had to wade through water up to their chests as they searched.

In excess of 1,900 burnt bone fragments – Aquilino’s remains – were discovered in a stream, while Coleman’s charred body parts were found in a shallow grave. A hatchet hung on a nearby tree.

Another unusual feature was that Desborough kept a beady eye on the search. Before there was enough evidence to remand him in custody, he hung around, at one point telling a forensic biologist that he liked the dismemberment scenes in the serial killer show Dexter.

Sometimes officers smelled burning and at other times heard digging, perhaps as Desborough tried to destroy evidence.

As well as discovering the victims’ remains, police came upon notes and plans Desborough had made that suggested he may have been planning to change his appearance through plastic surgery after the murders and flee the UK, perhaps to south-east Asia.

Detectives also discovered he had used his victims’ bank cards to buy goods and services, including a roast beef dinner soon after cutting up Coleman’s body.

He was eventually charged with the two murders and held in Exeter prison sharing a cell with Kempster, who had been jailed for drunkenly suffocating his 91-year-old father in north Devon.

Desborough’s appearance in the witness box was remarkable. He was considered so dangerous that he was handcuffed to an officer when he was moved from the dock to the main area of the court.

He was articulate when speaking about his time as a civil engineer and building regulations concerning his cabin, but he was less certain when he told the story of finding the bodies of Aquilino and Coleman.

He claimed he had come upon one hanging in a tree, the other naked in a stream. It was, in his words, a “series of unfortunate circumstances”.

Desborough repeatedly denying killing the pair, but accepted burning and hiding their bodies while high on ketamine and drinking tequila.

During the trial there was a suggestion that Desborough might have carried on killing, murdering members of his circle who could have implicated him in the deaths of his friends or who simply annoyed him.

In one note, he had written: “I’m a killer and ready to execute any predators.” In another, headed “bug out” – military slang for a retreat – he set out what appeared to be escape plans but added: “Take out the remaining muppets.”

Det Supt Rachael Bentley, the head of Devon and Cornwall police’s major crime investigation team, said of the murders of Aquilino and Coleman: “Both men were vulnerable and trusted James Desborough as their friend. Desborough not only brutally murdered both men, but then savagely desecrated their bodies, seeking to hide the evidence of his crimes. In doing so, he denied both men of dignity and their families of the opportunity to say goodbye.”

Almost 4,000 people evacuated from tourist sites near Bordeaux as wildfires rage in France and Spain

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 16:42:43 GMT

Return of winds and extreme heat threaten firefighters’ attempts to bring blazes under control

Nearly 4,000 people have been evacuated from tourist sites on France’s Atlantic coast as the return of winds and extreme heat jeopardises firefighters’ battles to contain wildfires raging in France and Spain.

The precautionary evacuation order in France, which covers campsites, holiday villages and other tourist accommodation around the resort of Lacanau to the west of Bordeaux, exacerbated a wildfire emergency described by the French president, Emmanuel Macron, as the “toughest” situation the country had dealt with since the second world war.

On a visit to a crisis centre in Bordeaux on Tuesday, Macron warned that “the coming weeks will be tough and we have to hold out”.

In Spain, meanwhile, a woman who had been injured in a wildfire in the southern province of Almería this month died in hospital, bringing the death toll from that blaze to 14.

The woman, who was not named, died at Seville’s Virgen del Rocío university hospital where she had been treated since suffering severe injuries in the wildfire, a hospital spokeswoman told AFP, without giving further details.

In France, Rémi Lassoureille, a fire commander in the Gironde department, was quoted by Le Monde as saying that the blaze there, which has destroyed 42,000 hectares (104,000 acres) of forest, was “relatively under control”, although firefighters feared a “potential flare-up of the fire on its north-west flank towards Lacanau”.

“That is why we decided to evacuate the campsites,” he said.

Other large fires have been contained in the nearby Landes, where thousands of evacuees were allowed to return home, and the Écrins massif in the French Alps, although one in the Gros Bessillon massif in the Var area of south-east France has not yet been fully brought under control.

Wildfires in France, Spain and Italy have forced the evacuation of about 330,000 people over the past week, with Spain entering Europe’s fourth intense heatwave of the summer attempting to contain some of the worst forest fires in the country’s history.

The Spanish prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said the country faced “difficult hours, complex hours” before the new heatwave, which is forecast to begin on Wednesday and warned about the urgency of responding to the climate emergency.

He later said authorities were beginning to “see light at the end of the tunnel in the fight against wildfires”. Spain’s interior ministry announced the end of evacuation orders for 15 municipalities on Tuesday afternoon in rare good news.

A fire in the hilly terrain of Ávila, west of Madrid, has become Spain’s largest on record, burning 50,000 hectares.

A firefighter, Javier García, told Associated Press he had never faced anything like it in his two decades protecting woodlands and rural communities.

“This doesn’t have a precedent,” he said, adding that the ferocity of the wildfire was forcing firefighters to fundamentally change their tactics by prioritising evacuations and property protection because of the danger from fast-moving walls of flames and blazes too powerful to attack directly.

“The evolution is alarming,” García said.

An EU spokesperson Anna-Kaisa Itkonen said a number of firefighting planes and helicopters from member countries had been deployed to France and Spain.

She said it was “important to clarify that no country can maintain alone all the resources that are needed to tackle every possible natural or other disaster and crisis”.

after newsletter promotion

EU officials have said wildfires could still be burning until early November in what threatens to be a record-breaking year of burnt land area.

Wildfire weather across the bloc has been more severe this year than ever before, according to data up to 22 July from the European Forest Fire Information System. In France, which had broken its full-year record for burnt area by then, and in Spain, the cumulative numbers of fires in 2026 have also set new records.

European wildfires have struck at the same time as ferocious North American ones, with hundreds of blazes continuing to devastate the western US and swathes of Canada. Meanwhile, torrential rains have flooded countries across Asia.

“The climate alarm is blaring, from every direction,” Simon Stiell, the executive secretary of UN Climate Change, said on Tuesday. With Europe now facing another heatwave, he said the human and economic costs of the climate crisis were reaching “national emergency” levels.

“These spiralling disasters are now the lived reality for billions in a world getting rapidly hotter, as humanity moves too slowly from fossil fuels to clean energy and to protect forests,” he said.

Western Europe had a wet winter and also, in some parts, a wet spring, which encouraged heavy plant growth. It has been followed by a dangerously hot and dry summer, with back-to-back heatwaves forcing moisture from plants and leaving behind a surplus of fuel that has fed the flames.

The climatic drivers have been made worse by the long-running abandonment of farmland that used to fragment the landscape, preventing small fires from growing into blazing infernos.

“If the issue of fuel load isn’t addressed, I think we’re going to have to get used to [fires too strong to put out],” said Dr Jesús Notario del Pino, a soil scientist at the University of La Laguna in Tenerife. “As many forestry specialists and engineers often say: what we don’t manage, the fire will.”

Dr Thomas Smith, a wildfire scientist at the London School of Economics, said: “If I was holidaying on the coast of Spain or the south of France, I would make sure I have any fire alerts or fire weather apps installed on my phone and familiarise myself with the evacuation plans for the hotel or residence. It’s very important to understand that timely evacuation saves lives.”

The June heatwave would have been “virtually impossible” without the added heat from more than a century of carbon pollution, a rapid analysis found last month, while the level of soil dryness in western Europe was made five times more likely by climate breakdown, according to a separate study from the same international research network last week.

Estimates of the death toll from the heatwaves, from national public health agencies and independent scientists, suggest they have claimed at least 10,000 lives.

Stiell said: “The science on the cause is unequivocal: global heating, driven by humanity burning colossal amounts of coal, oil and gas, is making protracted heatwaves, severe floods and violent mega-storms more frequent, more intense and more costly. “What needs to be done is equally clear: leave coal, oil and gas behind faster, scale up renewables, and protect people where the impacts are already hitting hardest.”

Scandinavia confirmed the form of his Ascot Gold Cup defeat of Trawlerman with a wide-margin win in the Group One Goodwood Cup on Tuesday, but the bare result does not tell the full story of a race in which a riderless horse led the field for much of the way and veered across the leaders with three furlongs to run.

The drama began at the start, when Hector Crouch was unshipped from Amiloc, the jockey catching his foot on the stalls as the horse jinked to the right. The gelding then worked his way to the head of the field with nearly 12 furlongs still to run and, having veered wide on the home turn, drifted sharply across both Scandinavia and Trawlerman soon afterwards.

Scandinavia, the favourite, was half a length behind Trawlerman at the time and Ryan Moore, his rider, did not stop riding but William Buick, on Trawlerman, lost all momentum. Scandinavia’s eventual winning margin of eight and a half lengths – with the riderless Amiloc still in front of him – suggests that the result was not affected, but the crowd was certainly denied the spectacle of two top-class stayers battling to the line.

“It’s significant,” Buick said. “It’s hard to say how significant but he’s a horse who is a Gold Cup winner [in 2025], so he stays.

“To try to manoeuvre around a loose horse is never easy and my worry was if I found myself on his outside, I could give away a lot of ground and be on the stands side, theoretically. I went the shortest route and he only got in my way in the most important part of the race.”

Moore, meanwhile, felt that the sight of a horse galloping in a clear lead might have benefited his mount. “It was nice for him to have a horse to follow all the way,” Moore said. “He probably thinks he got beat. His stride never shortened, he just kept galloping all the way to the line. He’s a high-class horse and hopefully there’s a few more good days to come.”

Lake Forest, who finished fast under Cieren Fallon to take the Group Two Lennox Stakes by a neck, could attempt to complete a remarkable double in the Group One Sussex Stakes here on Wednesday.

“I don’t see why he can’t come here again tomorrow, that’s the plan,” Maureen Haggas, the wife of Lake Forest’s trainer, William, said.

“We’ll see how he is. If we’re happy with him, then why not? He’s a five‑year-old gelding and he hasn’t got to travel anywhere. We don’t know about [the step up to] a mile, but he stays seven well.”

Earlier on the card, Kaiya Fraser came up with an early candidate for ride of the meeting as he threaded Oliver Cole’s Dr Rascal through a narrow gap against the far rail to take the Group Two Vintage Stakes by half a length.

Fraser, who was born and raised in Hackney, did not sit on a horse until enrolling on a foundation course for apprentice riders at the British Racing School in Newmarket as a 16‑year‑old. “It means everything, this is what we wake up for every morning,” Fraser said.

“I’ve put so much hard work in to get where I am today, and all the people around who have helped me – my agent James Forrest, and all the owners and trainers who put me up – I’m very grateful to them and I wouldn’t be here if it wasn’t for them.”

Bow Echo was the most impressive winner of the 2,000 Guineas since Frankel at Newmarket in May, and he will further enhance his status as one of the finest milers of recent decades if he can extend his unbeaten record to six starts in the Group One Sussex Stakes at Glorious Goodwood on Wednesday.

The parallels with the greatest Flat horse of recent decades do not end there, as Bow Echo’s next start was a less convincing success in the St James’s Palace Stakes at Royal Ascot. Frankel soon set the record straight, though, with a decisive success on the Sussex downs and there are sound reasons to think that Bow Echo can do the same.

Bow Echo was hampered in the early stages at Ascot and was lit up in the first half-mile, before being forced wide into the straight. He then held on by a short-head from Gstaad, who was nearly three lengths adrift in second at Newmarket.

Gstaad is back for a third tilt at Bow Echo on Wednesday, but the pacey four-year-old, Opera Ballo, may be a bigger danger from a low draw at a front-runner’s track.

Bow Echo (4.10), though, has several pounds to spare on Charlie Appleby’s colt on the ratings, has also drawn well in one and has scope to improve further after just five starts.

Goodwood 1.50 Tierra Del Toro has been better than the bare result on his last two starts and should be less susceptible to traffic problems in this smaller field.

Tory MP accuses French navy of firing ‘warning’ shots near him in Channel

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 16:26:53 GMT

Chris Philp says shots were ‘deliberate intimidation’ while he filmed interview on small boats crisis but France says it was training exercise

When Chris Philp heard a volley of shots on the high seas and spun round to see a French gunship, he believed he was the victim of naval aggression – and updated his social media feed accordingly.

The reality appears to be more mundane: it was, the French authorities said, a routine Channel training exercise by officers who had no idea that the shadow home affairs spokesperson was present, or who he was in the first place.

Philp was being interviewed by the BBC on a fishing vessel a couple of miles off Boulogne on Tuesday when the French boat Flamant passed by at a distance of about 300 metres. As it did so, a French navy officer standing at the stern fired 17 shots from a handgun, aiming away from Philp.

Philp, who was being questioned about the small boats crisis, turned to the BBC interviewer Michael Keohan and said: “Is that toward us? I dunno.”

After uploading a video of the incident to X, Philp claimed it could have been an attempt to censor debate about asylum seekers travelling to the UK in dinghies: “There was no notice or training exercise in place. Felt like warning shots or attempted intimidation.”

After several hours of online speculation that the shots could provoke a diplomatic incident, the French authorities said the gunfire had nothing to do with Philp or the BBC but was conducted to ensure “operation readiness” amid international tensions.

Earlier this month, a Russian warship, shadowed by a Royal Navy vessel, carried out a live-fire artillery exercise 46 miles south of Plymouth.

A statement from French defence staff said: “French navy units train regularly. Individual combatant training is a normal activity for a vessel on operations.

“The statutory signals required by international standards for this type of firing exercise were displayed, and all safety protocols were followed.

“This exercise is unrelated to the presence of a British ship in the area, which was outside the range of the firing. The Flamant was not engaged in an operation to monitor migrant vessels.”

Some were sceptical that a French gunship would have acted in response to Philp’s interview, or been aware of it.

One former senior Border Force officer said: “There are often exercises at sea involving the Royal or the French navy, and shots are occasionally fired, usually using blanks. This may be nothing at all.”

Kevin Rowlands, a retired Royal Navy captain and journal editor at the RUSI thinktank, said it was unlikely that the French were deliberately trying to intimidate Philp.

He said naval vessels train “pretty regularly” with small arms and the handgun appeared to be aimed “in a safe direction”.

“And so, on the face of it, I don’t think this appears to be an incident where the French are actively trying to intimidate a British politician or the BBC. That seems a little bit much, from what I’ve seen,” he said.

Those on the boat with Philp said that the incident was unsettling.

Keohan described it as “the most unusual moment … in the quiet of the Channel”. He said he saw a French patrol officer at the back of the boat pointing a pistol toward the sea and believed that was where the shots came from.

The journalist added: “There was no warning for our boat, no signs given that this was the French intention.”

The captain of the fishing boat, Matt Coker, said he also believed it was an attempt at intimidation.

Coker told the Times, which was also onboard the boat: “It’s a bit strange that as they approached us there wasn’t fire or anything and then as they went past, afterwards there wasn’t fire or anything,” he said. “They only seemed to be firing the weapons when they were right alongside us. So I find that a bit strange because we’ve got all this open sea out here.”

Asked to respond to the French authorities’ denial, Philp said it “was not credible”.

“They fired the live rounds at the closest point of approach to us – and didn’t fire anything that we saw before or after. It looked and sounded exactly like deliberate intimidation,” he said.

A Home Office spokesperson said: “This is a matter for the French authorities.”

Fifa accused of ‘selling the soul of football’ over $20bn World Cup commercial rights sale plan

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 16:17:42 GMT

World governing body set to raise millions from venture

Uefa hits out at proposal and could take legal action

Explainer: what Fifa’s plans mean and what happens next

Fifa has announced plans to sell the commercial rights to its tournaments, including the World Cup, to private investors in a controversial move that triggered an immediate backlash from Uefa, leading European clubs and politicians.

Uefa released a strongly worded statement accusing Fifa of “attempting to sell the soul of football” and is believed to be considering its legal position, while sources at numerous elite clubs were highly critical of the proposal in private. Andy Burnham, the UK’s new prime minister, condemned the move.

Fifa has confirmed it is working with the US bank JP Morgan on setting up a new entity – to be called Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) – that would raise hundreds of millions of dollars by selling a significant stake in the commercial rights of the men’s and women’s World Cups, and the Club World Cup to investors, with promises of an increase in distribution of “over $10bn” (£7.5bn) then being redistributed back to Fifa’s 211 member associations.

Thrive Capital, an investment company founded by Joshua Kushner – the brother of Donald Trump’s son‑in-law Jared Kushner – is leading the search for investors.

Gianni Infantino, the Fifa president, said the plan would see “the commercial side of the game [operating] as a focused, dedicated business, with its value shared more and better all around the world”. The plans are subject to approval by a “majority” of member associations, but Fifa declined to comment when asked when a vote will take place.

Numerous sources with knowledge of Fifa’s proposals said it is valuing the new commercial venture at about $20bn, with Infantino looking to cash in on football’s growing global popularity after this summer’s World Cup in the US, Canada and Mexico. The Guardian revealed this month that Fifa’s revenues for the tournament would exceed $15bn, a significant increase on the projected figure of $13bn, with such growth appearing to embolden Infantino to seek further riches.

The revelation of the plans provoked an immediate backlash from Uefa, with the European governing body accusing Fifa of attempting to sell the soul of football. Relations between the two most powerful organisations in the sport are at an all-time low, with Uefa claiming Fifa undermined the integrity of the World Cup this month when it intervened to overturn the USA striker Falorin Balogun’s red card after Trump called and asked Infantino to do so.

“This crosses a line that football’s governing institutions should never cross,” Uefa said of the FFE plan.

“Uefa takes it extremely seriously. So should every national football association. So should every stakeholder: leagues, clubs, players, supporters, governments and everyone who cares about the future of the game. The soul and governance of football are not assets to trade – especially with zero transparency as to who gains financially. None of us are the owners of football. It is not Fifa’s to sell.”

Burnham, an Everton fan, posted on social media: “Football does not belong to investors. It belongs to the people who fill the stands and who stand on the touchline week in, week out, rain or shine. The World Cup is not a product. It is the greatest competition in world sport, and it was never anyone’s to sell. Dress the deal up however you like. Once you have sold a piece of it, you have sold out.”

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

Infantino had succeeded in keeping Fifa’s plans under wraps until reports of the proposal first emerged in the Times and Financial Times. Fifa council members are understood to have been surprised by the announcement, having been sidelined from the decision‑making process.

It is the second occasion that Infantino has attempted to attract private capital to fund Fifa. In 2018, he agreed a deal in principle with the Japanese bank SoftBank to provide $25bn in funding for an expanded Club World Cup and global Nations League, but failed to get sufficient support, largely due to opposition from Europe. Uefa and the clubs are again united against Fifa’s plans, but Infantino may have enough backing from elsewhere to be able to disregard them.

In its statement, Fifa said the new enterprise would enable it to increase the funding provided to each of the associations from $8m to $20m each year, a huge sum for the majority of their 211 members.

Fifa insisted it would retain responsibility for football’s governance and the international match calendar, but in reality inviting private investment in its commercial rights would subject the decision makers to significant external pressures. Investors could ultimately be given significant influence over decisions that affect the entire sport, leading to fears they would seek to stage the World Cup more regularly and permit it to be hosted in only the most lucrative markets, such as the US. Fifa said it would “carefully select long-term investors who will purchase minority, non-controlling interests in FFE – all net benefits of FFE will be reinvested back into football worldwide”.

Infantino is expected to be re‑elected unopposed as president next year despite the huge controversy he attracts, but under Fifa statutes must stand down in 2031 after serving three full terms. The Times reported, however, that Infantino has aspirations to serve as chair of the new commercial company, which could earn him tens of millions of dollars.

Young people ‘expected’ to engage with new work support, says McFadden

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 16:12:25 GMT

Exclusive: Work and pensions secretary echoes Andy Burnham as he announces funds to stop families in England losing benefits

Young people will be expected to engage with new support to find work, Pat McFadden has said, as he announced parents receiving benefits could get £4,500 a year if their child starts an apprenticeship.

Speaking to the Guardian, the work and pensions secretary echoed the comments of Andy Burnham when he suggested that access to support would be conditional on young people properly participating in the support that would be provided. To help with that, the new funds announced would stop families losing benefits when teenagers take up apprenticeships.

“We have an obligation to put good support in place,” he said. “And then there is an expectation that people engage with the support.”

McFadden – one of the few ministers to keep his job in the reshuffle when Burnham became prime minister – said the new bursary would compensate for a quirk in the system that could mean families lose some benefits if a teenager took up an apprenticeship.

The penalty – where the family loses the child component of universal credit – is most likely to affect single parents or disabled teenagers under 18.

McFadden said that welfare reform would mean both “opportunities and expectations”. He said: “We are trying to get the system to ask: ‘How do we help you live your fullest life? How do we maximise your opportunities?’

“One of the things that struck me about the benefits system is how sticky it is, how when people get on to these long-term benefits they tend to stay in them for a long time.”

The new bursaries of about £4,500 will be offered to families, particularly single parents with a disabled child, where they could otherwise lose approximately £80 a week because the apprenticeship salary – £258 a week – is lower than the lost benefits of £340 a week.

Burnham is seeking to address the crisis of mounting unemployment among young people and said on Tuesday morning he would aim to implement fundamental changes in the education system to emphasise technical and vocational skills, especially those relevant to local businesses.

Both Burnham and McFadden have said they are determined to reform the welfare system, especially by providing more opportunities for young people on long-term sickness benefits to return to the workforce.

The prime minister also said on Monday he wanted to change the nature of the support and make some of it “conditional upon people taking opportunities that are presented in front of them … So you might increase the conditions required to receive benefits”.

McFadden said the bursary was part of removing those unintended barriers on young people taking up work – £30m funded through the current departmental budget – but added it was crucial that young people responded to the support on offer.

“The key to it is to remove this barrier to opportunity, really,” he said. “And to stop people being trapped in the benefit system when they would otherwise take up an opportunity which is in their interest, which would put them on to the next step of a career path.

“These cliff edges are never created by design – they’re just in a big complex system, they are just there and I’m very grateful to the charities and campaigners who drew this to our attention.”

Burnham has said he wanted to avoid “crude cuts to benefits to get the welfare bill down … Often that just pushes people into even more crisis and then even more public spending in another part of the system.”

McFadden said there would be a significant system redesign when the second stage of a report from the social security minister, Stephen Timms, and disability campaigners reports back in the autumn. An interim report has already found that the criteria for personal independence payments was not fit for purpose.

“We’ll need a whole government response, not just a [Department for Work and Pensions] response, because the issues affecting young people go way beyond the boundaries of the DWP. If you take mental health issues among young people, that’s obviously going way beyond the DWP,” he said.

The government is also expected to receive the second part of Alan Milburn’s review this autumn, looking at youth unemployment and lack of engagement with education and training. Charities have welcomed plans for the bursary but said young people needed to be directly made aware of its existence by potential employers.

Enver Solomon, the chief executive of the social justice charity Nacro, said: “If more young people are to take up apprenticeships it is vital their family isn’t worse off, so introducing a new bursary is a welcome step towards narrowing the income gap.

“As the new scheme is rolled out, the government must ensure it is as easy as possible for young people to apply, and that nobody loses out because they were not directed towards support.

“We know in families where wages should outweigh benefit payments there can still be real difficulty as payments shift from parents to young people who have to take on the responsibility of contributing to overall household income.”

It’s ‘Chico’ time: Glasgow curry restaurateur ready to face ‘creme de la creme’ of lawn bowls

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 16:05:46 GMT

Mohammed Ayub Qureshi has invited Pakistan’s opponents Australia for dinner at his restaurant – whatever the result

The invitation has already been extended. Even if Australia beat Pakistan in their men’s pairs match at the Commonwealth Games, they are still welcome to dinner afterwards. There is just one small catch. “If we lose, they are still invited to the restaurant, but I will probably give them a spicy vindaloo as revenge,” Mohammed Ayub Qureshi says with a smile.

Qureshi, better known around Glasgow’s bowls community as “Chico”, has spent decades serving food at Alishan Tandoori while also becoming Pakistan’s most recognisable lawn bowler. On Wednesday the restaurateur swaps the shirt and tie for Pakistan colours as he and his teammate, Maqsood Waseem Khan, face one of the toughest assignments in the sport.

Standing across the rink will be Australia’s Corey Wedlock and Aaron Teys. Wedlock is a three-time world champion after starring at the 2023 World Outdoor Championships, while Australia have already stamped their authority on these Games, leading the medal table with over 60 medals overall.

“I feel excited. I feel excited to be playing with the best,” Qureshi says. “Hopefully we’ll learn something and we’ll take something home. The experience, I mean, these guys, are the creme de la creme.”

Beside him sits Khan, the secretary of the Pakistan Lawn Bowls Federation, who needs no reminding of the challenge awaiting them. “These guys are serious so we know we have to be as well.”

Qureshi has lived in Glasgow for decades, while Khan remains based in Pakistan, training before flying in for international competition. “We make it work, it is not that difficult,” Khan says. “I play and train in Faisalabad or Lahore and he is here but it does not come to mind.”

Their journeys into bowls could hardly have been more different. For Qureshi, it started almost accidentally nearly three decades ago through a relationship forged in business. “I started playing bowls nearly 30 years ago. And the reason I got into it was because our bank manager at the curry house helped. He was a bowler,” Qureshi says.

“When we opened the business, we decided to do something for this club where I train, the Glasgow Indoor Bowling Club. We said to the manager: ‘We’d like to sponsor your club for the tournaments you hold every year.’ So for the last 30 years, we’ve been sponsoring them with three-course meals every year, trophies and prizes. Then I decided to join the club and play.”

Khan’s introduction to the sport required a bit more improvisation. “I was impressed by the bowls but I couldn’t buy bowling balls in Pakistan,” he says. “They never even heard of the sport. I got the balls to be made out of wood.”

Cricket remains the country’s overwhelming sporting obsession. Bowls, by contrast, is still fighting for recognition, facilities and even equipment. But Khan has made it his mission to change that. “I train young people in Faisalabad and in Lahore. Mostly young people are interested in bowls in Pakistan now. Pakistan is known for their love of cricket. Bowls is a sport of luxury. But I try to help them financially and try to get them interested. I am trying to create an academy which can provide easy access. Pakistan is my home and I want to bring my love there.”

Home, meanwhile, is a complicated concept for Qureshi. Born in Multan, he has spent more than 50 years living in Glasgow. He represents Pakistan but is cheered on by Scottish clubmates, loyal customers and friends. “My indoor club and the outdoor club and my customers, they all come and support me,” he says. “I see them in the crowd and sometimes I will give them a free poppadom in return.”

Running a successful restaurant and competing internationally might sound exhausting but Qureshi insists they complement one another. “Running a restaurant for 30 years, you get adjusted to it, you find a good staff who would cover you. Being a restaurateur gives me an income. Being an athlete gets you away from the public in a sense. You go on the green, relaxed, and just play balls at your leisure.

“Stressful days would be against the big teams. Like tomorrow. Your mind is always wondering what to do, what shot to play, all that sort of stuff. I mean, we’re kind of part-time club players becoming internationalists. It’s an amazing feeling. It’s a feeling you can’t describe.”

How to get a good night’s sleep in hot weather – and why it’s so hard

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 16:00:07 GMT

Avoid espresso martinis and wear the right pyjamas: experts give tips on how to sleep when it’s hot outside

Tell us: what impact have GLP-1s had on your relationships?

Getting a good night’s sleep when it’s hot out can feel impossible. Unfortunately, worrying about not being well-rested doesn’t help.

Experts say worrying about sleep in warm weather will inevitably make you feel worse. “When people cannot sleep because they are too hot, it often becomes both a physical and a mental challenge,” says Dr Shelby Harris, founder and director of NY Sleep and Psychology, and author of The Women’s Guide to Overcoming Insomnia. “They may start watching the clock, worrying about how tired they will be the next day, or trying harder to force themselves to fall asleep.

“If several hot nights occur in a row, the accumulated sleep loss can also affect mood, making people more irritable, emotionally reactive and less able to cope with everyday stressors,” Harris says.

If you’re on day three of bad sleep during a particularly heinous stretch of 100F days, here’s what experts have to say.

Understanding what happens physiologically and mentally when it’s hot will give you a framework for why you’re feeling – and maybe acting – different.

“The body is constantly trying to keep its core temperature stable,” says Dr Yi Cai, a sleep expert and the director of sleep surgery at New York-Presbyterian/Columbia University Irving medical center. “In hot weather, it does this by sending more blood to the skin and producing sweat, which cools the body as it evaporates. But when it’s very hot, especially if it’s also humid, those cooling systems become less effective.”

While your body is trying to cool itself down, your mind is also working overtime. “When someone is hot and struggling to sleep, frustration sets in and makes the problem worse,” says Janet Kennedy PhD, sleep psychologist and founder of NYC Sleep Doctor. “Core body temperature naturally drops 2-3 degrees at night, which triggers melatonin production. When it’s hot, that doesn’t happen, and it becomes difficult to fall asleep.” Melatonin is released by the pineal gland when it gets dark outside and tells your brain’s hypothalamus – which controls temperature regulation, among other things – to start preparing for rest.

“Tossing and turning, catastrophizing about the next day, and worrying about not sleeping activates the sympathetic nervous system, triggering adrenaline, which heightens discomfort and keeps you awake,” Kennedy says.

“If you cannot fall asleep because you are too hot, do not stay in bed becoming increasingly frustrated,” Harris says. “Get up, cool yourself down, and return to bed once you feel sleepy again.”

Keep the sun out: The temperature outside will influence the temperature inside your home, so blocking the sun’s rays out is key. “Keep the bedroom as cool as possible,” Kennedy says. “Close the blinds during hot days to keep the sun out.”

Sleep in the coolest part of your home: If you don’t have air conditioning in your bedroom, sleep in the coolest part of your home – usually on a lower floor, says Cai, with the blinds and curtains drawn. If the temperature drops a little at night, then you can open your windows to let some of the cooler air through. “Avoid adding unnecessary heat sources like bright lights or electronics before bed,” she says.

Use light, breathable bedsheets: For maximum comfort, sleep on the most cooling and temperature-regulating fabric possible. “Keep bedding light and breathable – cotton sheets are often more comfortable than heavy fabrics,” Cai says. Put your flannel bedsheets away for cozier times and pivot to natural materials; crisp cotton percale is a great option. Linen sheets are a great year-round choice and will keep you cool in the summer and warm enough in the winter. Other materials like bamboo, lyocell or any combination thereof can also work, but avoid cotton sateen, which is slinky, buttery, slippery and has a tight weave.

Wear breathable pyjamas: Now is not the time for footie pyjamas. Cai suggests loose fitting sleepwear or “as little as you’re comfortable with”.

Use cool, damp fabrics: Some of the traditional tricks for keeping cool actually do work, according to the experts. For instance, a cool, damp towel on your neck or wrists can help you feel more comfortable. Putting your pillowcase in the freezer for “a short time” before you sleep can also be pleasant, Cai says. (In my personal experience, 20 minutes should do the trick.) These temporary fixes can improve comfort, but Cai warns that “they’re not a substitute for a genuinely cool environment during extreme heat.”

Use cooling devices: Air conditioning is a straightforward way to keep the temperature of your room or home low. If you have a fan, try to maximize its effects: “A bowl of ice in front of a fan may provide some local cooling in a small space, but don’t expect it to cool an entire room,” says Cai.

after newsletter promotion

An espresso martini (or three) can feel divine in the moment, but at bedtime, you may regret your choices. “It helps to limit alcohol and caffeine, which compromise deep sleep and trigger night waking,” Kennedy says.

Heavy meals can also contribute to dehydration, Cai notes, which won’t help matters when you’re trying to get some rest. You should be drinking water when it’s hot, but don’t overdo it. “Avoid drinking large amounts [of water] right before bed if night-time bathroom trips are an issue,” Harris says.

If you do need to hydrate before bed, Kennedy suggests a compromise: “Stay hydrated, but taper before bed. Dehydration worsens heat strain, but drinking a lot right before bed increases wake-ups.”

On hot days, it might seem sensible to save exercise and other strenuous activity for the early morning or evening hours. But morning is a better choice. “Vigorous exercise close to bedtime can increase body temperature or interfere with sleep,” Harris says.

Many of us are unhappy and grumpy in relentless heat, but it can have worse effects for specific groups of people.

“Older adults are especially vulnerable [to heat] because the body’s ability to regulate temperature becomes less efficient with age,” Harris says. Infants, young children and pets are also regularly affected by extreme temperatures. “These groups are more vulnerable to heat and may not recognise or communicate that they’re overheating,” says Cai. “Check on older neighbors regularly, encourage regular fluids, and don’t rely on thirst alone as a signal to drink.”

Tending to the people (or pets) that are most vulnerable during heatwaves requires some forethought. Cai recommends dressing babies and young children in light clothing and keeping them in the coolest rooms of the house. Pets should be walked during cooler hours, usually in the early morning or evenings, and should always have plenty of access to water and shade.

Cai also urges people to pay attention to any possible symptoms of heatstroke. “If anyone develops confusion, becomes difficult to wake, stops sweating despite the heat, or has a very high body temperature, seek emergency medical care immediately,” she says.

Remember that sleep will eventually come. Locking into an anxiety spiral won’t do much good, and will potentially make things worse. “Try not to fight with things you can’t control,” Kennedy says. “Getting angry, frustrated or desperate will raise your body temperature and make it harder to sleep.”

Japan earthquake injures at least 100 and traps many inside shopping mall

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 15:43:42 GMT

Deaths expected as Kumamoto shaken by 6.8-magnitude quake, knocking out power and damaging buildings

A 6.8-magnitude earthquake has shaken south Japan, leaving at least 100 people injured. Some are trapped and presumed dead inside a shopping mall.

The earthquake hit Kumamoto prefecture on the southern Kyushu island late on Tuesday afternoon, knocking out power to thousands of homes and damaging roads, bridges and buildings.

Japan’s prime minister, Sanae Takaichi, told reporters authorities were still assessing the extent of the damage in the area, which was devastated by another deadly quake a decade ago.

“We have already been informed that people have been injured. Power outages and fires have occurred in some areas, and there has also been damage to roads and bridges and the collapse of buildings,” Takaichi said. “I ask everyone to take action to protect themselves, including evacuating to a safe location.”

About 300,000 people have been instructed to go to evacuation centres, the disaster management agency said. The areas with the biggest tremors will remain at risk of further strong quakes and landslides for about a week since the shallow earthquake is triggering seismic activity in the area, according to the Japan Meteorological Agency (JMA).

So far there have been more than 60 aftershocks ranging in magnitude from 1 to 4, the agency said. A tsunami warning was issued immediately after the quake, ​but was lifted within two hours.

One person was killed in south-west Japan when a house collapsed during the earthquake, Kyodo News reported.

Two hospitals reported ​more than 50 injuries each, including 10 in a serious condition, the public broadcaster NHK said.

“People are coming in with burns and fractures from being trapped under objects due to the earthquake, and ambulances are constantly bringing in injured people,” NHK quoted one hospital employee as saying.

“Inside the hospital, there are water leaks and electrical system failures.”

Several people on a high-speed ‌train at the time of the quake were also ‌injured and more were missing after a chimney collapsed at a Nippon Paper Industries factory, according to local media reports.

An explosion occurred in an Aeon shopping mall shortly after the earthquake, trapping “many people”, fire services said. The broadcaster TBS reported that police said “quite a few” were presumed dead.

As night fell, regional officials said they believed 10 people were unaccounted for in the mall, public broadcaster NHK reported. It earlier cited police as saying between 20 and 30 of the mall’s employees could not be contacted.

Takaichi pledged late yesterday that emergency responders would work “tirelessly” through the night “starting with the rescue and lifesaving of those affected”.

An Aeon spokesperson said customers and employees were evacuated after the initial quake and the cause of the explosion remained unclear. A government official subsequently told reporters that Aeon Kumamoto reported a gas leak, though it had not yet been determined as the cause.

Footage showed one side of the mall, the prefecture’s largest with roughly 200 shops, was torn away, exposing steel beams ‌and leaving debris strewn across the neighbouring car park. Several ambulances and fire engines were parked outside as rescue teams searched for survivors.

Footage from NHK showed several other buildings on fire or partly collapsed, along with large fissures on ‌major roads, including an elevated highway. TSMC, the world’s largest contract chip maker, Sony and Fujifilm evacuated workers from their factories in the area.

Chiharu Hara, a 35-year-old recruitment agent who was in Kumamoto, told AFP that she was “terrified” when the quake struck.

“The office swayed violently side to side. I was afraid it would collapse. Everyone panicked,” Hara said.

The quake’s epicentre was about 12 miles (20km) south of Kumamoto, central Kyushu island’s largest city, with a population of about 700,000. The US Geological Survey initially said the earthquake had a magnitude of 7.1, but revised it later to 6.8. The tremor at 4.27 pm local time had a magnitude of 7.1, the JMA said, but reached the highest level of 7 on Japan’s shindo scale. A subsequent aftershock with a magnitude of 6.1 was registered at 5.08pm.

Japan, which is located along the “ring of fire” of volcanoes and oceanic trenches in the Pacific basin, is one of the world’s most earthquake-prone countries, with a tremor occurring at least every five minutes. The country accounts for about 20% of the world’s earthquakes of magnitude 6 or more.

The massive earthquake in Kumamoto 10 years ago killed 275 people and injured a further 2,739. It damaged thousands of buildings including the city’s castle, a popular tourist site. Some of the castle’s stone walls were damaged in the most recent quake.

Kyushu Electric Power said 48,000 homes had ​lost power, while ​the railway company JR Kyushu suspended services, including its high-speed bullet trains. Kumamoto airport also shut its runway as airlines diverted and ​cancelled flights.

The telecoms operators KDDI and NTT Docomo ‌said there was disruption to their ​mobile phone services owing to power shortages ​and transmission-line failures. There were no irregularities reported at the nuclear power stations in the area, Japan’s nuclear regulation authority said.

The Japanese military has mobilised 3,600 personnel for disaster relief operations and sent 20 aircraft to assess the damage from the air, the defence minister said.

Japan is haunted by the memory of a massive 9.0-magnitude undersea quake in 2011, which triggered a tsunami that left around 18,500 people dead or missing and wrecked the Fukushima nuclear plant.

In an era of hyperpolitics, the left needs to organise

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 15:43:35 GMT

Mark Bergfeld and Derrick Joad on Zoe Williams’ interview of the political theorist Anton Jäger

Zoe Williams’ article on Anton Jäger (Meet the man whose groundbreaking book is being devoured by the left, 23 July) reminded me of something that I encounter in trade union meetings: people no longer come to them. But neither do they go to church or the synagogue, nor do they volunteer as the youth football coach. They work intolerable hours or are logged in, like me, writing this from my beach vacation in Greece.

In that sense, I agree with Jäger’s premise that we are in an era of hyperpolitics. Yet, as a trade unionist who dedicates his life to rebuilding the power of working people, I confront a problem that has led me to cave in to hyperpolitics. I co-produced a podcast on cleaners’ work and lives, and have been running an influencer campaign with hairdressers because that is how we get the union message out. People might not attend a meeting, but they will watch something on TikTok or Instagram, or listen to a podcast on Spotify.

Jäger’s argument appears to have a nostalgia for Christian democracy and the system of “pillars”: a society divided between Christian and social-democratic institutions, in which a person could spend their life within one denomination.

Living in Brussels, I met a trade union leader in his 60s whose father had been a miner. He joined the Christian union when he started in the printing trade, remained in the socialist health insurance system and joined the Christian Democrats because he thought it might help save his workplace. He attended one party meeting, hated the people there and never returned.

Jäger is right that intensity without organisation rarely produces power. But the task is to build plural institutions to counter the monopolistic tendencies of corporate power. The weakness of today’s organisations cannot be resolved by harking back to a golden age; it needs to draw its inspiration from the future. Mark BergfeldBrussels, Belgium

Hyperpolitics – politics practised now after the destruction of those institutions that gave the people a voice in politics – is a demonstration of the American political theorist Sheldon Wolin’s contention that democracy is a short-lived upsurge in people power that is soon nullified by the political actions of its powerful opponents. One example he quotes is the destruction of union power.

It was claimed that Margaret Thatcher’s reforms introduced the democratic decision process to industrial relations. Successive Labour leaders have defenestrated trade unions from the decision-making process, claiming this would made the party more democratic. This institutional destruction was a popular “democratic” reform, claiming to return power to the people while intending the opposite.

Anton Jäger is correct that the new hyperpolitics poses no threat to capital, as the real threat comes from the sustained struggle from organised interests. Some hope is to be found in the new trade unions such as the Independent Workers Union of Great Britain. Only they have put a check on the abuse of employer power in the retail trade. Ephemeral groups such as Occupy can be ignored as they lack the heft to force change.

Perhaps this is the reason for the popularity of the Green party among young people – they believe it is the only organised political group that is openly opposed to the inequities that characterise Britain today. Derrick JoadLeeds

Chicken farms and the reality of food production in Britain

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 15:37:47 GMT

Richard Griffiths and Will Raw respond to an article by George Monbiot in which he argues that industrial poultry farming is killing our rivers

George Monbiot is wrong in his belief that chicken farms harm rivers (Besieged by lobbyists, will UK ministers protect our ecosystems? No, they’ll chicken out, 23 July). Our farms have no direct contact with the soil and operate under permits issued and regulated by the Environment Agency, giving transparency on how manure is managed on site and where it goes when it leaves.

The chicken manure produced in the UK is used either for energy generation or as a fertiliser by other farming sectors. Each destination has full traceability, and manure will often be transported across the country to be used where it is most needed.

It may be convenient to blame a sector he does not like for a problem, but that diverts attention from addressing the issues that some of our rivers are facing. At some point, the reality of food production, and the fact that we do it well and responsibly, will have to supplant the social-media-friendly rhetoric. Richard GriffithsChief executive, British Poultry Council

By dismissing modern poultry farms as “factories”, George Monbiot does little to advance the serious discussion needed about the challenges of producing the nation’s food while also protecting and enhancing our environment.

Policymakers have a responsibility to hear from all those affected by their decisions, not least farmers who have long balanced their custodianship of the land with producing our food. Constructive dialogue between the farming sector, government, regulators and the public over issues such as planning reform is essential if we are to meet environmental requirements and achieve our pressing need to secure domestic food security.

British poultry farmers are continuing to support sustainability by investing millions of pounds into new technology and infrastructure, ensuring valuable nutrients that are crucial to producing food are utilised responsibly.

The real challenge is not choosing between food and nature, but finding practical ways to deliver both. If Mr Monbiot wants to be part of the solution, he should come out with me and visit one of our farms, where he will see that British poultry farmers remain fully committed to playing their part. Will RawChair, NFU Poultry Board

Why migraines are often undiagnosed

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 15:37:40 GMT

Dr Sally Cheseldine reflects on the experience of people who cannot articulate their pain and the significance of cravings

During my clinical career, I noticed that migraine was rarely diagnosed in individuals with severe intellectual disabilities or autism who were non-verbal and therefore unable to say that they had a sore head (Letters, 24 July). Instead, there was a high level of damaging head-banging, something that others say they feel tempted to do if they don’t have access to rapid pain relief for their migraine.

I was interested in the suggestion that cravings for cheese might be caused by migraine (The truth about migraines: what causes them – and how to find relief, 19 July). Cheese contains tryptophan, and it was shown in the 1990s (McDougle et al) that people with severe autism who had very low levels of tryptophan showed dramatic increases of several stereotypic behaviours, including banging.

In addition to headaches being misdiagnosed, I would also suggest that there is a significant part of the population in which it is completely undiagnosed due to the “diagnostic overshadowing” effect of other labels, with harmful consequences. Dr Sally CheseldineRetired consultant clinical psychologist

‘He liked to get people’s blood boiling’: metal masters Mastodon on the loss of bandmate Brent Hinds – and his shocking words before his death

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 15:00:07 GMT

The Grammy-winning band had an acrimonious rift with Hinds – then he died in a motorbike crash. They explain how they’re paying tribute on their new album, and why their love for each other never ended

Mastodon are near the end of a tour where they’re playing 22 shows in 14 different European countries during a record-breaking heatwave, when they video-call me outside a Bordeaux venue. Bassist and co-lead singer Troy Sanders says the experience has been “31 days of musical bliss”. He’s not being sarcastic, either.

“Things are super energetic, even at day 31,” he insists. “We’re contemplating even staying in Europe for a few days when this tour is over, because we’re enjoying ourselves so much.” It’s pleasantly surprising to see Sanders and drummer/co-vocalist Brann Dailor, sat to his left, in such high spirits, given the anguish and unrest they’ve endured over the last 18 months.

In February 2025, Dailor’s mother, Michele Lawrence, died aged 69. The next month, the band announced they’d parted ways with co-founding guitarist/singer Brent Hinds, ending a 25-year-long partnership. Hinds railed against his ex-bandmates on social media, calling them a “shit band with horrible humans … incapable of singing in key”, among plenty of other insults. He then died in a motorcycle accident, at the age of 51.

Mastodon are one of US metal’s most imaginative and successful acts, with a Grammy win and three Top 10 albums, and Hinds, a hard-partying maverick, had been a big part of what made them so distinctive and respected. Where contemporaries such as Trivium and Killswitch Engage were thoroughbred metal acts, Hinds gave Mastodon a defiant country twang, reflecting his Alabama upbringing and early years playing the banjo. Combined with Dailor’s virtuoso style, inspired by vintage prog, and co-guitarist Bill Kelliher’s primal riffs, “what we had sounded original and different,” Dailor says. “We always saw ourselves rooted in metal, but we could shape shift if we wanted.” When Black Sabbath played their farewell gig last year – two weeks before the death of Ozzy Osbourne – it was Mastodon who were selected to open the show, a band capable of igniting a stadium as well as inspiring reverence from the genre’s greats.

The deaths of Hinds and Dailor’s mother are the thematic core of the Atlantans’ upcoming ninth studio album, Marrow Deep. Its title references the fact that Dailor’s relationships with them were “the deepest you can get with a person. It’s hard to think of closer people that we could lose.”

The lyric-writing was the members’ way of processing those losses. Lead single Your Ghost Again dissects their complex relationship with Hinds, whereas Out Like a Lamb is for Lawrence, who died in her sleep after suffering cancer, rheumatoid arthritis and other ailments during her life. Dailor likens both Hinds and Lawrence to Keith Richards: figures who lived far longer than people assumed they would.

Hinds was arguably the most chaotic character in 21st-century metal. A former heroin addict, he lived in vans, boat sheds and abandoned apartments before joining Mastodon. He continued to party and drink long after his bandmates grew beyond such things – including co-guitarist Bill Kelliher, who almost died of alcohol-induced pancreatitis in 2009. “If any of us did half the stuff that Brent pulled off, we’d all have been dead years ago,” Dailor says. “We’ve always been a hard-partying band, but for the last 10, 15 years, the three of us really settled down and were focusing more on our live show and being productive in the studio. He was still rocking, which was, for a lot of people from the outside looking in, the most admirable thing about him. But from the inside it’s not always that much fun.”

In 2011, the drummer told Kerrang!: “People think [Hinds is] a fucking mental case, but there’s a beautiful person in there.” What was beautiful about him? Sanders answers: “He could find beauty in a lot of things: trees, mountains, caverns, oceans, music, people, handmade crafts. An appreciation for lots of originality and creativity.”

Dailor says Hinds loved “the honest things. He was the real deal, you know? His emotions were right there all the time and he could easily access them through his instrument.”

Following their breakthrough with 2004 single Blood and Thunder, the press touted Mastodon and their intellectual approach for “saving” metal. From 2007 to 2008, they supported Metallica on their stadium-filling World Magnetic tour. Their next album, 2009’s disorientatingly psychedelic Crack the Skye, was widely lauded; Hinds masterminded much of it, after being knocked out in a 2007 brawl outside an awards show and put into a three-day coma.

“He had vertigo for months and couldn’t really get up, so he was just sitting at home with an acoustic guitar,” Dailor recalls. “There were no bars for him to go to. He was forced to stay at home, so I think that, as a result, you have Crack the Skye.”

It started a string of successful records where the band wrestled with personal crises. The Hunter, a Top 10 hit in 2011, controversially stripped back Mastodon’s more brutal and progressive edges, was named after Hinds’s brother Brad, who died on a hunting trip in 2010. Dailor’s contributions to 2014’s Once More ’Round the Sun were inspired by his mother, who’d fallen off a chair in her kitchen and briefly been declared dead, and 2017’s Emperor of Sand was about cancer: Dailor’s mother and Sanders’ wife had been diagnosed with the disease, and Kelliher had recently lost his mother to a brain tumour. The album’s opener, Sultan’s Curse, won the 2018 Grammy for best metal performance.

“It summarised the story of us four dudes,” Sanders reflects. “Starting because we all appreciated Iron Maiden, Thin Lizzy and Neurosis, and then, 18 years later, we’re on this stage winning this award that was the furthest thing from our minds ever.”

Despite the increased success, Hinds’s involvement dwindled. According to Dailor, the guitarist grieved for his brother through “alcohol, drug abuse and self-medication”. From The Hunter onwards, the drummer tried to make the rehearsal room “fun” to tempt Hinds to contribute, inadvertently leading to their change in sound: “Come down and we’ll have some fun! We’ll write Curl of the Burl and Stargasm and it’ll be fun! It doesn’t have to be heavy!”

In 2015, Hinds made headlines when he told Guitar Player, “I fucking hate heavy metal, and I don’t want to be in a heavy metal band.”

“Brent said a lot of things that he probably didn’t mean,” Dailor counters when I bring up the quote. “He liked to talk some shit and stir the pot and get people’s blood boiling, I guess. I feel like he felt he could control a situation if he threw a wrench.”

The way that the band and Hinds parted ways remains a mystery. In their statement, Mastodon said it was a mutual decision; Hinds later claimed he was kicked out for “embarrassing them for being who I am”. Dailor and Sanders refuse to tell me what happened, but Dailor shoots down the rumour that Hinds punched him in the face, which stems from a public appearance he made just before the announcement where he had a black eye. “Brent texted me when that was all stirred up, and he was like, ‘Dude, I can’t believe people think I punched you in the face!’” he smiles.

So you were still in contact after everything happened?

“He reached out late at night sometimes, like, ‘Hey, I still love you, buddy.’ I was like, ‘Yeah, my mom just died, I don’t know. I love you too, but I need time in my life. I can’t even deal with Mastodon stuff right now.’ It was hard for me to get out of bed, to be honest with you.”

At the same time, Hinds was bitter towards his former bandmates on Instagram, where he left the “shit band with horrible humans” comment. Sanders reacts sternly when I mention it: “He was trying to be funny. It was pretty cute.”

Hinds later made more comments, in excruciating detail: “I’ve never seen anyone in my life look in the mirror more than Troy Sanders. He thinks he’s God’s gift to anything. I’ve never met three people that were so full of themselves. It’s disgusting.” But Dailor says that the drama became nothing but a “blip” after the guitarist’s death. The remaining members received the news over the phone from Hinds’s ex-wife while they were at Atlanta airport. “I was devastated,” Dailor remembers. “All the shit-talking that had happened – you reference the Instagram comment section shit – I didn’t think about any of that. We got 25 years of a deep relationship with this guy. I could tell who he was by the smell of his farts.”

Marrow Deep is dedicated to Lawrence and Hinds, but it’s a celebration of the present and future, as well. It marks the debut of new guitarist Nick Johnston and the first album where former session keyboardist João Nogueira is a full-time member, and it contains their most technical and metallic music since the 2000s. There are also a host of guest spots from peers and influences, including Gojira’s Joe Duplantier, Lamb of God’s Randy Blythe, Queens of the Stone Age’s Josh Homme and Black Sabbath bassist Geezer Butler.

“We listened to Geezer’s book and he name-checked us at the end, as far as being a band that he was into,” Dailor says. “Sabbath have been very kind to us over the years. The first time I ever met Tony Iommi, he came into the dressing room and he was like, ‘Oh, Mastodon! Me and Geez were listening to you guys on the bus last night.’”

At the start of second track Poisonous Weapons, there’s a sample from 1986 cult thriller film River’s Edge, where Dennis Hopper’s character Feck yells, “And I felt so fucking alive!” That’s because – for Dailor, who’s sporting a River’s Edge T-shirt – “the band Mastodon feels fucking alive”.

“When one of the integral members, one of your brothers, dies, it’s obviously a very painful thing to go through, but it also makes you question where you’re at,” he explains. “Seeing Brent in his casket was so difficult to wrap our heads around, and it makes you want to feel fucking alive. We’re still here, so we better get to it.”

Marrow Deep is released 28 August on Loma Vista

Captain Chris ‘Hunter-Killer’ Philp single-handedly takes on French navy

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 14:50:52 GMT

Shots fired in the Channel are all in a day’s work for the intrepid shadow home secretary

C’est magnifique, mais ce n’est pas la guerre. Captain Chris “Hunter-Killer” Philp had been on patrol since first light in the Channel. While the rest of the country was still asleep, the Philpster was scanning the horizon for rubber dinghies full of illegal immigrants. Something he had never done in his previous life as immigration minister. Back then he had sought to rehouse new arrivals in hotels. Now he wanted to send them to a watery grave.

It had been a quiet morning. Too quiet. Just the one sighting of a child with a rubber ring paddling off the beach in Boulogne. But Hunter-Killer was taking no chances. All it takes is one child and before long there will be hundreds of thousands making the crossing with swimming aids bought from the local Carrefour. So the Philpster had called in the RAF. Minutes later, a Typhoon FGR4 had blasted the kid out of the water. Job done. Pour encourager les autres.

Half an hour later, all hell broke loose. A French warship had appeared starboard. The next thing Hunter-Killer heard was the sound of 17 indistinct pops in the distance. “Get down,” he shouted to his crew. “We’re under attack.” Weirdly, no one on board the Philpster’s MTB disguised as a fishing vessel seemed remotely worried. How come they were so slow to sense danger? There again, few had the finely tuned antennae of the Philpster. Those years of training with the Special Boat Service had paid off.

Hunter-Killer threw himself on the floor of the wheelhouse, waiting for the gunshots to stop. “I think it’s safe now,” a deckhand said. “It was just some French sailor firing some shots from a handgun away from us into the sea. It wasn’t as if he was aiming at us or anything. He was probably just test-firing. It’s no big deal.”

“You don’t understand,” squeaked Captain Philpster. “This was a definite attempt by the French to intimidate me. Typical of Johnny Foreigner to send out a warship to track the shadow home secretary. They don’t like it up ’em. They’ve probably got special guns that fire round corners. So you think they’re shooting in a harmless direction but the bullets turn 90 degrees in flight. I came within a whisker of being hit. Not that anyone gets to intimidate Hunter-Killer. Help! Help!”

The crew looked rather nonplussed. Most of them hadn’t even heard the shots – “he was probably using a silencer”, said the Philpster – let alone had any idea they had come under serious attack. But Hunter-Killer was adamant. The Frenchies had been out to eliminate him. He had got too close to stopping the small boat crossings and Macron would never stand for that. So he was prepared to stop at nothing. Even risk starting a global conflict. Well, it had ended badly for Napoleon and it would end badly for Macron. Nor should the French forget that it had been the English who saved them in the second world war. Well, we wouldn’t make that mistake again.

“Sacré bleu!” said one member of Border Force. “There are often exercises at sea involving the Royal or the French navy, and shots are occasionally fired, usually using blanks. This may be nothing at all.”

The Philpster ordered him to keep quiet. The last thing he wanted was any collaborators speaking in French. Careless talk costs vies. He pulled the burner phone out of his pocket and speed-dialled Kemi. “I’m under attack,” he gasped. “Even though the French aren’t shooting at me, they are definitely shooting at me. They don’t want me to stop any small boats crossing the Channel, even though I haven’t yet seen any small boats. We need to be on our guard. The smuggling gangs must now be using invisible dinghies.”

Kemi’s eyes lit up. If only she was prime minister, she would be able to launch a tactical first nuclear strike on Calais. OK, there might be some collateral damage in Kent but it would still be worth it. Instead, she had to order the Philpster to disengage with the enemy.

“I can’t do that,” said Hunter-Killer. “While most politicians run from danger, I am trained to run towards it. So what I will do is film a clip of me being extraordinarily brave by doing nothing and then phone the French embassy to complain. If only they put as much effort into intimidating the people smugglers as they put into intimidating me. Not that I was intimidated. But it would be good to see the French navy also firing shots in the opposite direction to the dinghies.”

‘Topless modelling never aligned with me’: inside Everyone’s Seen My Tits, the play by a former page 3 model

The Guardian Tue, 28 Jul 2026 14:03:02 GMT

As she brings her memoir to the Edinburgh festival, Keeley Hazell talks about trauma, exploitation, the hollowness of the high life – and her new career as a writer on Ted Lasso

There was a time in the mid-2000s when it felt as though “everyone” had seen her topless, says Keeley Hazell. Page 3 was a staple of the tabloid press, lads’ mags were booming and she was one of the country’s most recognisable glamour models. “There was excitement, but also a lot of shame and embarrassment,” the softly spoken Hazell reflects. “Topless modelling never really aligned with me as a person.”

Hazell, who was born in Lewisham, London, left modelling in her early 20s and moved to LA to become an actor. But the emotional impact of her time in the industry has stayed with her, partly inspiring her 2025 book Everyone’s Seen My Tits: Stories and Reflections from an Unlikely Feminist. She describes the writing process as a “release” when we meet in London, where she has been preparing for an Edinburgh fringe theatre/comedy show based on the book. “I was able to give myself a voice,” she says, for “a period where I felt voiceless”.

The show makes her think “of the image of Russian dolls – I’m performing as me, but then I’m also performing as a version of me”. This sense of having multiple identities is nothing new for her. She remembers “presenting differently” to the Keeley Hazell people saw on magazine covers, “in vintage clothes and very grungey”. So much so that she was rarely recognised in the street, even at the height of her fame. When asked if she was a Page 3 model, she would deny it. “I’d be like, ‘Are you saying I look like a Page 3 model?’ And it was a really interesting experiment because they’d often be like, ‘No, no, you’re way more classy than that.’ It was weird because they were talking about me but I also felt separate from it.”

Hazell’s introduction to glamour modelling was fast and unexpected. At 16, she left school and started working in a hair salon, where a colleague encouraged her to apply to become a model. She had some photos taken and sent them off to “a bunch of addresses” given to her – one of which, unbeknown to Hazell, was the Daily Star’s “beach babe” competition. She won, and a few months later entered the Sun’s “Page 3 idol” competition. “I won that too, and that was the start of my career.”

Modelling was very different to her life at home on a council estate. “I went from growing up there to owning a luxury apartment overlooking the Thames.” Hazell was a “canvas”, and she knew she could be made up to fit a photographer’s image. “I was so young, there was so much exploitation, I was not emotionally or mentally prepared for it.” Safeguarding, she says, was basically nonexistent. “There was so little protection for women entering that industry. I had no idea about the things I needed in place, and my family didn’t either.”

Looking back, Hazell almost can’t believe Page 3 was real. “It was just a wild thing to grow up with … those images were so readily available in newspapers and in newsagents.” There are times when she thinks of those days fondly; she was earning more money than she thought possible and got to travel the world. But she regrets “not having more control” over things. “A lot of the time I was just numb. I’d drink a lot and tell myself to enjoy the party.”

Today, she gives carefully considered answers, with the air of someone who has had the time and space to process it all. Therapy has helped enormously, she tells me, particularly when it came to dealing with the fallout from a sex tape sold to the Sunday Sport. It was “terrifying” to write about the experience and “in a way relive it” Hazell says. “So many women experience some aspect of sexual violation and abuse in any realm, the shame for me needed to be ridded.”

The Edinburgh fringe show is the latest chapter in that process. It begins in 2019 with her auditioning to play Keeley Jones, a character inspired by her, in Ted Lasso. She didn’t get the part but she did land a recurring role in the series and serves as a staff writer. Hazell can’t tell me much more about her solo show’s structure – she’s still in the writing process. “Right now I’m just staring at a laptop, ordering food and thinking, this is difficult,” she says with a laugh. She is certain, though, that it will be funny. “Trauma and humour are intertwined … even within the spiralling and the PTSD of it all, it should be a humorous retelling.” And it feels freeing to have, at last, complete autonomy over the Keeley Hazell people see and hear from. “It is incredibly powerful to have a voice.”

Keeley Hazell: Everyone’s Seen My Tits is at Pleasance Courtyard, Edinburgh, 5 to 29 August
