Obama to Headline Democratic Redistricting Fund-Raiser

The New York Times July 28, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

After exhausting their gerrymandering options in 2026, the party is hoping to redraw more congressional maps ahead of the next election cycle.

By Nick Corasaniti

Former President Barack Obama will hold a fund-raiser in late August for the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, a fresh sign that Democrats intend to continue their aggressive push to gerrymander congressional districts ahead of the 2028 election.

The fund-raiser will take place on Martha’s Vineyard and will be hosted by Eric Holder, the former attorney general under Mr. Obama and the chairman of the committee, which is the main Democratic group focused on redistricting.

While Democrats appear to have exhausted all of their options for new maps before the midterm elections this year, their focus on the 2028 election still requires investment in crucial, state-level elections this fall. Democrats hope to protect or build trifectas in various states — single-party control of both chambers of legislatures plus the governor’s office — or Democratic supermajorities that would allow them to override a hostile governor’s veto.

The emergence of Mr. Obama on the political fund-raising circuit comes as Democrats, at least at the national level, are facing a significant cash shortfall.

Drawing even with Republicans in the national redistricting wars has been a top priority for Mr. Holder, Mr. Obama and Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic House minority leader. Mr. Obama, who remains one of the party’s most popular and influential figures, was a prominent supporter of a congressional gerrymander in California and an attempted one in Virginia.

“The race by Republicans to gerrymander is not over — and between potential redraws and the November election, the 2028 redistricting fight is already underway,” John Bisognano, the president of the National Democratic Redistricting Committee, said in a statement on Tuesday.

Details of the fund-raiser were first reported by Punchbowl News.

Democrats have largely been playing catch-up on the national redistricting front. Ever since President Trump sparked the battle by imploring Republicans in Texas to take the rare partisan step of redrawing their congressional map last year to benefit Republicans in the midterms, Democrats have faced a host of hurdles, in part because of redistricting reforms pushed by Mr. Obama, Mr. Holder and other Democrats.

The result has been the creation of as many as a dozen new districts that will favor Republicans this year.

Democrats have turned their attention to 2028 with the goal of reversing that new advantage and then some. States including New York, Virginia, Illinois and Maryland have all signaled a desire to redraw their maps for the next cycle. California could also try to redraw its map yet again, and some Democrats hope Washington and Oregon will join the battle, as well.

Republicans are also poised to redraw maps in many states in 2028, including Indiana, Mississippi, Nebraska and Kansas — as well as states redrawn in the past year, including Texas, Alabama and Louisiana, where further opportunities may lie.

Nick Corasaniti is a Times reporter covering national politics, with a focus on voting and elections.

How to Predict the Weather in Our Era of Freakish Storms

The New York Times July 28, 2026

I didn’t want to have to depend on a weather app to know when the storms are coming.

Fog approaching off the coast of Brooklin, Maine. Credit... Natalie Ivis for The New York Times

Supported by

By Heidi Julavits

On Thursday, June 19, 2025, the National Weather Service in Reno, Nev., issued a two-day forecast for the region that included Lake Tahoe, a popular and mystically blue-green body of water surrounded by mountains, some almost as high as 11,000 feet.

Friday, June 20, called for winds of up to 25 miles per hour, punctuated by 40 m. p. h. gusts in the lower altitudes, dangerous conditions for boating and severe enough to prompt a Wind Advisory. But Saturday’s weather — clear, with light winds, the high an unseasonably cool 61 degrees — seemed far more hospitable to recreational activities on the water.

On the morning of June 21, anyone looking out a window would have seen blue skies and white sheep-shaped clouds. Anyone reading the morning’s updated weather report would have noted how it validated the earlier one, with slight variations. The forecast called for increased cloudiness and even lower high temperatures, with a slight chance of showers and thunderstorms, the winds strengthening to a still moderate 10 m. p. h.

People piled into boats and onto the lake.

Around 12 p. m., the weather started to sharply veer from the predictions. Boaters couldn’t see the storm clouds building to the northwest, or the snow that began to fall on the mountain pass around 1 p. m., or the lightning that forced the cancellation of a foot race at a nearby ski resort.

Shortly after 2 p. m., the conditions began to rapidly, and startlingly, deteriorate on Lake Tahoe.

Over the next hour or so, the temperature dropped to 43 degrees from 55. Data from a weather buoy near Tahoe City reported winds increasing to over 29 m. p. h. from seven, with gusts as high as 45. The winds, traveling the length of the lake, had 22 miles of uninterrupted running room to push the water into increasingly higher, rowdier peaks. The earlier forecast called for waves of one foot. These waves reached 10.

It started to rain. Marble-size hail fell from the sky. At 2:20 p. m., a sinking boat, carrying 10 passengers, called 911. At 2:57 p. m., a 28-foot boat, also with 10 passengers aboard, capsized. At 3:24 p. m., a mutual-aid call went out to the Coast Guard and local rescue agencies for help responding to multiple boats in distress. The South Lake Tahoe Police Department alone received more than 50 calls.

By 4:25 p. m., the winds had dropped to a negligible three m. p. h., blue sky appeared between the dispersing clouds and six people — later eight — were confirmed dead.

I’ve been caught in a handful of unpredicted storms — squalls, we’ve always called them — when the formerly scrutable world, within minutes, turns lawless. Water shoots upward and sideways. The wind transforms into a solid, high-speed object. Harbors and bays I’ve navigated for years morph so violently that it’s like being trapped inside the psyche of a raging planet. Since my first squall encounter, in my early teens, I’ve been on wary alert whenever getting into a boat. The weather report. The blue sky. The safe harbor. My own judgment. Whom, or what, should I trust?

These questions were live in my mind when I first learned about what people in the media and online were calling the “freak storm” on Lake Tahoe. Versions of the refrain “No one saw it coming” seemed to expose a logical, yet apparently fallacious, notion about how meteorology works: The more ferocious the weather, the harder it should be for computer models to miss it.

An article in The New York Times succinctly corrected that assumption: “The technology meteorologists use to predict weather failed to pick up the localized conditions.”

At the time, I was 3,000 miles east of Lake Tahoe on the coast of Maine, where technology regularly fails to pick up our localized conditions, too. Given how many people work and relax on the ocean around here, nearly everyone’s got a hairy weather story; like me, no one is eager to repeat the experience. Yet our forecasts can be so head-scratchingly wrong, people in town often ask other people in town: Where do you get your weather? Responses vary and can resemble idiosyncratic, highly personalized divining systems. This wind app plus that website’s radar plus that guy on that radio station plus my barometer.

I get my weather at the nearby dock. The people who work and loiter there know the area and its weather vicissitudes well. Whenever I think a forecast might be worse than just comically wrong, I drive down to the harbor and ask around.

Because it’s not true that nobody sees the sudden storms coming. Perhaps they aren’t as freakish as portrayed. In the case of the Lake Tahoe storm, one man said that a “sixth sense” told him something unpredictable, or unpredicted, was about to happen. He noticed “the lake was laying down, the clouds were building up.” While others stayed on the water, trusting the morning forecast would hold, he returned to shore.

I wanted to develop a sixth sense like this man, and not because I distrust science or support the budget cuts to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration, though maybe those cuts will make sixth senses a compulsory skill. Sixth senses are also increasingly recommended because of climate change. As Phillip LaFrance, who runs a boat charter and is one of the people I regularly consult on the dock, told me: “I’m no longer saying, ‘Oh, it’s only a thunderstorm.’ They should be feared more.”

I was ready to fear. I was also ready to hone my weather literacy so that I could distinguish, if only in our tiny coastal notch, a day that might turn wicked from one that probably wouldn’t. I wanted a sincere response to a rhetorical question I once heard posed to a salty weather wizard: What magic are you pulling out of the air?

Natural weather forecasting, and old sailors’ aphorisms such as “rainbow to windward, rain ahead,” would seem to be of increasingly quaint irrelevance as technological advances in weather science continue to improve. Eric Sloane, author of the 1949 “Weather Book” — which looks like a children’s illustrated guide to clouds but is actually a complex meteorological primer for weather enthusiasts — drolly nodded toward the ongoing jostling for authority between science and wisdom. “Anyone who has known a sailor with ‘a weather eye’ and who has also seen the inside of a weather bureau,” Sloane wrote, “knows the difference between being weather-wise and being meteorologically accurate.”

One person who has managed to seamlessly combine traditional forecasting methods with science is Maine Public Radio’s meteorologist Lou McNally. For many, McNally has been a part of their mornings for 30 years. In addition to his jobs as a radio meteorologist and a professor at Unity Environmental University, where he teaches a course on climate change (“Some people would call it indoctrination, and I would agree”), McNally previously worked as the “folklore editor” at the National Weather Digest and wrote a weekly column called “Weather Whys” that ran in local Maine newspapers.

A proponent of the “lost art” of natural weather forecasting, his radio reports are more like informative, chatty yarns, weighed down by none of the usual bland meteorologicalities. “‘Considerable cloudiness,’” he told me. “What the heck is that? You go outside and consider it? I need to think about people who are going to be out in it and how it will affect them.”

A typical McNally report might begin: “The steam bath that was yesterday’s weather is being pushed south into the Mid-Atlantic, where our friends and neighbors will continue to cook.” He famously ends each report by reminding listeners of the limits to his predictive powers: “And that’s the way it looks from here.” Within his sign-off is a question his listeners might be asking themselves: How does it look where I am?

When we spoke, McNally was surrounded by files and books organized enough to suggest some sort of system, and scattered enough to suggest he regularly consults them all. He approaches weather — even, or especially, weather that’s already happened — as an unending mystery to probe rather than a bulletin to receive and deliver. Many meteorologists, he notes, use “canned forecasts, canned information.” These people are not, McNally said, “opening the window and taking a whiff.”

For a person hoping to acquire some natural weather forecasting basics, he advocates comparing the eventual weather against the prediction and “seeing how the forecasts played out.” He gave an example from early in his broadcast career, when, he said: “I got fried. I got burned.” He failed to predict a storm where “three-quarters of an inch of icy snow just falls out of the sky.” Afterward he studied the storm’s unusual confluence of factors to better spot one like it in the future. “The three or four times over the last 40 years that I have seen that happen [again],” he said, “I’ve forecasted it and nobody else has.”

People’s individual weather experiences — even people who’ve been dead for hundreds of years — have, for McNally, always been an inextricable facet of meteorological inquiry. When he decided, as a doctoral student, to map the path of the jet stream in 1785, he collected weather reports printed in newspapers, then filled the data gaps with descriptions of weather he found in old diaries. “I don’t know if it was just to get the mind and the hand going, or whether to get the ink flowing out of the pen,” he said of diarists’ tendency to start by noting the weather. He’d earlier tested this diary-as-data theory by comparing the weather passages in a diary from the 1940s belonging to a woman in Waterville, Maine, against the published reports. “She was saying things like, ‘Cloudy and dark, foggy, cool and damp,’ and then all of a sudden she said, ‘Sunny, dry, I could put out my whites.’” The weather reports from that same period validated his meteorological interpretation of her descriptions. “Cold front! Poof! Right there.”

My conversation with McNally suggested two important mental shifts.

One: Where forecasting is concerned, I should be as curious about the past and the present as I am about the future. This echoed some advice I’d already received from Maynard Bray, another trusted dock source, and more notably an engineer, writer and foremost expert on small North American wooden boats. He recommended the lessons inferred by the diary practice of the famed naval architect and design innovator Nathanael G. Herreshoff, who recorded the weather in Bristol, R. I., three times a day, from the age of about 20 until his death, 70 years later, in 1938.

Two: Weather isn’t a set of conditions locked into place at the beginning of the day.

“The first thing I ask them is, ‘Why?’” McNally said, when people want to know the forecast. Because the fact is: “They don’t care about the weather — they want to know if they can go to the beach.” A morning report can give people permission to do what they want with their day. Yet once that initial permission is given, they tend to stop seeking it.

Deriving useful intel from other people’s weather (or weather-keeping habits) is something I had, in theory, already learned from two of the canniest mariners I know: Jane Ahlfeld and Gretchen Snyder, who teach a course called “Elements of Sailing” at the wooden boatbuilding school in our town. I’ve studied with them twice.

“The hardest part of teaching,” Ahlfeld told me, “is figuring out the weather and using it the best you can.” A 37-year veteran, Ahlfeld is a uniquely positioned observer of not just our local weather peculiarities but also its longer-span climate evolutions. The challenges of her job have changed over the decades because “there are more days when we’re getting strong winds that we can’t go out in.”

(LaFrance, one of my dock consultants, has observed similar changes. Our once-reliable southwesterly summer wind is “all over the place,” and the gusts are higher. “It used to be 10-15 with gusts to 20,” he said, citing a typical forecast, “now it’s 10-15 with gusts to 30.”)

When I was Ahlfeld and Snyder’s student, class began each morning in an old shingled boathouse, listening to the NOAA buoy report on the weather radio, Channel 02. NOAA sets weather buoys up and down the coast to record data such as air and water temperatures, wave height, wind and gust speeds. Our report covered buoys starting in Boston and painstakingly worked its way northward. If we tuned in just after our local buoys were read by the monotonous, automated voice, we had to endure the entire 10- to 15-minute loop before returning to the information that presumably mattered. This exercise in patience underscored how our weather was connected to the weather of others — how, to use a local meteorological construction, if it was “blowing stink” in Boothbay, it might eventually be blowing stink where we were, too.

Ahlfeld kindly agreed to reacquaint me with the weather basics she taught me years ago. While we sat in my hot barn, she showed me handouts from our class that I should have found more familiar than I did. Beyond the diagrams explaining, say, cold fronts, Ahlfeld’s most instantly graspable takeaway involved change.

“I don’t know what that change necessarily is going to be,” she said, if she notices the wind dying or the temperature dropping or any abrupt shift in the conditions, “but I don’t want to be on the water, because something could boil up.” She added, “That’s air saying, ‘I’m not going to behave well, because I’m transitioning.’”

Another telling change is air pressure, which can be monitored with a barometer. Barometers resemble clocks, if minutes of time were inches (or millibars) of pressure. Like clocks, barometers have two hands. One is a measuring hand, which moves on its own; the other is a marker hand, which allows the observer to mark their last reading. If the measuring arm moves counterclockwise, the pressure is changing from higher to lower — low-pressure systems produce wetter, stormier weather — and people might ominously say, “The barometer is falling.”

If a person had no access to a barometer, Ahlfeld told me, here is how they could anticipate, 24 to 48 hours in advance, the arrival of a low-pressure system: First, high cirrus clouds, wisps of white called “mares tails,” appear. Then come “mackerel skies,” clouds that are “a little chunkier, like cottage cheese,” followed by fully overcast skies. That’s when, if it’s available, Ahlfeld consults her barometer.

“How concerned should I be about this system that’s coming through?” she asked. If the barometric pressure starts to fall quickly — if the distance between the marker arm and the measuring arm rapidly widens — that’s when people need to pay attention, because the faster the change, the more powerful, and potentially dangerous, the approaching system will be.

But a storm system isn’t the same as a sudden squall, defined by McNally as a “quick onset of wind, lasting just a short while and decreasing rapidly afterward,” behavior that inspired the weather adage “The sharper the blast, the sooner it’s past.”

I wanted to know how to foresee those.

Again, clouds. “Funky” clouds, Ahlfeld said, that are not “happy and floating along, these little puffs of wool,” but ones that start to pile up high and resemble curdled explosions (what I’ve known as “thunderheads”) or tall anvils, the tops flattened by the strong, upper-altitude wind.

“That is a bad sign,” she said, then added, circumspectly, “or whatever. It’s just a sign.”

(LaFrance also cited such clouds as a mandatory call to attention. “Vertical development,” he says, “or V. D. Which is not a medical problem.”)

But they still might be a problem. To know how much of a problem requires a person to know from which direction their weather comes. On this part of the Maine coast, ours comes from the direction of Waldo County, which Ahlfeld refers to as “a weather maker.” This is where our thunderstorms are forged. If I see an ominous cloud building between the distant uprights of a suspension bridge, it’s something to keep an eye on, because whatever that cloud contains is possibly headed toward me.

Finally, Ahlfeld shared one of her local rules of thumb.

“Never trust a west,” she said. During the summer, a wind blowing from the west means that a cold front is moving through our area, and a dry, cool, higher-pressure system is behind it. Here on land, the west wind is good news. It hearkens azure skies and sheep clouds. On the water, it arrives with an asterisk. The winds forcing the change can result in conditions that are, as Ahlfeld says, “strong and puffy, punchy.” Whatever winds and gusts are forecast, she said, they can build over the day and exceed — possibly far exceed — the predictions.

In the 1970s, the National Weather Service initiated a program called SKYWARN, which still solicits local volunteers as observers and reporters of “ground truth,” because they “can see things that radar and other technological tools cannot,” a handy rebuttal to anyone believing technology has eliminated the need for civilian input.

The concept of a person knowing the ground truth or their ground truth, besides being one of the most marvelous discoveries of my middle life, intersected with two words I heard when interrogating people around town about the source of their natural weather forecasting savvy.

Those two words were “intuition” and “gut.”

McNally also emphasized that you should “trust your gut first,” and “you need to pay attention to your gut,” because, he said, the forecast “is never 100 percent.”

“Gut,” in this case, isn’t only a synonym for a sixth sense. McNally is basically advocating a bodily approach to diary keeping. All of us contain whole lifetimes of weather data in the form of physical experiences. The more you pay attention to details around you, he said, and connect cause and effect, then the more you know to perk up “when you get a little gurgle in your stomach.”

A body, and other nearby bodies, can act as barometers, based on scientifically explicable causes. There’s a dozen or so colleges, McNally said, “where you can find a major, or at least a minor, in biometeorology,” which is the study of weather’s impact on plants, animals and humans.

“You heard the one about cows lying down means there’s going to be a storm?” McNally asked.

I had not.

Cows, he clarified, lie down because they’re tired. But, if you pass a field of cows lying in all different directions, and then a few hours later the cows are all pointed in the same direction, this indicates that the wind has shifted from light and variable to stronger and prevailing, meaning a new weather system is possibly on the way. Cows are considered prey, he explained, and “prey is going to put their tails into the wind.” A predator, catching the cows’ scent, will approach from downwind. The cows, thus, need to face in the direction of whatever predators might be coming to kill them so that they can run away.

Dogs are barometers, too. If you let your dog into the backyard during a high-pressure system, McNally said, it “goes to the corner, does what it does and then comes back.” But if the dog runs “this way and that way and this way and that way,” its zig-zaggy behavior indicates the pressure is dropping and a low is on the way. Why? Smells are held down by high pressure, released by low. The dog, he said, “is chasing yesterday’s squirrel, last Thursday’s rabbit.”

(By this same rough principle, swamps are “another natural weather indicator.” Swamps contain decomposing matter that releases methane gas bubbles. These bubbles rupture when the pressure drops. If the swamp “doesn’t stink when you drive by in the morning but it does in the afternoon,” then you know a low is approaching.)

Ahlfeld also mentioned how bodies function as atmospheric instruments. On low-pressure days, people take more naps. So do pets. The reason isn’t heaviness, as I had assumed, but its opposite. High pressure presses on the body, buttressing it. The body doesn’t need to reinforce its own boundaries because it gets an assist from the air around it. For this reason, dry days make a person feel lifted, spiritually but also physically. On low-pressure days, the interior is out of harmony with the exterior, which can be both physically and emotionally disorienting. Why am I so down when the world isn’t against me?

Pressure imbalances are the reason that more babies are born during storms — babies are suspended in a hermetically sealed “bag of water,” McNally says, and “you have to have the same air pressure outside as in or it will pop” — and also why some people’s joints hurt before it rains. Gasses in the blood expand when the pressure beyond the body starts to drop. Generally, “we’re porous enough to balance out that pressure,” he said. But knuckles and old knee injuries, i. e. places in the body with worn cartilage and scar tissue, can’t expand as quickly, and hurt.

I assembled some barometric facts about my own body. I get migraines before big blizzards — very low-pressure systems — arrive. I also thought more about those uneasy days, the ones when I’m venturing farther into the world, specifically the more tenuous watery part of it, and I’m inexplicably in a more heightened state and worried that the wind will get stronger, and the creased foil ocean will rip into whitecaps, and that the whole situation will become quite a bit sketchier than the forecast suggests.

I mentally walked myself through one of these days. What I first register as I approach the dock is the wind hitting my cheek from a certain direction. Given what I’ve most likely, unwittingly, associated with that angle of impact on my skin — weather that may eventually turn gnarly — it probably prompts me to scrutinize the harbor more closely and notice anomalies. The dark navy blue of the water, the individual boats, pointed toward the harbor’s mouth rather than the island, suddenly caught in what resembles a slow-motion shark attack, invisible jaws whipping them back and forth.

Finally I pieced it together. The wind on these days blew from the west.

When Ahlfeld and I first spoke in my barn about all-of-a-sudden storms, she remarked, “We haven’t had one this summer, which is sort of shocking to me.”

Then we got one.

On Aug. 27, my basic weather app showed sun, no rain and decent winds. Based on this forecast, my husband I decided to sail into a nearby bay.

Around noon, right before we left the harbor, he received a notification on his phone.

“It might rain around 5,” he said, and we rolled our eyes. A few days earlier, the first notable storm clouds in many weeks appeared. The sum result? A shallow palmful of drops scattered over the entire harbor.

Also, a rain warning wasn’t a storm warning. Rain was just wet; and recently, not even.

We sailed into the bay, rounded a navigational buoy and started the four-mile trip home. In the far distance, between the uprights of the bridge, we saw a dark mood gathering. Around 3:15 p. m., back in the harbor, the wind picking up, I noticed a clutch of small boats from the school where Ahlfeld teaches, one of which carried a friend of mine, heading back toward their harbor in the stiffening breeze. My son and I gaped at the cartoonishly looming clouds while we drove up the peninsula to the supermarket.

At 4:42 p. m., as we were going home, my husband texted: “Thunderrrr.” When we crossed the small causeway that spans a usually protected stretch of river, the river’s surface was white-capping. I had never seen this before. Then around the next bend we caught sight of the open water, its surface stoked into a half-white, half-black fury.

Once it was over, about 30 minutes later, I started texting. First to make sure people were OK; then to find out if anyone knew in advance that the squall was coming.

One friend, known for his abundant, triple-back-up caution, wrote: “No warning! We were in a boat, too, and had some rather hair-raising moments!” My friend in one of the school boats reported that the second-in-command radioed an alert, and that her instructor, for a moment, wasn’t too concerned — in front of them, the sky was clear — then turned around and clocked the darkness bearing down. They made it safely to their moorings before the wind hit.

The next day I went down to the dock to conduct a squall post-mortem. I spoke to Bray, who had also been on the water — “Came out of nowhere,” he said — and then to LaFrance, who said, “V. D., V. D.” He had rechecked the radar around 2 p. m. because he, too, noticed the clouds starting to build in the distance. The radar then had predicted the squall to hit precisely when it did, between 4:30 and 5 p. m.

Yet I hadn’t bothered to revisit the forecast since the morning, when my app suggested it was safe to go out. Ahlfeld succinctly and calmly repeated in a text what she’d been saying all along. “Watching those clouds approach [should] have you running to get back on land.”

Which, to be fair, we did do. Ahlfeld’s response seemed to indicate not that I hadn’t been properly vigilant, rechecking the radar throughout the day, but that I’d done exactly as she’d taught me. I also didn’t think, as I might have in the past, that meteorology had failed to adequately warn us about the squall. Instead I marveled at how well the system here worked. Even the people who claimed the storm “came out of nowhere” saw it with enough time to get to safety.

Which means — if people have honed their weather eyes, if they’re in touch with the ground truth — that the difference between a “freak storm” and a forecasted one is measurable in minutes. Possibly meteorology’s most trust-inspiring feature is that an informed, engaged citizenry must work with computer-model-generated forecasts rather than submit to their authority completely. Rightness and wrongness maybe aren’t related to whether earlier predictions come to pass; they’re instead determined by an ongoing set of decisions I’m making, based on the forecasts I’m perpetually receiving. The most up-to-date weather is at my fingertips — if my fingertips, and the body attached to them, touch not a screen but the ground, the water, the air.

In the past, when I’ve returned to New York City, where I work as a professor, I still check the daily forecast in Maine. But this tracking habit quickly dies, and I eventually return to my weatherless city life, where the most pressing concern is whether to pack an umbrella.

Increasingly, however, the weather does matter in the city; or as Sloane put it in “Weather Book,” “the weather is with us wherever we are.” People drown in basement apartments during flash floods caused by torrential rains. The wind gusts are regularly strong enough that the local meteorologists warn about “unsecured objects” on fire escapes or construction sites.

That same June morning I learned about the Tahoe storm, our daughter, 450 miles south of us, was slow-poaching in a New York City heat wave that broke numerous longstanding records. Then on July 14 came a rainstorm so dramatic it made international news. (“Watch: Flash flooding sweeps through New York City subways.”) Phone videos on social media, shot by alternately panicked or enthralled subway passengers at Manhattan’s West 28th Street station, showed water rushing down the stairs, onto the platform and into the train. The videos resembled outtakes from a submarine disaster movie where not all the extras received the same script. Some people stood on the seats as water seeped into the car, while others didn’t really seem to notice anything unusual happening at all.

Reports after the July storm referred to “localized” flooding around the city. (I’ve since identified which subway stations are most likely to flood when heavy rain is predicted, so that I can avoid them.) The city’s weather, and the specific alertness it requires, can vary greatly from one neighborhood, or even one block, to the next. “That’s the way it looks from here” is as applicable an adage to an urban location as it is to a rural one.

These days — actually all days, every day — I’m talking about the weather with the people in and around my apartment building. The lobby and the sidewalk are my urban docks. Local, “it happened to me” (or my neighbor or my friend or my friend’s neighbor’s friend) stories transmit not just specific conditions and their outcomes; through them I can learn to make better future decisions based on other people’s less fortunate ones.

Leave the basement, the train, the station. Take the plants off the fire escape. Stay clear of construction sites and big trees.

And while weather talk is sometimes derided as small talk, deployed to ward off more personal interactions, it’s also how to know an individual intimately. The sole experience I might share, in any given moment, with any given person in my immediate vicinity, is the weather around us. Even so, a person’s body is the ultimate microclimate, as local as local gets. The same weather impacts each of us differently, given how old we are, how many scars we have, how many air-conditioners we have in our windows, if we have a house at all. Telling others about our local conditions — and expanding what counts as weather literacy, as our local new normals tilt ever more extreme — that’s part of talking about the weather, too. When the wind reaches 35 m. p. h., it’s difficult to hear what people are saying. During the first five months of 2026, the wind gusts in New York City registered between 35 and 70 m. p. h. on 26 percent of the days.

But other connections — equally vital survival skills — might be blunted, as well, if the weather remains inscrutable and unknowable, and understood, or misunderstood, as a whimsically destructive force that no one can predict. What we risk missing is an opportunity for collective curiosity about, and appreciation of, our shared conditions. On Aug. 27, after Ahlfeld texted about the storm clouds, she wrote: “Sun and rain have me looking for rainbows 🌈. Nothing yet.” And then: “Rainbow! To the east.” I walked outside and faced east. The setting sun flared orange against the trees, as if to remind me that fall, my favorite Maine season, was on the way. A full rainbow arched above them, earth to sky to earth.

Heidi Julavits is a writer who grew up in Portland, Maine. Her most recent book is “Directions to Myself.”

Cyclospora Cases Are Rising. Here’s What to Know.

The New York Times July 28, 2026

Cyclospora Cases

Advertisement

Supported by

The parasitic infections have reached unprecedented levels in the United States. Experts have tips on how to stay safe.

By Alice Callahan and Caroline Hopkins Legaspi

The United States is in the midst of its worst year yet for cyclosporiasis, an intestinal illness caused by a parasite transmitted through food or water contaminated with human feces.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has confirmed or is investigating more than 11,500 cases in 41 states — the most cyclosporiasis cases ever recorded in a single year in the United States — and it has reported 308 hospitalizations. Since the agency’s last update on July 21, state health departments have logged thousands more cases.

Federal officials are also investigating an outbreak including nearly 2,000 people in nine states — Michigan, Ohio, Indiana, Kentucky, West Virginia, Illinois, Kansas, Oklahoma and Pennsylvania — that has been linked to iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms and grown in central Mexico. On July 17, Taylor Farms recalled potentially contaminated lettuce from 27 states, including products sold to restaurants, retail stores and food service distributors, including Taco Bell and Walmart. Details on the exact products and retail outlets affected have been sparse.

The Food and Drug Administration said it was investigating several other, smaller outbreaks, including one with 72 cases, but it did not disclose their locations or potential sources.

Health officials are scrambling to understand the true size and scope of the illnesses across the country, and are investigating multiple types of produce as potential sources. The number of cases is expected to rise in the weeks ahead, they have said. It can take up to six weeks for federal and state officials to determine if an illness is linked to an outbreak, according to the F. D. A.

Cyclospora is a microscopic parasite that infects people when they consume food or water contaminated with human feces containing its oocysts (or eggs), said Keith R. Schneider, a professor of food safety at the University of Florida.

Infections tend to rise from May through August in the United States because the parasite thrives in warm temperatures.

After the parasite is ingested, it can take from two days to two weeks or more for it to infect the intestinal lining and cause symptoms, including cramping and watery diarrhea.

An infected person will then shed the oocysts in their feces, but it takes another week or two for the parasite to become infectious outside the body. That lag most likely explains why the illness does not seem to spread directly from person to person, Dr. Schneider said.

The scale of the current cyclosporiasis outbreak is unlike any seen before in the United States, said Frank Yiannas, a food safety expert and former top official at the F. D. A.

The thousands of cases across multiple states imply a “massive degree of human fecal contamination,” said Matthew Moore, a food safety microbiologist at the University of Massachusetts Amherst.

It’s possible that tainted agricultural water is behind the unparalleled surge in infections, said Randy Worobo, a professor of food safety microbiology at Cornell. One possibility is that water used to irrigate fields or wash produce may have mixed with runoff from nearby toilet facilities, though health officials are still investigating the source of the contamination.

Michigan is currently reporting the most infections in the country: 9,680 cases and 160 hospitalizations as of Tuesday. The state typically records only 40 to 50 cases per year.

The C. D. C.’s current cyclosporiasis figures are most likely an undercount, health experts say, as some people who are ill are never diagnosed. When they are, it can take time for states to investigate cases and report them to the C. D. C., and for the agency to confirm these cases before sharing them with the public.

This helps to explain why many states report cyclosporiasis totals that do not match the C. D. C. numbers. States may also count cyclospora cases differently. For instance, some states report cases based on positive laboratory tests while others only report cases after health officials follow up with people to confirm their symptoms. Some states also update their case counts more frequently than others.

Note: Data as of July 28. There are variations in how state health departments define cases and how frequently they update case counts. Some states report cumulative case counts for the entire year so far, though most cyclosporiasis cases usually occur between May 1 and August 31.

Source: Case data are from state health agencies.

Arfa Momin, Alice Callahan and Caroline Hopkins Legaspi/The New York Times

The New York Times contacted state health departments for their current case counts, which collectively exceeded 18,500 cases as of Tuesday afternoon.

The previous largest outbreak in recent decades occurred in 2020 and sickened 701 people across 14 states, according to the C. D. C. That outbreak was linked to Fresh Express bagged salads. A 2022 Florida outbreak was also linked to bagged salads.

Lettuce sold by Taylor Farms and grown in central Mexico likely accounts for many — but not all — of the reported illnesses this year, health officials have said.

Nearly 2,000 cases have so far been linked to iceberg lettuce supplied by Taylor Farms and served at Taco Bell locations in nine states. But Taylor Farms has also recalled bagged lettuce sold at Walmart and shipped to a number of food service distributors in 27 states, so the affected lettuce may have reached restaurants, cafeterias or other establishments that have not yet been publicly named.

On July 23, for instance, health officials in New Hampshire reported that nine people had become ill after eating Taylor Farms lettuce at a medical center cafeteria.

The current surge in infections may be a result of multiple outbreaks happening simultaneously, said Kalmia Kniel , a microbiologist at the University of Delaware.

In North Carolina, which had recorded 718 cases as of July 27, people have frequently reported consuming parsley and cilantro before becoming ill. Some who have become ill in Michigan reported eating at restaurants, including fast food chains, but not everyone reported eating out, said Natasha Bagdasarian, the chief medical executive for Michigan.

Because it can take up to a few weeks or more for people to develop symptoms and get diagnosed, public health investigators often ask people what they ate during the weeks before they became ill, which can be difficult for people to remember, Dr. Bagdasarian said.

Cyclospora is a “tricky” organism to study, Dr. Kniel said. It’s challenging to detect in food or water. And compared with other pathogens like bacteria, it’s harder to link cases from a common source using genetic analysis.

Previous cyclospora outbreaks in the United States have been linked to lettuce and salad mixes, raspberries, basil, cilantro, fruit mixes, snow peas and snap peas.

Produce is probably contaminated in fields or in processing facilities, Dr. Bagdasarian said, and a supplier selling a product like bagged lettuce to restaurants may also be stocking grocery stores with it.

Some health experts are recommending that people take extra precautions with produce that has been implicated in past outbreaks — especially bagged lettuce.

Whether you choose to avoid certain types of fresh produce right now comes down to your own risk tolerance, said Barbara Kowalcyk, director of the Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition Security at George Washington University. She said that she was avoiding higher risk items for the time being. “Quite honestly, I don’t have time in my life for explosive diarrhea,” she said.

Cyclospora isn’t typically life-threatening, but lengthy bouts of diarrhea can cause severe dehydration, which is especially dangerous for those in vulnerable groups, including children, older adults and people who are pregnant or otherwise immunocompromised.

Telling healthy people outside of those groups to avoid entire categories of fresh produce is an “overly broad” recommendation, said Craig Hedberg, a professor of environmental health sciences at the University of Minnesota School of Public Health. Doing so could result in people eating less healthfully and food waste, he said.

Some public health departments are advising people to cook higher-risk produce to at least 158 degrees. This is a more reliable way to kill the parasite than rinsing or freezing.

Health officials in Michigan are advising people to use whole heads of lettuce rather than bagged salad kits, toss the outer two or three layers of leaves and then rinse with water.

In fact, all fresh produce should be rinsed before eating, health officials recommend. Scrub firm fruits and vegetables like melons and cucumbers with a clean brush, and cut away any damaged or bruised areas. When feasible, peel produce before eating.

The most common symptom of cyclosporiasis is watery diarrhea. The illness can also cause a loss of appetite, cramping, bloating, gas, nausea, fatigue and weight loss. Some people may experience a low-grade fever, said Dr. Adam Ressler, an infectious disease physician with Michigan Medicine.

People with symptoms should see a health care provider for testing and treatment, Dr. Ressler said. “I wouldn’t wait too long to get in and get tested,” he said.

Without treatment, symptoms can last anywhere from a few days to a month or more. And they may “wax and wane,” he said.

The most effective treatment for cyclosporiasis is Bactrim (a combination oral antibiotic also sold under the brand names Septra and Cotrim). It’s typically taken for seven to 10 days, Dr. Ressler said.

For those who are allergic to or intolerant of that medication, a doctor can recommend other treatment options, such as different types of antibiotics, he said.

Untreated, symptoms like chronic diarrhea can last for a month or more, Dr. Ressler said.

Staying hydrated is important, said Dr. Thomas Moore, a clinical professor of medicine at the University of Kansas School of Medicine-Wichita. He recommended making a simple rehydration solution with water, sugar and salt to replace electrolytes and fluids.

It’s possible. State and local health departments rely on federal funds to monitor, detect and respond to food-borne illnesses. In 2026, those agencies received only about 40 percent of what they requested for those efforts, Dr. Kowalcyk said.

During the coronavirus pandemic, state health departments received emergency federal funding to support their response to the virus. Many of those departments used that money to improve their ability to respond to other types of future outbreaks. That stream of funding has since ended, Dr. Kowalcyk said, resulting in many staff and program cuts.

Last summer, the C. D. C. quietly scaled back its Foodborne Diseases Active Surveillance Network, or FoodNet, which made it optional for the 10 member states to track cyclospora cases and report them to the C. D. C. While those states still have other ways to report infections, experts say that this change may result in many cases going uncounted.

Alice Callahan is a Times reporter covering nutrition and health. She has a Ph. D. in nutrition from the University of California, Davis.

Caroline Hopkins Legaspi is a Times reporter focusing on nutrition and sleep.

Graham and Netanyahu Worked Together to Denounce International Criminal Court

The New York Times July 28, 2026

Lindsey Graham (1955-2026)

Advertisement

Supported by

Senator Lindsey Graham helped to coordinate a group of lawmakers to rebuke the I. C. C., which was investigating Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel.

By Maggie Haberman

Senator Lindsey Graham, the South Carolina Republican who died this month at 71, worked privately with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of Israel to coordinate a bipartisan group of lawmakers to denounce the International Criminal Court investigation into Mr. Netanyahu just before the 2024 election, footage of their discussions shows.

The conversations were among roughly 400 hours recorded by the British filmmaker Alex Holder, who trailed Mr. Graham for roughly four years for a planned documentary project titled “Lindsey’s Game.” The footage of two discussions with Mr. Netanyahu about rebuking the I. C. C. was reviewed by The New York Times.

The calls took place just days before the 2024 election, on Oct. 29, as Mr. Graham was in Ohio, where he was campaigning with Donald Trump Jr. for Bernie Moreno in a Senate race, according to Mr. Holder.

The discussions underscore the significance of the relationship between Mr. Graham and Mr. Netanyahu and its impact, including with the senator’s colleagues. The two men were days away from an election that would return Donald J. Trump to the White House. Mr. Graham was a valuable interlocutor for Mr. Netanyahu even before that, but the call took place as the prime minister was prepared to discuss with Mr. Trump waging an increasingly expansive war against Iran.

Mr. Netanyahu was in Washington on Tuesday for Mr. Graham’s funeral, as well as a meeting with Mr. Trump about the war in Iran, which is becoming an intractable problem for the president.

Mr. Netanyahu remains the subject of an arrest warrant by the I. C. C., but Israeli officials have called the effort politically motivated. Mr. Netanyahu has made foreign trips since it was issued, and is set to travel to the U. N. General Assembly in New York in September.

Mr. Trump has declared that he will not be arrested, despite Mayor Zohran Mamdani calling Mr. Netanyahu a war criminal and saying he had reviewed whether city officials had the power to make an arrest. The mayor later said officials concluded they did not.

In the first call with Mr. Netanyahu, which was recorded on video, Mr. Graham is seen and heard talking to the prime minister, whose voice is occasionally garbled as it comes through the line and is picked up on the senator’s microphone. But Mr. Netanyahu could be heard clearly as he discussed a pending decision by the I. C. C. about whether to seek his arrest for alleged war crimes, as a prosecutor with the court had recommended earlier in 2024.

“A three-judge panel,” Mr. Netanyahu said in the first call with Mr. Graham, will be “making the decision very soon.” He noted that the court’s chief prosecutor, Karim A. A. Khan, had faced allegations of sexual misconduct, and suggested to Mr. Graham that “the great cloud that it shed” could help delay the arrest warrant (Mr. Khan was removed from his position last week, the court’s oversight body announced.)

“It is possible to have to appeal to the court to say, ‘OK, we want to review this before you do anything, before you issue an arrest warrant. There has to be a review about this entire process,’” Mr. Netanyahu said, adding that “this cloud or this stain has to be removed” before moving forward.

“And I suggest that you send a letter, with, maybe some other senators,”Mr. Netanyahu said. When Mr. Graham offered up Speaker Mike Johnson as the “perfect person” to sign such a letter, Mr. Netanyahu replied, “Would he get Democrats?”

Mr. Graham said that he would try for a bipartisan approach.

Mr. Holder recorded the audio, without video, of a second call between the two men that he said took place later that day. Only Mr. Graham’s voice could be heard.

On that call, Mr. Graham joked to Mr. Netanyahu that he should “pay me for all this. I should get tons of shekels.” It would take “more than dinner,” he added.

He then said that “we got them both,” appearing to refer to Senators Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Ben Cardin of Maryland, two Democrats, who said they would sign a letter protesting the efforts to move ahead with an arrest warrant.

“So here’s why I’m calling you,” Mr. Graham told Mr. Netanyahu, saying he hoped to get the letter “out the door Wednesday,” appearing to refer to the next day, October 30. “So send me over whatever you want to say. And they want to say two things” to the I. C. C.

One was that the prosecutors should speak with the Israeli government and not move ahead with the case until “the cloud is lifted” from the prosecutor’s own problems.

What Mr. Graham requested in exchange, he said, was for Mr. Netanyahu “to call Blumenthal and Cardin and thank them for being fair-minded on this, and also thank them for trying to help with Saudi-Israel normalization. You appreciate it. You’re very interested in it, and that will encourage both of them.”

The letter was released on Nov. 1, 2024, and included Mr. Blumenthal and Mr. Cardin as signers. In addition to noting the allegations against Mr. Khan, the letter said that the I. C. C. did “not comply” with the law by declining to keep a planned meeting with Israeli representatives before applying for the arrest warrant.

A spokesman for Mr. Netanyahu did not respond to an email seeking comment on the calls.

Mr. Blumenthal declined to address questions about the calls Mr. Graham had with Mr. Netanyahu. An aide to Mr. Cardin did not respond to an email seeking comment.

Maggie Haberman is a White House correspondent for The Times, reporting on President Trump.

ICE Arrests Surge at Airports, Opening New Front in Deportation Drive

The New York Times July 28, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

Times Exclusive

Federal agents are arresting spouses of Americans, tech workers and others whose visas have expired, including many who have active applications to stay in the country.

By Hamed Aleaziz and Miriam Jordan

The Trump administration has begun arresting foreign citizens with expired U. S. visas as they travel through airports, including spouses of Americans, according to documents obtained by The New York Times and interviews with immigration lawyers — a tactic that opens up a vast new pool of people for deportation.

Immigration agents in plain clothes have whisked away targets at check-in counters and arrival gates, with enforcement actions in at least 15 airports in recent weeks. Some of the arrests have occurred quietly, while others have happened as angry fellow passengers filmed the encounters.

The recent arrests appear to be an expansion of an arrangement between the Transportation Security Administration and Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The Times reported in December that ICE officers were arresting people with deportation orders at airports with the help of information provided by airlines to the T. S. A.

Now, through a review of Homeland Security Department documents and interviews with lawyers for more than 25 people from more than a dozen countries recently detained at airports, The Times has learned that the program apparently now includes people with expired visas — a much larger group.

Hundreds of thousands of immigrants and visitors overstay visas each year. Many with expired visas occupy a legal gray area, as they are awaiting visa extensions or green cards and have been issued work permits. Such individuals were not prioritized for deportation in the past unless they had committed crimes, and they were rarely detained while waiting for visa extensions or green cards. But that has changed under President Trump, whose administration has undertaken a campaign of mass deportation and views all visa overstays as illegal.

“This administration is working diligently to ensure that aliens in our country illegally can no longer fly unless it is out of our country to self-deport,” a spokesperson for the Homeland Security Department said in a statement. The agency did not confirm the expansion of the program.

The department, which oversees ICE, has not disclosed how many people have been detained at airports as overstays under the new initiative. The arrests come during a period in which the White House has pushed ICE for more arrests across the country, and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin has pledged to turn “up the heat on the streets.” To that end, the administration has set a target of 2,000 immigration arrests a day, roughly double the pace from earlier this year.

Interviews with more than a dozen immigration attorneys, advocacy organizations and an airline employee reveal a broad cross-section of targets: an engineer awaiting a work-visa extension, several newlyweds married to U. S. citizens, and a former au pair.

Footage of encounters between travelers and ICE officers have flooded social media. In one widely circulated video, Chantal Morales Rojas, a 27-year-old from Ecuador, was detained by plainclothes officers as she boarded a Southwest Airlines flight from Denver to Oakland, Calif., on July 20. She had been spending the weekend with the family for whom she had worked as an au pair, according to the family.

When Ms. Morales Rojas scanned her boarding pass, an alarm sounded and the gate agent asked her to wait. Moments later, two plainclothes agents intercepted her in the jetway.

“They said they were going to be respectful, that they would be polite,” Alicia Dantzker, a friend of the family, who was on the same flight and filmed part of the encounter, told The Times in an interview. The video captures the men encircling Ms. Morales Rojas, and then ushering her through a side door and down steps to the tarmac as Ms. Dantzker screams for help.

Also among those detained was a Ugandan woman in a wheelchair who has sickle cell anemia and an active asylum application, according to her lawyer.

In another case, ICE attempted to arrest an Australian citizen who had overstayed his visa at the Las Vegas airport, according to the Department of Homeland Security. The scene was recorded by a bystander whose video of the encounter drew wide attention. Officers let him go “to de-escalate the situation and for officer safety,” but ICE ended up taking him into custody a day later when he tried to board a flight in Los Angeles, the department said in a statement.

“In 38 years practicing immigration law, I had never seen this,” said Charles Kuck, who is based in Atlanta and is representing an Indian engineer who was detained while awaiting a work-permit extension. “And I know it’s happening to lots of people.”

Shannon Shepherd, an immigration lawyer who is vice chair for the Chicago chapter of the American Immigration Lawyers Association, said she and other lawyers were revising longstanding advice about domestic air travel.

“Before, I was saying, ‘As long as you have an ID, you can travel domestically,’” Ms. Shepherd said. “Now I am turning around and saying, ‘If you are in the process of changing status, avoid any travel.’”

The original collaboration between T. S. A. and ICE began in May 2025, when the airport security agency started sharing information with the immigration agency for enforcement purposes, according to a document obtained via the Freedom of Information Act from the government transparency group American Oversight and shared with The Times.

ICE shared names of individuals with deportation orders with the airport agency, which would run them through its databases and report any hits to ICE for potential arrest. It was a remarkable shift from past practices, when the federal government avoided involving the T. S. A. in immigration enforcement for fear of disrupting domestic travel.

Now, “the net they are casting for people they want to detain is far wider,” said Ghassan Shamieh, an immigration lawyer in San Francisco.

“It’s not people with criminal records” being targeted, Mr. Shamieh said. “You are talking about people with legitimate pending applications.”

Mr. Shamieh has four clients who were detained at airports in the last 10 days, including two women who recently married Americans and are in the process of obtaining permanent residency through their spouses. One of the husbands was with his wife when she was taken into custody after they landed in Burbank, Calif.

On Tuesday morning, an immigration judge granted her release on a $35,000 bond. But D. H. S. lawyers reserved the right to appeal within 30 days, and she is likely to remain detained until they decide.

Ms. Morales Rojas, the au pair, entered the United States lawfully in January 2023 as a J-1 exchange visitor, a legal status that allowed her to work for two years, according to her lawyer. Her visa expired Jan. 4, 2025, according to D. H. S. Before the exchange program ended, Ms. Morales Rojas filed an application with immigration authorities to remain in the country, said the lawyer, Laura Lichter.

“During the last three and a half years, Morales Rojas lived openly in the United States with the government’s knowledge of her pending case, passed repeated background checks, and received work authorization from D. H. S. while waiting for her application to be reviewed,” Ms. Lichter said. “The process she’s pursuing is completely lawful.”

But homeland security officials said in a statement that “in violation of our nation’s laws, she overstayed her visa.” On Tuesday afternoon, a judge granted her release on a $3,000 bond, and she is likely to leave detention by Wednesday.

Ms. Lichter has filed suit challenging the government’s decision to arrest and detain Ms. Morales Rojas without a proper arrest warrant and without an individualized determination that detention was necessary.

Lauren and Scott Cahr, her former employers, said they had hired Ms. Morales Rojas when their first child, Silas, was 6 months old. The Cahrs said in an interview that they had flown Ms. Morales Rojas to Denver during an Ultimate Frisbee tournament that they attended, and she had helped care for Silas and his little brother.

The family formed a deep bond, and the Cahrs created a custom photo book titled “The Adventures of Chanty and Gordo,” the nicknames Ms. Morales Rojas and their son called each other, as a parting gift.

“She is an amazing young woman who we were so lucky to have in our lives,” Ms. Cahr said. “We have tried to maintain a consistent relationship with her.”

Ms. Cahr has visited Ms. Morales Rojas in detention, while members of the Cahrs’ Ultimate Frisbee community have launched a GoFundMe campaign to help cover legal costs.

Houthis Claim Strike on Another Saudi Oil Tanker

The New York Times July 28, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

With their ally, Iran, bottling up the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthi group in Yemen is escalating its declared blockade of Saudi shipping in another vital waterway, the Red Sea.

By Pranav Baskar and Shirin Hakim

The Iranian-backed Houthi militant group in Yemen said on Tuesday that it had targeted a Saudi oil tanker with missiles in what would be the latest attack in an emerging front of the war between the United States and Iran.

The skirmishes between the Houthis, who control a large part of Yemen, and the Saudis risked igniting another conflict and infused more volatility into world energy supplies.

Saudi authorities did not immediately confirm the attack on the latest tanker, the NCC Ghazal, which is listed by public maritime monitoring services as Saudi-flagged. The ship was last located five days ago, along Saudi Arabia’s Red Sea coast, by MarineTraffic, a ship-monitoring firm.

The Houthis said the tanker ignored repeated warnings and was forced to reverse course. They did not say if the ship was actually hit, or where the vessel was at the time.

It was at least the fourth oil tanker to be attacked since the militia announced that it would blockade shipping to and from Saudi Arabia in the Red Sea. A monitoring group run by the British navy said, hours after the Houthi claim, that a tanker heard an explosion while transiting the Red Sea and all crew members were safe.

Shortly after the Houthis claimed the attack, the Saudi ministry of defense said that for the second consecutive day, it had destroyed several drones launched by Iran-aligned militias in Iraq aimed at Saudi oil facilities.

Since the Houthis announced their blockade earlier this month, each side has claimed attacks on the other. A Saudi-led military coalition has carried out airstrikes in Houthi-held territory for the first time in years. Separate from shipping attacks, the Houthis on Monday said they had targeted crude oil supplies and transport routes linking Saudi Arabia’s eastern oil fields to the Red Sea hub of Yanbu. The kingdom’s defense ministry has not yet addressed that claim.

Since March, Iran has effectively blockaded the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow portal to the Persian Gulf. That has forced Saudi Arabia to rely more heavily on exporting oil and gas through its Red Sea ports, hundreds of miles away.

The Houthis control most of Yemen’s Red Sea coast, where the southern part of the sea narrows to meet the Bab al-Mandab Strait — the link to the Indian Ocean and the shortest route to Asian markets. If ships cannot use that passage, they must instead go north through the Suez Canal, adding thousands of miles to some voyages.

In the last week, the Houthis claimed attacks on two tankers in the Red Sea, only one of which Saudi Arabia confirmed. Later, on Friday, the hull of a Saudi-owned vessel was damaged after being targeted in the Red Sea, Saudi officials said.

The Houthis form part of Iran’s broader “axis of resistance” alongside Iraqi factions, Hamas in Gaza and Hezbollah in Lebanon. With Iranian backing, they fought a civil war against the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government of Yemen, taking over a swath of the country.

While the Saudis and the Houthis have been in a fragile stalemate since a cease-fire in 2022, tensions erupted this month when the Houthis accused Saudi Arabia of striking Yemen’s main international airport in Sanaa, the capital, in a dispute over an Iranian plane that tried to land there. The Houthis retaliated by attacking the Abha airport in southern Saudi Arabia, the first direct Houthi strike on Saudi soil since early 2022.

The Houthis have weaponized their ability to disrupt shipping in the Red Sea before.

During the war in Gaza, which began in late 2023, the Houthis attacked commercial shipping in the Red Sea with drones, missiles and hijacking, trying to exert pressure on Israel and its allies. By some estimates, a Houthi blockade could affect more than 3 percent of the global oil market.

The latest Houthi threats come at a particularly difficult time, with Iran’s attacks on ships transiting the Strait of Hormuz prompting many shipowners and operators to decide it is too dangerous to use that waterway. The strait has been practically at a standstill, with the exception of a brief cease-fire, since the United States and Israel launched strikes on Iran on Feb. 28, and the number of crossings has hit some of its lowest levels in months.

Jewish Terrorism Is Also a Threat to Zionism

The New York Times July 28, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Bret Stephens

By Bret Stephens

Opinion Columnist

Because Israel is routinely the victim of double standards — Will Zohran Mamdani ever make a personal cause of denouncing his native Uganda for criminalizing homosexuality? Or tell a human-rights malefactor like Turkey’s president, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, that he, too, isn’t welcome in New York? — it’s tempting for the Jewish state’s stalwart defenders, including me, to downplay its failings.

That goes especially when we see the country having to defend its legitimacy against scoundrels. Or when allegations made against it later prove sloppily reported or entirely unfounded. Or when the chorus of condemnation is loud enough already without lending our voices to it.

But anyone who cares about Israel’s well-being shouldn’t be silent about anti-Palestinian settler terrorism in the West Bank and the nothing-much-to-see-here policy of Benjamin Netanyahu, the prime minister. That’s not only because the terrorism is a menace to Palestinian lives and property, or an affront to Jewish ethics, or a stain on Israel’s reputation — though it’s all those things. It’s also a direct threat to Israel’s security and statehood, and thus to Zionism itself.

That’s the point of a public letter to President Trump, issued Sunday by Matan Vilnai, a retired deputy chief of staff of the Israel Defense Forces, on behalf of an organization that includes hundreds of retired senior Israeli officers.

“Whereas our security agencies excel in dealing with Hamas and other West Bank Palestinian terror groups, they are severely constrained when it comes to Jewish terrorists,” the letter notes. “It is no secret that certain members of our current government orchestrate much of this chaos, including by shielding their followers — who are armed and driven by messianic impulses — from the law and its enforcement.”

“Unless arrested swiftly and decisively,” the letter bluntly warns, “escalating violence in the West Bank is poised to ignite the region and carries severe ramifications for both Israeli security and U. S. regional interests.”

That reality was again brought home last week, when extremist settlers went on a rampage in several Palestinian villages, reportedly setting fire to a home and two mosques, attacking a stonecutting factory and committing other acts of outright terrorism. That followed an incident in which four Palestinians and two Israelis were killed after a confrontation involving a group of Israelis who, without prior coordination, had trespassed into an area under Palestinian civil control.

This sort of episode has become routine. As The Times of Israel reports, “the I. D. F. recorded 867 incidents of nationalistic crime and settler violence in 2025.” That’s up from 682 the previous year.

Netanyahu’s answer to all this, as he told CNN’s Dana Bash, is that the violence is the work of about 150 “juvenile delinquents” and that he doesn’t accept “vigilantism.” But it’s preposterous to think that a government that can assassinate a Hamas leader in a Tehran guesthouse finds itself unable to contain a wave of Jewish thuggery. If the prime minister wanted to end the problem, he could. Like Bartleby, he would prefer not to.

That’s largely because his Likud Party depends on the parliamentary support of extremist settlers led by Itamar Ben-Gvir, the minister of national security, and Bezalel Smotrich, the finance minister, and Netanyahu has learned to stay atop Israeli politics by never letting go of his right flank.

In an interview, Eran Shamir-Borer, who spent many years in the I. D. F.’s Military Advocate General’s Corps and is now with the Israel Democracy Institute (on whose advisory board I sit), listed for me the specific decisions by Netanyahu’s cabinet that have brought Israel to this pass. Chief among them is Defense Minister Israel Katz’s refusal to use administrative detention as a legal tool to rein in suspected Jewish terrorists. David Zini, the current head of Israel’s internal security service, avoids the term “Jewish terror” in favor of the euphemism “frictions.” And Ben-Gvir is himself a product of the same milieu that produced the rampaging settlers.

“Everyone hears the music,” Shamir-Borer said, “and it legitimizes this kind of conduct.”

That’s what makes Vilnai’s letter significant, particularly during the same week that the prime minister visits Washington to meet with Trump. Vilnai is no peacenik: He served in a previous Netanyahu government as the minister of home front defense and was one of the commandos who, 50 years ago this month, liberated Jewish hostages in the Entebbe raid. But like many other patriotic Israelis, he’s aghast at a government that prioritizes the prime minister’s political needs and his cabinet’s ideological obsessions over the rule of law.

There is an immediate danger in that the spiraling West Bank violence could easily produce a third intifada that an exhausted Israel can ill afford militarily or diplomatically, to say nothing of the human cost in both Israeli and Palestinian lives. There’s a still greater long-term risk that the Netanyahu government’s excuse making for Jewish lawlessness and terrorism leads to what the scholar and diplomat Michael Oren, in a prescient Commentary essay from 2009, called “the hemorrhaging of sovereignty.”

Any nation in which broad segments of the citizenry are either untouched or untouchable by the law — in Israel’s case, not just radical settlers and ultra-Orthodox draft shirkers but also Arab citizens badly underserved by law enforcement — is on the road to its own kind of Lebanonization. That’s where every group is a law unto itself and the state’s powers, including its monopoly on the use of force, wither.

I’ve written before that the purpose of Zionism — for which I’m a lifelong advocate — is Jewish self-rule: “Neither rule by others nor rule over others.” It’s why I still believe in a Palestinian state, even if the conditions for it are probably far off. It’s why I more fervently believe in a Jewish state, governed by law and recognizing limits. Under this Israeli government, that’s slipping away.

Noncitizen Voter Error Puts an Ambitious Democrat in the Hot Seat

The New York Times July 28, 2026

U. S. Immigration Crackdown

Advertisement

Supported by

After disclosing that thousands of ineligible people were added to the voter rolls, New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill is trying to bring accountability while resisting President Trump’s narrative.

By Tracey Tully

The discovery of as many as 6,600 noncitizens on New Jersey’s voter rolls has thrust the state’s Democratic governor, Mikie Sherrill, onto a political tightrope.

And her balancing act is about to intensify.

Ms. Sherrill, who took over in January, on Tuesday defiantly refused the Justice Department’s demand that the state turn over personal details about the thousands of residents affected by what she has called a software error. “The request had no legal basis,” she said in response to the Trump administration’s request for the “full names, dates of birth, nationalities, residential addresses” of noncitizens who were inadvertently registered to vote between June 2023 and June 2024.

Ms. Sherrill has instead stressed that the noncitizens placed on the voter rolls when seeking driver's licenses or IDs were not at fault and has vowed to do what she can to protect them.

She has chastised President Trump, accusing him of chasing ghosts of elections past and weaponizing elections “for political gain.” At the same time, the governor, a moderate in her party, signaled last week that she was open to “suggestions that make our elections more safe.”

She has also made it clear that the mistake did not happen on her watch. Ms. Sherrill has cast blame on the technology vendor that supplied the software, the Motor Vehicle Commission and the administration of her predecessor, Philip D. Murphy, a fellow Democrat.

“Unacceptable,” she said in a news conference — five times.

She merely inherited this mess, but cleaning it up could be complicated — both practically and politically.

About 400 of the wrongly registered noncitizens have cast ballots since June 2023, Ms. Sherrill said. The governor has said that she had no evidence, “at this time,” that any election was swayed, but has ordered an independent investigation. (In recent years, no statewide or New Jersey federal election has been close enough to have been decided by 400 votes.)

Nevertheless, the New Jersey situation has given Mr. Trump and his fellow election truthers an example of unlawful voting that everyone agrees happened and is a problem.

“The president has made it a national issue,” said Benjamin Ginsberg, a prominent Republican election lawyer, who has been critical of the president’s unsubstantiated claims of stolen elections.

“And Governor Sherrill,” he continued, “whether she likes it or not, is now the face of that issue.”

Ms. Sherrill served in Congress before being elected governor by a 14-point margin last year. She has established a federal political action committee to support “cleareyed leaders who are unafraid to challenge the status quo,” and has said that she expects the next president to be from the Democratic Party.

“I want to be influencing that ticket very heavily,” Ms. Sherrill said in a July 20 interview about what she considered her state’s successful handling of its World Cup hosting duties.

A day later, she held a news conference and disclosed that a flaw in software used at motor vehicle offices between June 12, 2023, and June 25, 2024, had resulted in thousands of noncitizens being registered to vote, even though they had marked that they were not U. S. citizens and were therefore ineligible.

The software was fixed, Ms. Sherrill said, but the Murphy administration never notified affected residents or removed their names from the rolls. Mr. Murphy, through a spokesman, has said that he was unaware of the breach.

Knowingly registering to vote or casting a ballot as a noncitizen is illegal. And as many as 6,600 people now stand in harm’s way as the Trump administration intensifies its immigration crackdown.

Since last year, when the Justice Department began demanding voter rolls nationwide, more than half of the states, including New Jersey, have refused, leading to lawsuits. Judges have repeatedly ruled against the Trump administration, finding that states were not obligated to release the data to the federal government.

A Justice Department official could not be immediately reached for comment about Ms. Sherrill’s decision to withhold the wrongly registered residents’ personal information.

Ms. Sherrill said Tuesday that the state was moving to quickly delete about 4,500 of the affected residents from the rolls.

The remaining 2,100 registrations are being referred to county election officials. “We are taking this extra step because our initial review indicates that a number of these individuals may be citizens,” she said in a statement. “Just as we have an obligation to remove everyone who is not eligible to vote, we also have a responsibility to protect the voting rights of eligible New Jersey citizens and ensure no one is improperly removed from the rolls.”

Last week, the Motor Vehicle Commission began mailing letters, in English and in Spanish, alerting those affected. “Notwithstanding your selection of ‘No’ to the U. S. citizenship question, your information was transmitted to the Statewide Voter Registration System for voter registration,” the letters read. The state also set up an information portal, “MVC System Error 2023.”

Fear in immigrant communities, already high during Mr. Trump’s second term, has soared, said Maria Juega, a founder and former executive director of the Latin American Legal Defense and Education Fund, an immigrant rights group in Trenton, the state’s capital.

“The atmosphere couldn’t be more tense,” Ms. Juega said. “People are scared to death of leaving their houses.”

New Jersey is one of 19 states that both allow undocumented immigrants to obtain driver’s licenses and make it easy to register to vote at motor vehicle offices. A website where users can look up whether they are registered to vote is cranky and in English, Ms. Juega noted, fueling confusion among immigrants who now fear they may unwittingly be at risk.

“It’s just a mess — a total mess,” she said.

Ms. Sherrill has promised transparency and committed to holding those responsible accountable.

“We inherited a problem. We didn’t hide it. We didn’t deny it,” she said Tuesday.

But the timing of the discovery could hardly be worse, with less than 100 days until the midterm elections.

“She doesn’t have the luxury of time,” said Micah Rasmussen, director of the Rebovich Institute for New Jersey Politics at Rider University.

It remains an open question how much the controversy will resonate beyond New Jersey. But Republicans in Trenton and in Washington have said that Ms. Sherrill’s effort to make clear that the error took place on Mr. Murphy’s watch is a distinction without a difference.

Joe Pennacchio, a Republican state senator, said Democrats were to blame. “They were in charge of the hen house,” he said.

The Democratic response in New Jersey has been notably muted.

State Senator Andrew Zwicker was one of the few Democrats who offered a full-throated defense of New Jersey’s elections after Ms. Sherrill’s disclosure, stressing how small a fraction of the total vote was involved.

Still, Mr. Zwicker acknowledged that New Jersey’s voter-registration error has “been sucked up into” Mr. Trump’s narrative of widespread illegal voting.

“It’s utterly discouraging,” he said.

The discovery coincides with Mr. Trump’s efforts to persuade Congress to adopt his SAVE America Act as he pushes for more control over voting ahead of November’s elections. On Monday, the Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to clear the way for the president to restrict mail voting by executive order.

Mr. Ginsberg, the election lawyer, said it was possible for Ms. Sherrill to turn the controversy to her advantage, if, for example, she were able to create a bipartisan model for auditing voter rolls that other states could emulate.

“It’s an interesting test for somebody who wants to be on the national stage,” he said. “There’s a chance for her to turn something really messy into an opportunity.”

Tracey Tully is a reporter for The Times who covers New Jersey, where she has lived for more than 20 years.
