Who Wins (and Who Loses) in the Democrats’ New 2028 Primary Calendar?

The New York Times July 28, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Democratic Party officials have approved a new calendar that puts South Carolina at the head of the line. Black and Latino voters will gain new clout.

By Lisa Lerer

Democrats across the country agree that their new primary map will redraw the road to their party’s 2028 presidential nomination. But, as they look to what’s widely expected to be a crowded and competitive contest, no one is quite sure what turns it will take.

Instead of Iowa and New Hampshire, long the traditional openers of the primary process, Democratic candidates will navigate their way through a six-state gantlet that starts in South Carolina on Jan. 22, winds through Nevada, New Hampshire, New Mexico and Michigan and ends in Virginia on Feb. 29.

The cross-country sprint has significantly broadened the race — geographically, racially and ideologically, Democratic strategists say.

“It really could benefit anyone,” said Rob Flaherty, a deputy campaign manager for former Vice President Kamala Harris’s 2024 run and the co-host of “Nobody Knows Anything,” a podcast about national politics. “I follow things pretty closely, and I have no idea how it’s going to bounce.”

Here’s what the calendar does — and doesn’t — tell us about the 2028 Democratic primary race.

The new map is good news for Black voters, increasing their power in the earliest stage of the contest. While the electorate in Iowa and New Hampshire is largely white, a majority of South Carolina Democratic primary voters are Black.

“Black voters are the backbone of this party,” said Christale Spain, the chair of the state’s Democratic Party, in an interview with the political commentator Roland Martin last week. “We should continue to elevate Black voters role in the process.”

Harris, who has floated the possibility of a third presidential run, remains popular with Black voters and could be advantaged by South Carolina’s spot at the head of the line — but it’s hard to predict. In 2020, she exited the race before the state even voted, with her fund-raising having run dry.

Some commentators pointed to the possibility that multiple Black candidates — including perhaps Gov. Wes Moore of Maryland and Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia — could split the electorate, sending the race into the next contests with muddled results.

Senator Jon Ossoff of Georgia, who has a history of building coalitions with Black voters, could be strong in the state. Pete Buttigieg, the former transportation secretary, struggled there in 2020.

The new map more than doubles the share of Latino voters across the first four states from 2020, the last time Democrats had a competitive presidential primary, according to an analysis by Decision Desk HQ, an election results reporting website.

The heavy Latino populations in Nevada and New Mexico give those voters a pivotal role in culling the field as the candidates move through the early contests.

While Latino voters are generally considered more socially moderate, Senator Bernie Sanders, the liberal Vermont independent, won big in Nevada after investing heavily in organizing there in 2020. Working-class Latino voters could also be inclined toward candidates like Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York or Senator Ruben Gallego of Arizona.

“The Black voters are going to kick off the calendar,” said Xochitl Hinojosa, a Democratic strategist. “But I do think that Latino voters will ultimately decide who the nominee is.”

The announcement of the new calendar prompted grumbles from some corners of the progressive world that the Democratic National Committee had created a schedule designed to hamper insurgent left-wing candidates.

But it’s not clear what kind of candidate is favored by the new calendar.

The six early states are relatively inexpensive to advertise in, which could provide the opportunity for an insurgent to catch fire — though in 2020, South Carolina elevated Joseph R. Biden Jr., an establishment candidate, over Mr. Sanders.

On the other hand, the new map rewards campaigns with the money to build a six-state, cross-country organization that can reach diverse constituencies. That may benefit candidates like Ms. Harris and Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, who could enter the race with well-established political brands and expansive fund-raising lists.

One of the biggest changes to the calendar is bumping New Hampshire from its vaunted “first in the nation” position.

New Hampshire law requires the state’s presidential primary to be held at least seven days before any “similar election.” That standard would bump its primary into mid-January, before South Carolina.

In past elections, New Hampshire has been immovable. In 2024, party leaders also tried to move the state back in the calendar. It voted first anyhow, risking its delegates in the process.

Local officials have promised to once again defend the state’s tradition. But in 2028, the penalties for candidates could be onerous: The party has threatened to bar any candidate who campaigns in a state that jumps the calendar from participating in official party debates.

That change could hurt Mr. Buttigieg, who has shown strength in the state.

New Hampshire also runs an open primary, allowing independent voters to participate in party contests. That dynamic has made it a place where moderates can gain steam — a benefit such candidates will no longer get.

Lisa Lerer is a national political reporter for The Times, based in New York. She has covered American politics for nearly two decades.

Senators Forge a Deal on Graham’s Russia Sanctions Bill

The New York Times July 28, 2026

Lindsey Graham (1955-2026)

Advertisement

Supported by

Senators announced a breakthrough on the long-stalled measure as Senator Lindsey Graham, its main champion, was memorialized.

By Robert Jimison

Reporting from the Capitol

Senators on Tuesday announced a breakthrough in a long-stalled bipartisan effort to advance sweeping sanctions against Russia, paving the way for an evening test vote on the compromise bill after the Washington funeral of Senator Lindsey Graham, its main champion.

Republicans and Democrats said they had addressed concerns from members of both parties and were ready to push ahead in efforts to pass the measure in honor of Mr. Graham, who spent the final hours of his life working in Ukraine to cement it.

The measure would impose harsh new penalties on countries that purchase oil and other energy products from Russia, as well as extend existing sanctions against Iran seeking to limit its ability to fuel its wartime economy.

“We are proud to announce an agreement on legislation to stop purchasers of Russian oil and gas from fueling Putin’s war machine and to continue restricting the Iranian regime’s ability to support terrorism and build its nuclear program,” said a joint statement from the Republican senators Darline Graham of South Carolina, Jim Risch of Idaho, Roger Wicker of Mississippi and Katie Britt of Alabama and the Democratic senators Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut and Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire. “There is no greater way to honor Senator Graham’s legacy than to move forward with this bipartisan agreement, and we look forward to today’s vote.”

The announcement came just as lawmakers and his family gathered at the Capitol to honor Mr. Graham’s life, and hours before the president and world leaders convened at the National Cathedral for his funeral.

An initial vote was expected on Tuesday evening, just after President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine, who has long pressed for such a sanctions package, was to meet with senators on Capitol Hill.

The revised legislation reflects an intense round of negotiations to narrow the measure’s provisions and ensure tighter congressional oversight over the penalties it would impose.

To appease Democrats who had balked at handing President Trump new tariff authority, the revised measure would require that the president impose the sanctions rather than simply permit him to do so — though Mr. Trump could still waive them if he certified that it was necessary for national security reasons. Negotiators also added requirements that the administration regularly report to Congress on how the penalties were being carried out.

Senators also said they had adjusted language governing the bill’s secondary tariffs to exempt American allies that still purchase small amounts of oil, gas and other energy from Russia if they were demonstrably reducing their reliance on Russian-produced energy.

Mr. Blumenthal, who had worked with Mr. Graham on the measure for more than a year, said he was confident the changes would secure enough backing to overcome any objections from Democrats and yield the votes necessary for the measure to move ahead.

“We’ve got a solid core of 60-plus senators,” Mr. Blumenthal said.

Robert Jimison covers Congress for The Times, with a focus on defense issues and foreign policy.

The New York Times July 28, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Bill Pulte, the acting director of national intelligence, said he has terminated nearly a third of the officials in his office, but others doubt the figures are accurate.

By Julian E. Barnes and Dustin Volz

The reporters cover the U. S. intelligence agencies.

Bill Pulte, the acting director of national intelligence, has spent his final days on the job celebrating his efforts to terminate employees in his office.

But current and former officials said few people have actually been fired in recent weeks from the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, despite a flurry of social media posts by Mr. Pulte. And members of Congress have been left scratching their heads about whether Mr. Pulte has cut nearly as many employees as he has claimed.

Mr. Pulte said on Tuesday, hours before the Senate is expected to confirm his replacement, Jay Clayton, that he had reduced the staff at his organization by nearly a third since taking the job of spy chief in June.

“Good News! In addition to the Historic DECLASSIFICATIONS (Transparency!) by the President, we are, this morning, Executing a 5th and Near Final Round of TERMINATIONS, an approximately 30% Staff Reduction from Weeks Ago,” Mr. Pulte wrote in an X post that mimicked President Trump’s social media patois. “The Intelligence Community must protect the American people, NOT the political whims of the bloated and corrupt elite class.”

But Mr. Pulte’s office has provided no details or explanations of the purported cuts, sowing doubts on Capitol Hill.

Mr. Pulte, who also oversees a federal housing agency and has pursued campaigns of retribution against Mr. Trump’s perceived enemies, lacked any national security experience before he was tapped to run the spy office.

“The acting D. N. I. has been quick to announce firings and make public claims about them, but has so far declined to provide the Senate Intelligence Committee with the information necessary to assess the accuracy of those statements or the basis for those decisions,” said Rachel Cohen, a spokeswoman for Senator Mark Warner of Virginia, the top Democrat on the committee.

Mr. Pulte has not laid out the goals of his purported reductions. A spokeswoman for Mr. Pulte did not respond to questions about his social media posts.

But several former U. S. intelligence officials expressed disbelief about the claim of reductions. They said Mr. Pulte was counting people whose tour of duty at the office was complete and were returning to their home agencies as previously planned. He also appears to be counting unfilled positions at the National Counterterrorism Center and other parts of the spy office as terminations, former officials said.

Still, current and former officials said, the elimination of jobs and returning officers to their home agencies have hit hardest at the National Intelligence Council, a group that reviews the conclusions of a variety of spy agencies.

In many respects, the council is a core part of the spy chief’s office, developing authoritative analytic judgments supported by a variety of intelligence agencies, while guarding against groupthink.

Last year, Tulsi Gabbard, the previous director, fired the head of the council in a dispute over intelligence about a Venezuelan gang. She also eliminated the council’s Strategic Futures Group, arguing its work was at odds with Mr. Trump’s policies.

The Office of the Director of National Intelligence had about 1,700 employees when Ms. Gabbard announced in May that she was stepping down, including around 1,300 full-time government employees and 400 contractors.

Mr. Pulte initially put a handful of close aides to Ms. Gabbard on administrative leave, allowing them to find other jobs in the government. He also directed about 75 intelligence officers who formally worked for other spy agencies, like the C. I. A., the National Security Agency, the Defense Intelligence Agency or others, to return to those agencies.

Julia Curlee, a former longtime C. I. A. analyst who left the agency this year, criticized Mr. Pulte’s efforts to cut intelligence professionals as a performance intended to please Mr. Trump that may have long-term consequences for America’s spy agencies.

“The bill will come due in low morale and in Americans who now won’t apply,” said Ms. Curlee, who served on the White House National Security Council during the first few months of the second Trump administration. “Congress should demand to know what this is meant to achieve, and which national security functions will go unperformed.”

Julian E. Barnes covers the U. S. intelligence agencies and international security matters for The Times. He has written about security issues for more than two decades.

Dustin Volz writes about cybersecurity and intelligence for The Times. He is based in Washington.

Iran Publicly Hangs 2 Protesters, Rights Groups Say

The New York Times July 28, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Human rights activists say the Iranian government has been rapidly escalating executions. The latest prompted public protest, videos appear to show.

By Leily Nikounazar and Sanjana Varghese

The Iranian authorities publicly hanged on Tuesday two participants in the country’s widespread January protests, human rights groups said, the latest executions in what activists describe as a rapid increase in the government’s use of the death penalty this year.

The hangings were carried out at dawn in Isfahan’s Shahid Alikhani Square, according to the Washington-based Human Rights Activists News Agency, and appeared to draw a rare public backlash.

Several videos verified by The New York Times show large crowds of chanting protesters near the site. Blurry footage circulating on Telegram and social media early on Tuesday morning in Iran showed protesters around the corner from the square, chanting “shameless” and booing.

Iran has long been one of the world’s most frequent users of capital punishment, but public executions are extremely rare. Several human rights activists described Tuesday’s hangings as an escalation by a government seeking to stifle dissent after the unrest in January, particularly during the war with the United States.

Mahmood Amiry-Moghaddam, director of the Norwegian-based Iran Human Rights group, called the executions “a brutal form of state terror that the international community must not tolerate.” He said, “Public executions are among the regime’s most potent instruments for instilling fear and fostering a sense of helplessness among the public.”

The two men executed on Tuesday were Amirhossein Safari and Abolfazl Sepahi, according to Mizan, the news agency associated with Iran’s judiciary. Mizan did not mention a public execution, but two other media outlets in Iran described the hangings as being conducted “in the presence of the public.”

The men were part of a group accused by security forces of killing four police officers during protests on the night of Jan. 8. According to an indictment, the assailants attacked the officers with knives, machetes and axes, then doused them with gasoline and set their bodies on fire.

Lawyers representing the two men did not publicly comment on the charges, but both men gave televised confessions broadcast on Iran’s state news channel several months ago. Iranian rights groups and human rights lawyers say such confessions are often made under duress, frequently after psychological or physical torture.

Several human rights groups said that the men, like other protesters sentenced to death after the January demonstrations, had not been given due process.

A report released by Human Rights Activists News Agency, or HRANA, said that lawyers for Mr. Safari and Mr. Sepahi had faced difficulties gaining access to their case files and that the court rejected what could have been exculpatory evidence. The families were kept in the dark about the details of the verdicts, the report said.

According to HRANA, fourteen men have been sentenced to death on charges of involvement in the police officers’ killings, though it identified only 12 of them by name.

The selection of Shahid Alikhani Square for the execution was likely symbolic, because it is where the authorities allege that the four officers were killed, said Hassan Nayeb-Hashem, founder of the Vienna-based All Human Rights for All in Iran.

Saeid Dehghan, an Iranian human rights lawyer based in Toronto, described the event as the government “baring its teeth in an effort to suppress the public.”

Yet several videos appear to show that the hangings had the opposite effect on some people.

In one video, a crowd can be heard booing as the Islamic call to prayer rings out. Another video shows more crowds in a different area on the outskirts of Shahid Alikhani Square. In the footage, shots are heard ringing out, and the person filming begins to run.

Several Iranian-focused rights groups have warned for months that the pace of sentencing and hangings appears to have surged amid the war.

Mahya Ostovar, founder of the Iranian Democratic Diaspora Network in Ireland, said that more than 800 executions had been verified this year. “As the world’s attention has focused on war and diplomacy, the human rights catastrophe inside Iran has only intensified,” she said.

The United States and Israel launched their war against Iran just weeks after security forces crushed nationwide demonstrations. The government says some 3,000 people were killed in the protests, while activist groups like HRANA put the toll above 7,000.

“These executions should also serve as a warning that the real war in Iran has never been the one dominating international headlines,” Ms. Ostovar said. “The real conflict is the ongoing struggle between the Iranian people and the Islamic Republic. That struggle is far from over.”

Sanjana Varghese is a reporter on The Times’s Visual Investigations team, specializing in the use of advanced digital techniques to analyze visual evidence.

Aide Who Had Affair With Newsom 20 Years Ago Details Her Experience

The New York Times July 28, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Ruby Rippey had stayed mostly quiet since her relationship with the San Francisco mayor rocked the city.

By Heather Knight

Heather Knight covered San Francisco City Hall while Gavin Newsom served as mayor.

An aide who had an affair with Gavin Newsom more than 20 years ago when he was the mayor of San Francisco has written a detailed account of the relationship, which Vanity Fair published on Tuesday.

The first-person essay by the aide, Ruby Rippey, who was working as Mr. Newsom’s appointments secretary at the time, was published just as Mr. Newsom finishes his final year as California governor and lays the groundwork for a possible presidential run in 2028.

Ms. Rippey, 54, has rarely spoken publicly of the affair, but it was the talk of San Francisco in 2007 when Mr. Newsom stood before reporters and a bank of television cameras at City Hall to announce, “Everything you’ve heard and read is true.”

He explained that he’d had an affair with Ms. Rippey, the wife of Alex Tourk, a close friend who was then serving as his re-election campaign manager after working as his deputy chief of staff. Mr. Tourk had just told Mr. Newsom that he was resigning after learning about the affair from his wife.

In her essay, Ms. Rippey does not use Mr. Newsom’s name, but she describes him as the mayor of San Francisco and a man “often described as Kennedy-esque.” (Vanity Fair mentions his name once, in its summary of the essay below the headline.)

She seems to blame herself for betraying her husband and says that her life spiraled as she drank heavily and used cocaine.

She indicates that she was not coerced, but she also held Mr. Newsom responsible for holding power and proceeding with the affair anyway. “Power does not need to coerce,” she writes. “It only needs to exist. The responsibility to hold the line belongs to the one who holds it. That didn’t happen.”

She writes that their relationship began in the summer of 2005 and lasted for months, with off-and-on encounters.

“I always go to him — his penthouse in Russian Hill, a private back room at a North Beach bar, the W Hotel in Los Angeles,” Ms. Rippey writes in her essay.

“We meet and we drink. There is sex, but it isn’t the point,” she continues. “The point is proximity — to power, to being chosen.”

Mr. Newsom announced in January 2005 that he was divorcing Kimberly Guilfoyle, a former San Francisco prosecutor who is now President Trump’s ambassador to Greece. But even though he was single, the revelation of his affair with Ms. Rippey shocked San Francisco residents and California political circles because he’d had a relationship with his subordinate and upended his close friend’s marriage.

By the time the affair became public knowledge in early 2007, Mr. Newsom was dating Jennifer Siebel, now his wife, who caused her own brouhaha by publicly dismissing the affair as “a couple nothing incidents” and by calling Ms. Rippey “the culprit.” Ms. Siebel later apologized for the remarks.

Izzy Gardon, a spokesman for Mr. Newsom, said on Tuesday morning: “The governor acknowledged his role and publicly apologized for his conduct nearly two decades ago when he was still mayor. In the time since, he met his wife, started a family and has focused on serving Californians.”

“He addressed this chapter of his life, including in his memoir, and out of respect for everyone involved does not have anything further to add,” Mr. Gardon continued.

Ms. Rippey declined to be interviewed on Tuesday. She is being represented by Dini Von Mueffling, a public relations strategist who has also worked with Monica Lewinsky and Kristin Cabot, the woman seen on a “kiss cam” being held by her married boss at a Coldplay concert.

Mr. Tourk did not return a text and email seeking comment. After resigning as Mr. Newsom’s campaign manager, he founded Ground Floor Public Affairs and has represented companies that include Anthropic, Lyft and the San Francisco Giants.

Ms. Rippey says in Vanity Fair that she considered writing a memoir after the affair became public, but that Kamala Harris, then the city’s district attorney, advised her to say nothing and take time to gain perspective. “It turns out to be the best advice I receive,” Ms. Rippey writes.

The affair was raised by Mr. Newsom’s opponents during his 2018 run for governor. At the time, Ms. Rippey wrote on Facebook that she did not see it as part of the growing #MeToo movement, because while she was his “subordinate” she was also a 33-year-old married woman and mother who was “free-thinking.”

In the Vanity Fair essay, she writes that she received a phone call in January from an adviser to Mr. Newsom who let her know that she was mentioned in his new memoir. Mr. Newsom primarily discusses her in two paragraphs, calling their relationship “the stupidest and also briefest of affairs.”

She takes issue with Mr. Newsom’s portrayal in the memoir of owning up to his role in the affair. He wrote that he had “come clean” to Mr. Tourk, which she felt mistakenly “gives him credit for something I had already done.”

In a Facebook post on Tuesday, Ms. Rippey explained why she told her story in such depth, so many years later, and implied that it was partly a response to Mr. Newsom’s memoir.

“Until now, silence felt like the right choice,” she wrote. “Now it feels necessary to offer a fuller account of what happened, rather than allowing a misleading account to stand as the whole story.”

She added that her essay was not intended as “a hit piece or a redemption story.”

“It’s about accountability, consequences and earning the right to tell the truth after 20 years of silence and repair,” she wrote.

Ms. Rippey, now 20 years sober, lives in Mill Valley, Calif., just north of San Francisco in Marin County. She writes that she and Mr. Tourk have divorced and co-parent their son, who is now an adult. She says it took more than a decade for Mr. Tourk to look her in the eye after the affair, but that they had since become close enough again to consider each other family.

Ms. Rippey has remarried and has an 11-year-old son with her second husband.

Heather Knight is a reporter in San Francisco, leading The Times’s coverage of the Bay Area and Northern California.

How A. I. Books Sneak Their Way Into Stores

The New York Times July 28, 2026

What to Read

Advertisement

Supported by

Big booksellers are taking different approaches to dealing with the deluge of titles generated by artificial intelligence.

By Alexandra Alter

Jess Michaels, a historical romance writer, has released 117 novels since she started writing full time in 1999, most of them self-published. She’s built a devoted readership, and has had 10 USA Today best sellers.

But lately, sales have been so dismal that she might stop publishing.

“The glut of the A. I. work makes discoverability very difficult,” Michaels said. “You’re talking about directly pirating my work, putting it into an engine so that you can produce a ‘Jess Michaels-type book,’ and then glutting the market with it.

“I cannot tell you how soul-crushing it is,” she added. “It essentially erases actual authors.”

It didn’t take long for chatbot writing to spill into books after artificial intelligence models capable of spitting out sophisticated prose arrived several years ago. But many in the book world held out hope that fiction would be the last fortress to fall — that readers wanted stories full of human emotions and could tell when they weren’t written by humans.

A few years into the A. I. era, there is sobering evidence that a significant and growing portion of the novels being sold are written with or by chatbots, and that readers are buying them.

A new study conducted by computer scientists using A. I. detection software to analyze thousands of self-published novels on Amazon, found that a substantial number of those novels contained chatbot-generated prose.

“In genre fiction, people are using A. I. to write these books, and readers are not able to tell,” said Tuhin Chakrabarty, a professor of computer science at the State University of New York at Stony Brook, who led the research.

After setting aside books that weren’t selling, the team looked at a random sample of 14,419 self-published novels released on Amazon between January 2023 and March 2026 using A. I. detection software from Pangram, which many computer scientists consider to be one of the most reliable programs of its kind. The study found that in 2,168 of those books, more than 50 percent of the prose was A. I. generated, and that 970 of the novels were more than 90 percent A. I.-generated.

The researchers estimate that the sales of all novels in their sample including at least 25 percent A. I.-generated text totaled in the tens of millions of dollars in the last three years. The findings, which have not yet been peer-reviewed, seem to confirm what many in the book business feared: A. I. writing is now an inescapable fixture of the retail landscape.

Amazon doesn’t prohibit the sale of A. I.-generated books on its site. The company asks self-published authors to disclose to Amazon whether or not they used A. I. to create their books, and limits the number of books each author can upload to the site to 10 per week.

But writers are not required to flag their A. I. use for readers. And the 10-book limit still allows for the sale of A. I.-assisted works at a scale and speed that would be practically impossible for even a prolific human to match.

A spokesman for Amazon, Josh Pflug, said the company has clear content guidelines regarding the sale of books on its site.

“We take proactive and reactive measures to prevent, detect, and remove content that violates those guidelines, whether A. I.-generated or not,” he said.

Other researchers have also found an alarming number of books containing A. I. writing on Amazon. A study from the National Bureau of Economic Research that came out earlier this year found a correlation between the spike in the number of books that contain A. I.-generated prose and the rapidly growing number of e-books on the site — a finding that Amazon disputes.

“The claims about title growth in our store are not consistent with what we are seeing,” Pflug said, although he declined to provide internal figures.

The researchers used Pangram to analyze text from around 60,000 books sold on Amazon. From that sample, about 53 percent of the books published in 2025 contained A. I.-generated text, compared to 23 percent in 2023.

The study found A. I. use to be higher in nonfiction categories like travel and outdoor sports, and comparably low in fiction. It also showed that the average rating of new books on Amazon has dropped as A. I. use has spread.

“If all of these new books are much worse than what we already have, then there’s little to be gained by consumers,” said Imke Reimers, an associate professor of strategy and business economics at Cornell University, who coauthored the study.

Both studies could add fuel to copyright cases that authors and publishers have brought against A. I. companies. In a barrage of lawsuits against OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and xAI and Meta, publishers and writers have argued that the surge in A. I.-generated works has flooded the market, diluting some of their sales.

Over the past several months, a string of A. I.-related scandals has unsettled the literary world. And the explosion of A. I. writing has put distributors and retailers in an awkward spot. Amazon’s stance toward selling A. I.-generated titles has generally been lenient, but other retailers have tried to take a more nuanced approach toward stocking them.

In May, James Daunt, the chief executive of Barnes & Noble, caused an uproar in the book world when he said in an interview on the “Today” show that he has “no problem” selling A. I.-generated books if they are labeled. His remarks were widely condemned on social media by readers and writers, who said he was opening the door to selling slop at a major bookstore chain.

Daunt later clarified his remarks in a statement he shared with The New York Times, noting that Barnes & Noble takes “active measures to exclude all A. I.-generated books from our online catalog and never knowingly order any for stocking in our stores.”

He added that while “the store will sell A. I.-generated books if there is clear demand, we think it very unlikely that there will be customer demand for A. I.-generated books.”

There are at least some A. I. novels for sale on Barnes & Noble’s website, including “Fighting Love’s Flame,” a steamy romance about an Alaskan smokejumper and a documentary filmmaker who falls for him, and “Tumbleweeds & Tequila,” about a woman who is stranded in the desert and rescued by a hot ex-Navy Seal. Both books were published by Future Fiction Press, a new publishing company that produces novels using A. I. The books’ overviews on the Barnes & Noble website disclose that they were “produced using author‑directed A. I. tools.”

Other booksellers are drawing a harder line against A. I. generated works.

“Are you going to allow scammers to rip off your customers? The answer has to be no,” said Andy Hunter, the founder of Bookshop, an online book-selling platform that bills itself as an independent business alternative to Amazon.

Hunter said Bookshop asks Ingram and Draft2Digital, companies that distribute books to the site, to filter out A. I.-generated works. But he worries there is no reliable way to fully block them. With more than 800,000 self-published books available for purchase on the site, it’s inevitable that some slip through the cracks.

Other online retailers say they have been flooded with A. I. slop and are struggling to stay ahead of the torrent.

“We’re on the receiving end of an avalanche, an avalanche that is only going to get bigger,” said Michael Tamblyn, the chief executive of Rakuten Kobo, an e-reader producer and e-book retailer.

Klaus Kremmerz

Charlotte Coppin for The New York Times

Ahmed Gaber for The New York Times

Last year, Kobo’s self-publishing platform rejected 45 percent of the books submitted. Of those, 85 percent were not accepted because Kobo determined them to be A. I.-generated.

“You can say, This probably isn’t a publisher, this is three LLMs in a trench coat,” Tamblyn said.

Other times, it’s a harder call. Kobo is now evaluating whether A. I. detection software, along with human review, can assess titles. But it’s becoming more difficult to catch scammers, who are using chatbots that produce more sophisticated prose, and can also use A. I. agents to create multiple accounts on publishing platforms.

Kris Austin, the co-founder and chief executive of Draft2Digital, which distributes independently published books to retailers, libraries and subscription services, said that the company saw an explosion of high volume uploads and low quality books over the last 18 months — a surge partly driven by A. I. He worries about how that will affect self-published authors, many of whom are struggling to find an audience in a flooded marketplace.

“This rise of low-quality slop, it’s threatening what the indie community has built,” he said.

Alexandra Alter is a features writer for the Styles section of The Times.

Ukraine’s Strike on an Iranian Ship Could Bring Two Wars Closer

The New York Times July 28, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

The attack in the Caspian Sea was an unusually direct encounter between two countries that have been on opposite sides for years.

By Constant Méheut and Qasim Nauman

Constant Méheut reported from Kyiv, Ukraine.

A Ukrainian strike last weekend on an Iranian cargo ship in the Caspian Sea has underscored the links between the wars that the two countries are fighting, raising tensions between them as well as the risk of more direct confrontation.

Ukraine said the ship was carrying military equipment between Iran and Russia. Iranian officials said it was a commercial vessel, and it accused Ukraine of killing a sailor in the attack.

Iranian officials threatened retaliation in a series of statements and comments to the news media. Ukraine’s foreign minister, Andrii Sybiha, snapped back, telling Iran it had “no standing to pretend to be a victim” given its military support for Russia in its war with Ukraine.

Here’s a look at how Iran and Ukraine became adversaries through two separate wars — and why their indirect conflict now risks becoming a direct one.

Iran and Russia have had a close military relationship for decades. The most visible recent example of this is the long-range attack drones that Tehran has supplied to Moscow.

Russia launched swarms of the drones across Ukraine within months of its 2022 invasion, to deadly effect. Russia later began manufacturing its own versions of the Iranian drones.

The United States has accused Iran of supplying Russia with short-range ballistic missiles as well. And Ukraine said Iran had sent trainers to help the Russian military use drone systems, a claim that Iran denied.

The widespread use of drones, particularly the relatively cheap types provided by Iran, transformed the war in Ukraine and, more broadly, changed how military planners assess the needs of modern armies. It also forced Ukraine to develop counter-drone technologies that analysts say now rival conventional air defense systems.

Four years after Russian unleashed those Iranian drones against Ukraine, Kyiv has now brought its hard-earned expertise in countering them to the Middle East.

After the United States and Israel began their war with Iran in late February, the Iranian military launched waves of drones at U. S. military targets in Gulf countries. Ukraine saw that as an opening to showcase and export its low-cost anti-drone systems.

President Volodymyr Zelensky of Ukraine said in March that more than 200 Ukrainian military experts had been sent to the Middle East to help defend allies against Iranian drones. “We do not want this terror of the Iranian regime against its neighbors to succeed,” he said during a speech in Britain’s Parliament.

Ukraine has also sealed defense deals with Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates focused on countering Iranian missile and drone threats.

Ukraine has increasingly portrayed its war with Russia and the war in the Middle East as intertwined, saying Iran and Russia were aiding each other in their respective conflicts.

On Saturday, Mr. Zelensky said Ukraine’s intelligence services had gathered evidence that Russia was providing Iran with satellite surveillance of Gulf states and U. S. military bases in the region, helping Tehran plan and carry out attacks. He said Ukraine would share the intelligence with its Western allies.

On the same day, Ukraine struck the Iranian ship in the Caspian Sea, accusing it of transporting military cargo between Iran and Russia, without specifying in which direction — the clearest suggestion yet that Kyiv’s long-running proxy conflict with Tehran could evolve into a more direct confrontation.

Mr. Zelensky may also use the attack to try to persuade President Trump that Ukraine and the United States share the same enemy and to advocate for closer military ties. The Ukrainian leader met with Mr. Trump on Tuesday afternoon and said the two leaders discussed securing more air defense capabilities for Kyiv.

In a post on X, Abbas Araghchi, the Iranian foreign minister, tied the attack on the ship directly to the Middle East conflict, calling the strike “a blatant U. N. Charter violation” and claiming it had been “done at Israel’s behest to drag Europe into its war.”

Mr. Araghchi added that he had spoken with both the European Union’s top diplomat and Russia’s foreign minister to make clear that the attack “CANNOT GO UNANSWERED.”

The first signs of a diplomatic off-ramp appeared Tuesday night, as Mr. Araghchi and Mr. Sybiha spoke by phone, with both calling for de-escalation. “Our position remains unchanged: Europe and the Middle East deserve stability, security, and peace,” Mr. Sybiha said in a social media post.

Leily Nikounazar and Shirin Hakim contributed reporting.

Constant Méheut is a Times correspondent covering the war in Ukraine.

Qasim Nauman is a Times editor in Seoul, covering breaking news from around the world.

A Six-Pack of Beer Might Close a Constitutional Loophole

The New York Times July 28, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By James J. Sample

Mr. Sample is a professor at Hofstra University’s law school.

Ken Jouppi has wanted to fly since boyhood. He fixed up Boeing B-52s as an Air Force mechanic, earned his pilot’s license in the late 1960s and moved to Alaska, where he made his living flying a one-man air taxi, KenAir, over some of the emptiest country in America.

In 2012, Mr. Jouppi agreed to fly a woman up north, to Beaver, a village of fewer than a hundred people, to visit her husband. He loaded her luggage and groceries into his plane. But before they could take off, troopers searched the compartment and found a six-pack of beer, clearly visible. Alcohol is banned in Beaver, so they charged Mr. Jouppi, his company and the passenger with importing alcohol into a dry village.

Mr. Jouppi claims he didn’t see the beer, but a jury convicted him of a misdemeanor anyway, and the judge gave him three days in jail and a $1,500 fine — the minimum sentence. But because Alaska law says that bootleggers have to forfeit any airplane used to smuggle alcohol, the prosecutors then tried to seize his plane, a 1969 Cessna, worth about $95,000.

Mr. Jouppi has been fighting to keep the plane ever since. Last week, the Supreme Court agreed to take up his case to answer an important and neglected question: When is a fine so excessive that it becomes unconstitutional?

The Eighth Amendment forbids “excessive fines.” The Supreme Court has defined that term exactly once, in 1998. A fine is unconstitutional when it is “grossly disproportional to the gravity of a defendant’s offense,” the court held in United States v. Bajakajian. In 2019, the court confirmed that the Eighth Amendment restricts not just the federal government from imposing excessive fines, but also states, cities and counties. That is nearly the whole of the doctrine, and the lower courts have split over what “the gravity of a defendant’s offense” means. The justices now can create the yardstick every court must use before calling a punishment excessive.

Ask what Mr. Jouppi did, and the confiscation of the plane looks wildly out of scale. Ask how serious alcohol smuggling is in the abstract, and he loses before the facts are heard. Alaska’s struggle with rural alcohol abuse is real and grievous. Mr. Jouppi was a professional pilot who, a trooper testified, would “have to be blind not to know” what he was loading. Weighing the harms alcohol visits on rural villages — crime, alcoholism, fetal alcohol spectrum disorders, death — the court concluded that “the illegal importation of even a six-pack of beer causes grave societal harm.”

Mr. Jouppi has a legitimate defense. He was a first-time offender, convicted of a misdemeanor over a customer’s beer and given the lightest sentence the law allows. To take a $95,000 airplane on those facts is the very picture of a punishment that does not fit the crime.

The Supreme Court has spent three decades reining in excessive punishments, just not under the Eighth Amendment. The court’s decisions have come under the 14th Amendment’s due process clause, in cases about punitive damages, and the beneficiaries have overwhelmingly been corporations. In one case, the court threw out a multimillion-dollar award against BMW, which had sold a repainted car as new, by evaluating the conduct’s reprehensibility, comparable penalties and the ratio between punishment and harm. Another ruling for State Farm suggested that punitive awards more than nine or 10 times a victim’s actual losses will rarely survive. And a decision in favor of the cigarette company Philip Morris added a rule that reads as if written for Mr. Jouppi: A state may not punish a defendant for harm to people who are not before the court.

Unfortunately for Mr. Jouppi, those rulings do not apply directly to his Eighth Amendment claim. But their insight should. Corporations — BMW, State Farm and Philip Morris — got individualized review and protection from being charged with society’s wider wounds. An 82-year-old pilot, invoking the one clause the Constitution devotes to excessive economic punishment, had the harms of statewide alcoholism laid at his feet.

Since those punitive-damages rulings are civil and Mr. Jouppi’s forfeiture is criminal, they travel on different constitutional tracks. Even so, the gap is hard to unsee, and there is nothing partisan in naming it. The justices most alarmed by aggressive fines and forfeitures span the court’s ideological spectrum, from Justices Neil Gorsuch and Clarence Thomas to Justice Sonia Sotomayor. Their concern is practical: When governments lean on fines and forfeitures for revenue, the burden falls hardest on those least able to fight back.

The justices need not minimize Alaska’s grave concerns about alcohol to hold that this forfeiture went too far. They need only say that fines must reflect the seriousness of a defendant’s actual offense, not the broadest social problem the legislature was trying to address.

The case comes down to a single question: Who decides how grave an offense is — Alaska’s legislature writing a law intended for the worst imaginable alcohol smuggler, or a judge looking at the man in the actual case?

However the justices answer in the coming term, they will tell us whether the Eighth Amendment means as much for a pilot in Alaska as due process has come to mean for BMW.

James J. Sample is a law professor at Hofstra University and the author of the Substack Who Decides Who Decides?

Trump Loved Graham, Not So Much His Beloved Senate

The New York Times July 28, 2026

Lindsey Graham (1955-2026)

Advertisement

Supported by

News Analysis

The South Carolinian relished serving as a “bridge” between the institution he revered and the president, but now that bridge is gone.

By Carl Hulse

Reporting from the Capitol

President Trump may have loved Lindsey Graham, but he loathes the Senate, an institution that Mr. Graham revered for the way it empowered individuals like himself in a way that is currently bedeviling the president and his hard-right allies.

The president’s second-term power grab has gotten scant pushback from Republicans on Capitol Hill, but what little there has been has emanated mainly from the Senate.

Senator John Thune, Republican of South Dakota and the majority leader, has so far refused to acquiesce to presidential demands to gut the filibuster and pass a voting restrictions bill. A handful of other Senate Republicans have bucked the president on policy and nominees, drawing Mr. Trump’s social media wrath and the attendant electoral consequences.

One of Mr. Graham’s multiple self-appointed roles was to interpret the Senate for Mr. Trump — and vice versa. The senator relished his role as an intermediary to the institution that has often angered the president, who has never understood or appreciated its complex ways or why it won’t simply bend to his will as the Republican-led House does.

“It’s overused, but I guess you could call him a Trump whisperer or translator or interlocutor,” Senator John Cornyn, Republican of Texas, said of his South Carolina colleague, whose absence remains acutely felt in the Senate. “We are going to miss him, because the relationship between the president and the Senate is not great anyway, and Lindsey was sort of a bridge that no longer exists.”

The loss of Mr. Graham comes at a particularly fraught time as Mr. Trump has escalated his criticism of the Senate and Mr. Thune. The president is demanding that Mr. Thune keep the chamber in session over the August recess to push ahead with a stalled voter bill and adopt a Republican-only budget framework with funding for the war with Iran and other administration priorities.

Senators, however, are exceedingly reluctant to give up their monthlong recess, particularly in an election year, when there is little to no chance of a legislative breakthrough.

“It’s just a fact, and the facts don’t change,” Mr. Thune told reporters on Monday about the lack of votes for Mr. Trump’s priorities. “Now, if he can change the facts and start moving some of those senators who are noes into yeses, then we’d have a different conversation. But it’s just — that’s just the reality.”

With tensions rising between the Senate and the White House, the White House press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, warned last week that the president’s patience is “running out” on Mr. Thune.

Yet Mr. Trump on Monday downplayed any differences between the two, saying that Mr. Thune has “got to get his job done.”

“It’s fine,” Mr. Trump continued. “I have a good relationship with John Thune. He’s got to get his job done.”

Asked if he had ever considered trying to oust Mr. Thune as majority leader, the president said that “I haven’t even thought of it.”

One reason the president might have said he hadn’t thought of it is that Mr. Thune retains very broad support among Senate Republicans, who show no signs at all of wanting to make a change in their leadership to appease Mr. Trump.

Even some G. O. P. senators unhappy with the legislative agenda Mr. Thune is pursuing remain solidly behind him. All of them see Mr. Thune as a buffer between them and a tempestuous president. Calling for Mr. Thune’s ouster and failing to achieve it would leave the president in a significantly weakened position as far as the Senate is concerned.

After Mr. Graham’s death, the president briefly tried to jump-start his restrictive elections overhaul, which would impose new voting registration and identification requirements, by noting the senator’s support for it and saying its enactment would be a tribute to Mr. Graham. But that effort went nowhere.

His colleagues were fully aware that Mr. Graham had not been particularly outspoken on the voting issue and had instead put his legislative heart and soul into a package of sanctions on Russia. It was that legislation, not the SAVE America Act, that he would have seen as a fitting memorial, and senators were expected later on Tuesday to take their first step toward passing it.

Mr. Graham’s willingness to break with Mr. Trump’s America First tendencies and the increasing isolationist bent of the Republican Party to stand resolute in support of Ukraine won him the admiration and affection of Democrats, despite deep differences on the conduct of the war in Iran.

“Lindsey Graham is the type of senator who is most known for their focus on the role of America in the world,” said Senator Tim Kaine, Democrat of Virginia. “The number of senators who’ve really kind of made it their business to really talk about the role of America in the world, as opposed to domestic policy, has really shrunk.”

Mr. Trump and Mr. Graham didn’t always have a strong relationship. Mr. Graham briefly sought the Republican presidential nomination himself in 2015 and harshly criticized Mr. Trump and his presidential ambitions before they mended fences.

In a phone interview with Fox News on Tuesday morning, the president noted that “we started off a little bit on the rough side” but added that Mr. Graham “really became like a member of the family.”

Mr. Graham, for his part, saw the relationship as partially strategic, wanting to keep a direct line to the president to make his case on issues where he saw Mr. Trump drifting in what the senator considered the wrong direction. He was not afraid to be blunt, and saw the golf course as a convenient venue for candid discussions with Mr. Trump.

“He had a unique relationship with the president, which allowed him to say things to the president that I don’t think a lot of senators would be comfortable saying because he won’t like to hear them,” Mr. Cornyn said, noting that Mr. Trump typically showed little tolerance for the slow-moving Senate. “He’s a businessman and he doesn’t have any patience for process. But that’s what the Senate is all about, is process in order to ultimately get a result.”

Who — if anyone — can now take on the role of Mr. Trump’s Senate confidant remains to be seen, though several Republicans, including Senator John Barrasso of Wyoming, the No. 2 G. O. P. leader, talk frequently with him and carry some influence.

But Mr. Graham’s death has left a void in the Senate’s tense relationship with a mercurial president that will not be easy to fill.

Carl Hulse is the chief Washington correspondent for The Times, primarily writing about Congress and national political races and issues. He has nearly four decades of experience reporting in the nation’s capital.

F. D. A. Official Says Food Supply Is Safe as Cyclosporiasis Cases Climb

The New York Times July 28, 2026

Cyclospora Cases

Advertisement

Supported by

The acting deputy commissioner for food said the agency was taking action even though finding the root cause of the outbreaks is difficult.

By Julie Creswell

Reporting from New Orleans

Even as the number of cyclospora cases in the United States hit record levels, top health regulators insisted that consumers could still trust what they were eating.

“The U. S. food supply is safe,” Donald Prater, the acting deputy commissioner for food at the U. S. Food and Drug Administration, told attendees Monday at the annual meeting of the International Association for Food Protection.

“However, there’s a couple of challenges,” he said, referring to the cyclosporiasis outbreaks that have sickened more than 11,000 people across the country. “It will take a little time. But we do believe we’re taking action and we’re protecting public health.”

It has been a rough summer when it comes to food-borne illnesses.

Nearly 100 people have been reported ill with salmonella, leading to the recall last week of 19 million eggs linked to part of the outbreak. An E. coli infection was traced to some organic blueberries. And earlier in the summer, a listeria outbreak led to the recall of various soft cheeses.

Still, the outbreaks of cyclosporiasis sweeping the country are top of mind for the hundreds of food-safety experts gathered for their annual conference in New Orleans.

“One of the things I’m personally concerned about, we’re starting to have more and more of these outbreaks here in the United States,” German Rios, the senior director of food safety and quality at the produce manufacturer Fresh Express, said during a panel discussion. “I am concerned that we may not have really hit the peak of the outbreaks.”

Across many conference panels and in hallways between meetings, some participants expressed concern that the root causes of the ongoing multiple cyclosporiasis outbreaks may never be known. And without understanding how certain produce or other foods became contaminated in the first place, some said they feared there might not be an end to what some had deemed cyclospora season for consumers.

One pocket of the cyclosporiasis outbreak that has sickened 1,947 people and hospitalized 98 has been linked to iceberg lettuce grown in Mexico and served at some Taco Bell locations. That led Taylor Farms, the country’s largest produce supplier, to voluntarily recall lettuce shipped to 27 states.

The F. D. A. identified a new outbreak that has sickened at least 72 people, according to an update posted to the agency’s website last week. At the same time, health officials in North Carolina are trying to track down an outbreak that they do not believe is related to the iceberg lettuce served at Taco Bell, but that has resulted in more than 300 cases of cyclosporiasis in the state. They are eyeing parsley, cilantro and lettuce as potential culprits there.

Even though regulators have identified iceberg lettuce from Mexico as the source for one of the outbreaks and that lettuce has been recalled, the number of cases of cyclosporiasis and of unrelated outbreaks keeps climbing, Mr. Prater of the F. D. A. said.

“Once we’ve identified the contaminated product, we will, of course, work to initiate and effectuate recalls, removing the contaminated product on the market, alert consumers and conduct root-cause investigations,” he said. “We’re right in the middle of all of that.”

But if identifying the food that is the source of a cyclosporiasis outbreak is difficult, pinpointing where and how the contamination occurred is even more challenging, many scientists in attendance said. Cyclospora is a parasite that spreads through human feces, and it’s rare for investigators to locate a precise source of contamination.

Produce — whether cilantro, berries or leafy greens — is imported nearly every day from other countries.

When two separate cyclosporiasis outbreaks in 2018 and 2020 were traced back to its leafy in greens, Fresh Express took a hard look at what was happening in some fields in Mexico where some of its produce was grown. The company found that farm owners and workers needed increased education around how cyclosporiasis was spread, Mr. Rios of Fresh Express said.

“We needed to focus and emphasize training and help the employees, help the individuals, understand why it is important and what is cyclospora and how does it occur,” he said.

The company hired additional people to ensure bathrooms in the fields were being regularly used and cleaned. Employees were told to throw out gloves more frequently. Hand washing stations that featured spigots that needed to be turned by hand were reworked so that employees could turn faucets on using just their forearms.

But Fresh Express has also examined where the water that it uses to irrigate crops in the United States comes from. In the Salinas Valley in California, Mr. Rios said, there is what he called purple-valve water, which is recycled or reclaimed wastewater that has been treated and used for irrigation.

“In our case,” he said, “we try to stay away from purple-valve irrigation water.”

Julie Creswell is a business reporter covering the food industry for The Times, writing about all aspects of food, including farming, food inflation, supply-chain disruptions and climate change.

On sites like X and TikTok, the conversation about Taylor Farms is dominated by conjecture about the produce firm’s donation to a Trump-linked PAC.

Credit... Michelle V. Agins/The New York Times

Supported by

By Tiffany Hsu

The public discussion around the cyclospora outbreak, the largest in U. S. history, initially focused on food safety: How could the parasite be killed? What foods were affected?

Then, suddenly, social media chatter lurched into conjecture about politics.

Much of the online discussion turned — in the span of a single day — to whether the Trump administration was meddling in the investigation that linked the outbreak to the food producer Taylor Farms, which donated $1 million in March to a super PAC for President Trump and has a history of supporting the Republican Party.

And days after the government first linked Taylor Farms to the illnesses, the politicized narrative continued to make up a significant portion of the talk of the outbreak. More than 62 percent of the online conversation about Taylor Farms over the past week referred to the claims, according to research from PeakMetrics, an analytics company.

The administration firmly denied any connection. The Department of Health and Human Services said on X that “nothing influences our decisions except science and the safety of the American people.” But the government’s conflicting announcements have helped fuel the speculation.

Narratives, particularly sensational ones, often take root online and spread quickly. The cyclospora situation, however, has been especially fertile ground: a public health emergency playing out in a country with waning faith in the public health apparatus, involving close ties between an implicated produce company and a president long accused of self-dealing.

To disinformation experts, the speed with which speculation about political machinations overtook fact-finding conversations demonstrated how fully primed the online ecosystem has become to accept rumor and falsehoods.

“There is massive distrust right now in these institutions, and now you’re layering on top of that the conspiracy theories that emerge so incredibly quickly on social media,” said Timothy Caulfield, a professor studying health misinformation at the University of Alberta.

Health officials across multiple states have recorded more than 11,000 confirmed or suspected cyclospora infections this summer, but the true scale of the outbreak is difficult to discern. The parasite, transmitted through tainted food and water, causes symptoms that can take days or weeks to emerge, making its origins difficult to trace.

Federal health officials publicly linked Taylor Farms to the outbreak on July 16. Two days later, the Food and Drug Administration said a test of shredded iceberg lettuce that had been processed by Taylor Farms de Mexico found cyclospora. A day after that, however, the agency said that the finding was actually a false positive. Taylor Farms, which had issued a voluntary recall of lettuce from 27 states, said that the F. D. A. had apologized. The agency said it hadn’t, at least not officially, and added that there was still strong evidence tying the producer to the outbreak.

As the public back-and-forth unfolded, social media users also discovered the $1 million donation from Taylor Farms’ corporate parent to MAGA Inc., one of the main super PACs supporting the president. The company recently hired Mr. Trump’s former deputy director of White House personnel.

Taylor Farms executives met with officials from the White House and the F. D. A. the same day the company was first linked to the outbreak. There, they sought to distance the company from it.

Taylor Farms’ links to conservatives led people online to claim, without evidence, that the Trump administration had a hand in the F. D. A.’s walking back its test result — purportedly as a quid pro quo for the company’s financial backing. Some of the posts were viewed hundreds of thousands of times. (PeakMetrics said in a blog post that a third of the initial references to the politicized rumors seemed to originate from bot accounts.)

Kush Desai, a spokesman for the White House, said in an email that “any notion that the White House or Trump administration would ever compromise on the health and safety of the American people is absolutely false.”

Taylor Farms did not directly address the online rumors but said in a statement that it would “continue to be transparent as more information becomes available” and that as of July 19, no tested samples of its produce had been confirmed positive for cyclospora.

Scientists have said that false positives are common when testing for the pathogen, a difficult process that they said had likely been undermined by cuts to federal surveillance programs as well as funding limitations and staffing shortages at state and local public health departments.

Tiffany Hsu reports on the information ecosystem, including foreign influence, political speech and disinformation

Why Iran Is in No Rush to Return to Talks With United States

The New York Times July 28, 2026

War in the Middle East

Advertisement

Supported by

Amid a reprieve in the fighting, Iran’s leaders are betting that they can endure more pain than President Trump can, and they have leverage over the Strait of Hormuz, analysts say.

By Yeganeh Torbati

Yeganeh Torbati has reported for years on Iranian politics and society.

Iran’s skies have been free of the sound of explosions and airstrikes for the past several days, after a bout of renewed fighting with the United States. But Iranian officials say they have not agreed to a cease-fire and are in no hurry to hold direct talks with American negotiators.

Instead, Iranian officials insist that they are in a position of strength, military leaders boast of battlefield successes, and diplomats dismiss U. S. claims that they are eager to return to negotiations.

The rhetoric coming from Iran indicates that its leaders are comfortable with the state of limbo with the United States — something between peace and full-fledged war — believing that they can handle renewed conflict and that they have leverage over President Trump. The priority for Iran seems to be gaining recognition of its control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz waterway, a concession that the United States has been unwilling to make.

Despite the bluster, the uncertainty is a challenge for Iran, analysts say. Fighting could break out again at any time, a final settlement appears distant and Iran’s economy is almost certain to deteriorate further because of instability, wartime destruction and a U. S. naval blockade.

Ramazan Sharif, a former spokesman for Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps, the ideological military force that has solidified its control over Iran during the war, said on Sunday that Iran’s “enemy” had “faced strategic defeat at every step,” Iranian state media reported.

Iranian diplomats have reacted with more restraint to the pause in the fighting over the past few days, after two weeks of trading attacks. But there is little hint that they are in a mood for compromise.

“At present, what exists cannot be described as a cease-fire,” the Iranian foreign ministry spokesman, Esmail Baghaei, said at a news conference on Monday.

Mr. Trump said on Monday that Iran had asked for a pause to meet for talks, and that the two sides were engaged in discussions.

“We’re talking right now,” he told reporters aboard Air Force One, adding that there was “a good chance” a new round of diplomacy with Iran could yield a breakthrough. Last week he said at the White House, “they want to meet desperately to try and end it.”

Mr. Baghaei denied that there were any negotiations with the United States currently.

Iran faces stark internal divisions over the diplomatic contacts, with hard-liners opposed to resuming negotiations and denouncing the elected government, which has engaged in talks in pursuit of a cease-fire.

Iran’s negotiations, Mr. Baghaei said, were with Oman, over management of the Strait of Hormuz, the critical waterway for oil and gas shipments that Iran effectively shut down after being attacked by the United States and Israel in late February.

“They believe that time is on their side, that they can absorb pain and pressure more successfully than Donald Trump can, and that ultimately he will agree to a deal that fits their demands without any concessions from their side,” said Gregory Brew, a senior analyst on Iran at the Eurasia Group, a political risk advisory firm.

The recent resumption of fighting caused oil prices to surge, raising prices at the gas pump for American consumers. Oil prices had fallen sharply, after the United States and Iran paused their attacks.

Mr. Trump faces a painful dilemma in deciding his next step on Iran.

The New York Times reported on Saturday that private U. S. deliberations over the war have focused on the Pentagon’s shrinking stockpiles of air defense munitions, making a return to war high risk. That is just one of several concerns for U. S. officials, along with the danger of a widening war, the effect on Gulf allies and global energy supplies.

It is difficult to know the state of Iran’s missile supplies, said Farzin Nadimi, a senior fellow with the Washington Institute and an expert on Iranian military affairs. Iran is believed to have produced between 700 and 1,000 solid-propellant ballistic missiles between the brief war with Israel in June 2025 and the outbreak of the current war, he said. Its output of liquid-fuel and cruise missiles is less quantifiable, he added.

Open-source information on Iran’s missile production can be fragmentary, Mr. Nadimi said. That opacity means that less is known about how Iran would fare in a return to full-blown war.

Still, Iran does not “want to return to a full-scale war that involves both the U. S. and Israel, and also one with open-ended prospects,” he said. Iranian officials have hinted in recent interviews that they agreed to the cease-fire partly because missile stocks were running low or were not fully accessible, he added.

Iran is at risk of overreaching, Mr. Brew said. For Mr. Trump, escalating the war could be more appealing than accepting a deal that gives Iran control over the strait, he added, and other countries are unlikely to accept tolls on ships. There is scope for both sides to de-escalate if Iran can accept a compromise arrangement for the future of the waterway.

Yeganeh Torbati is the Iran correspondent for The Times.

What to Know About the Kumamoto Earthquake in Japan

The New York Times July 28, 2026

Earthquake in Japan

Advertisement

Supported by

At least one person who was found in a collapsed house was killed, and about 50 others were injured on Tuesday in the southwestern prefecture of Kumamoto.

By Johnny Diaz

A powerful 6.8 magnitude earthquake struck southwestern Japan on Tuesday afternoon, damaging buildings and homes, igniting fires and injuring dozens, prompting a search for people who may have been trapped in rubble.

Here’s what to know.

The earthquake hit around 4:30 p. m. local time in Kumamoto Prefecture on Kyushu island, the southernmost of Japan’s main islands.

The earthquake’s intensity led to buildings collapsing in the region. Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi of Japan said people were trapped inside some structures. Fires also erupted in Kumamoto City, the regional capital, which has a population of more than 700,000.

The epicenter of the quake was near Uto, a smaller coastal city around 30 miles south of Kumamoto City, according to the U. S. Geological Survey

The U. S. agency had earlier reported a magnitude measurement of 7.1 for the earthquake before it adjusted the figure to 6.8.

View the location of the quake’s epicenter and shake area.

The second floor of a shopping mall in southern Kumamoto City collapsed, injuring two people. Crews were working to rescue people who may have been trapped inside. Video footage posted on social media showed debris scattered inside and outside the mall.

Aerial footage showed a flipped train carriage on tracks in the city and widespread damage to buildings and bridges. Other images recorded by the public broadcaster NHK also captured elevated sections of the Kyushu Expressway that had split into two pieces, as other footage showed a wall that had partly collapsed at Kumamoto Castle, a landmark in the city’s center.

The prime minister said the authorities were still assessing the severity of the damage to buildings and bridges.

At least one person died in a hospital after being found in a collapsed house in Kumamoto, according to the police.

At least 50 people were being treated for injuries at a hospital in Hikawa, a town to the south of Kumamoto City, according to NHK.

The last major quake in Japan in 2024, centered on the Noto peninsula farther north, killed hundreds of people, with more succumbing to disaster-linked causes afterward, according to NHK.

In April 2016, the Kumamoto region also experienced days of deadly seismic events that killed at least nine and injured hundreds, according to the U. S. Geological Survey.

The Sendai Nuclear Power Plant appeared to be secure and had no reports of abnormalities, Minoru Kihara, a top Japanese cabinet official, said during a news briefing.

The power plant, which has two reactors and supplies electricity to the Kyushu region, is in Kagoshima, south of Kumamoto.

Johnny Diaz is a reporter for The Times covering breaking news from Miami.
